An American astronaut on board the ISS recently snapped a spectacular "fireball" streaking across the nighttime sky over West Africa. The striking "light show" shows a Russian rocket being vaporized as it reenters the upper atmosphere.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What's in the photos? Space debris from a Russian rocket burning up upon reentry

Who took the photos? NASA astronaut Chris Williams

Earlier this year, an astronaut on board the International Space Station (ISS) snapped some striking photos, and an eerily beautiful video, of a "fireball" streaking over Earth as chunks of space debris burned up in the nighttime sky.

NASA's Chris Williams, who lived and worked on the ISS between November 2025 and July 2026, captured the eye-catching images from the station's cupola — a large, roughly dome-shaped series of windows that constantly points down at our planet — and later shared them on the social media platform X.

"Just as we were passing over West Africa, I saw a bright object directly below us, streaking through the upper atmosphere," Williams wrote in the post. "I saw its tail grow and then split apart into a shower of smaller pieces," he added. "It was quite a light show!"

Williams initially peered down at Earth to catch a glimpse of the Russian cargo spacecraft Progress 95, which successfully delivered essential supplies and additional equipment to the ISS later the same day. Instead, he saw what he believed was "some piece of orbital debris or a satellite breaking up as it entered the atmosphere."

Live Science's sister site Space.com later revealed that Williams had actually witnessed the burning remains of the Russian Soyuz rocket that had carried Progress 95 into space, after it lifted off from a recently repaired launchpad at the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.

The Soyuz rocket launched the cargo spacecraft Progress 95, which later docked with the ISS. (This photo shows the Progress 46 mission docking with the station in 2011.)

Shortly after deploying the resupply shuttle into low Earth orbit, the rocket's fairings and booster fell back toward our planet as expected, breaking apart into smaller pieces that were superheated and later vaporized by intense friction as they hit the upper atmosphere, according to Space.com. A very similar fireball was seen above Australia in August 2023, when another Soyuz rocket reentered the atmosphere.

Russia's prior resupply mission, Progress 94, also made headlines earlier this year when one of its antennae failed to deploy after separation from its Soyuz rocket, forcing cosmonauts (Russian astronauts) to use a remote control "backup system" to dock the spacecraft to the ISS.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Historically, the only fireballs visible in Earth's skies have been those caused by meteors, which can similarly break apart in flames. We were recently reminded of this when fireballs were spotted above the U.S. this spring, including one space rock that exploded with a massive sonic boom over Ohio and another that crashed through the roof of a house in Houston. (A NASA statement said the fireball Williams witnessed also may have been caused by meteor activity but was more likely to be the Soyuz rocket.)

However, fireballs from human-made objects are becoming more common. The number of spacecraft orbiting Earth has skyrocketed (pun intended) in recent decades, and "what goes up must come down."

Williams' photographs show how the remains of the Soyuz rocket exploded in a bright flash before stretching out into a train of flaming debris.

Most spacecraft and large pieces of space junk burn up around 50 miles (80 kilometers) above Earth's surface — just below the imaginary boundary with space, known as the Kármán line. While this may lead to visually stunning spectacles like the one Williams captured, scientists are starting to realize that these fireballs may be having a bigger impact on the upper atmosphere than they previously expected.

In recent years, researchers have detected a sharp increase in atmospheric metal pollution from vaporized spacecraft. And while they are still trying to figure out what effect this may have, some scientists have proposed that it could affect the ozone layer or potentially alter Earth's magnetic field.

Additionally, as the number of falling spacecraft rises, the chances that debris may fall to Earth's surface — after failing to properly burn up upon reentry — also increase. This came to the fore in March 2024, when the remains of a 3-ton battery pack that was discarded from the ISS crashed into a family home in Florida.

This 2011 astronaut photo captured one of NASA's iconic space shuttles passing between Earth and the International Space Station for the very last time.

During the Sept. 11 attacks, NASA astronaut Frank Culbertson — the only American not on Earth at the time — snapped a "sobering" shot of smoke pouring across New York City as the second tower fell.

A 2016 satellite photo shows Hurricane Madeline and Hurricane Lester heading straight toward Hawaii. When viewed from above, the twin cyclones and the surrounding clouds look eerily like a giant smiley face.

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. His recent work on the solar maximum won "best space submission" at the 2024 Aerospace Media Awards and was shortlisted in the "top scoop" category at the NCTJ Awards for Excellence in 2023. He also writes Live Science's weekly Earth from space series.

#6493. Sausage Stuffing Recipe

This sausage stuffing has everything you want on your Thanksgiving plate: crisp, craggy edges, a plush, savory center, and plenty of browned sausage throughout. Torn pieces of country-style bread soak up the broth and eggs without falling apart, turning golden and crunchy on top while staying tender underneath.

Breakfast sausage does much of the heavy lifting. Once browned, its drippings join plenty of butter to cook the onions, celery, and garlic. Fresh sage, parsley, and thyme bring balance, while optional fennel seeds add a little extra aromatic punch.

Uncooked pork breakfast sausage is the first choice. Typically seasoned with sage and black pepper, it brings familiar Thanksgiving flavors and plenty of richness. For some heat, choose spicy breakfast sausage. If you can't find the packaged kind or want to avoid pork, try making your own with our breakfast sausage recipe, using ground dark-meat turkey in place of pork.

This stuffing relies on the fat from breakfast sausage for its flavor. Want a vegetarian version? Our Simple-Is-Best Stuffing is a long-standing reader favorite and was the inspiration for this version; use that recipe with vegetable broth for a meat-free stuffing.

What’s the best bread for sausage stuffing?

Look for a sturdy country-style white loaf or sourdough with a relatively thin crust. Avoid soft sandwich bread, which can turn mushy, and very crusty artisan loaves, which won’t absorb the broth as readily. Even if your bread is a day or two old, don’t skip drying it in the oven—that’s what helps the stuffing hold its shape.

Can I make sausage stuffing ahead of time?

You can dry the bread a day ahead and store it loosely covered at room temperature. For more ways to get ahead of Thanksgiving, including cooking, refrigerating, and reheating stuffing, see our make-ahead stuffing guide.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Grease a 13x9" baking dish with unsalted butter. Arrange one 1–1¼-lb. loaf country-style white bread, torn into 1" pieces, in a single layer on a large rimmed baking sheet and bake until dried out and golden around the edges, 30–40 minutes. Let cool.

Meanwhile, melt 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high heat. Cook 1 lb. breakfast sausage, casings removed if needed, stirring and breaking into small pieces, until well browned and cooked through, 8–10 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer sausage to a small plate, leaving fat behind.

Reduce dial to medium heat and add remaining 8 Tbsp. unsalted butter to fat in pot; heat until melted. Cook 2 medium onions, finely chopped, 6 celery stalks, finely chopped, 8 garlic cloves, coarsely chopped, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. fennel seeds (if using), stirring occasionally, until onions are softened and golden around the edges, 12–15 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 2 cups low-sodium chicken broth or vegetable broth along with sausage, ½ cup (packed) coarsely chopped parsley, 2 Tbsp. finely chopped sage, 2 Tbsp. finely chopped thyme, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Whisk 3 large eggs and remaining 1 cup low-sodium chicken broth or vegetable broth in a small bowl to combine, then stir into pot (don’t worry, eggs won’t scramble). Add bread to pot and toss gently to combine. Let sit, tossing occasionally, until liquid is almost completely absorbed, about 10 minutes.

Transfer stuffing to prepared dish (don’t pack or press down) and cover loosely with foil. Place dish on a clean large rimmed baking sheet and bake until stuffing is hot throughout (an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 160°), 35–45 minutes. Increase oven temperature to 400° and remove foil (no need to remove stuffing from oven while heat increases). Continue to bake until stuffing is light golden brown on top, 25–30 minutes longer.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 1 day ahead; store loosely covered at room temperature. Stuffing can be assembled 1 day ahead; cover and chill. Bring to room temperature before baking.

Editor’s note: This sausage stuffing recipe was first printed in our November 2023 issue; it has been updated for style. Head this way for more of our favorite Thanksgiving side dishes →

#6492. Keeping the Diwali Flame Burning in New York City

The akhand diya, the continuously burning flame, has one purpose: to stay lit. It is a small but enduring presence, tended to around the clock, its care passed from one person to the next so that the light never goes out. I’ve often thought about how much of life is like this, how we are constantly passing the torch from one version of ourselves to another.

As a teenager, I remember feeling that I had crossed an invisible threshold into womanhood. I was becoming someone different from the girl I had been, carrying parts of her with me but beginning to understand the world through a new lens. Now, years later, I find myself at another such transition: I am becoming a different version of a woman, one I am still getting to know.

In many ways, this transition is happening outside of me. Thirteen years ago, I moved away from my family in Mumbai and the home where Diwali had always been celebrated. For all those years, the rituals continued, even as I participated in them from thousands of miles away, mostly over video calls. Back in Mumbai, Diwali meant a house full of family and friends, kitchens bustling with cooking and frying, and the warm glow of diyas illuminating the mandir. I was no longer physically there, but I remained part of it. This year, for the first time, I hosted my parents for Diwali in the home I’ve built for myself in New York City.

It felt cataclysmic, or at least I was making it feel that way in my head. As I welcomed a different version of myself, I was also taking on a new role within my family. I was no longer simply the daughter returning to their house for Diwali; I was the one opening my home, preparing the food, tending to the rituals, and making space for the people who first taught me what this celebration means. There is perhaps no greater joy than watching the people I love receive and experience care. And yet, this was a responsibility I had chosen to take on, and one that felt particularly daunting as the eldest daughter. I wanted to get it right.

For me, that care has always found its way to the table. Food is how my family celebrates, how we mark occasions, and, perhaps most importantly, how we look after one another. So naturally, much of my energy went into planning the meal. Despite my best efforts, my dad promptly assigned himself the task of making the goat kari—apparently, even after 13 years away, some things hadn’t changed. We headed to our local butcher in Brooklyn to buy fresh goat meat, and almost immediately, his attention turned to the spice tolerance of my guests.

“How much spice can your friends tolerate?” he kept asking me. “Should I keep it at a level six? But our level six might be their level ten. What do I do?” he lamented. “Relax, they’ll be able to handle it! Just make it our level five,” I told him.

I gave in and handed over part of the kitchen to my mother, too. She took charge of the paneer, cooking generous chunks in a luscious onion-tomato gravy and making the chapatis. Selfishly, I didn’t mind relinquishing that responsibility: This would be my one chance for the year to eat chapatis fresh off the tava, puffed up and piping hot, and made by my mother.

As the days drew closer, I found myself loosening my grip on the plans I’d made. My parents had their own ideas about what needed to be cooked, and while I was initially resistant to them taking over (any immigrant will tell you how hard it is to get our parents to just relax!), I was learning that hosting didn’t necessarily mean doing everything myself. It also meant making room for everyone to contribute and allowing new rituals to form.

The evening began with freshly fried moong vadas. My mother, of course, insisted on frying them for everyone, right before serving. Made from soaked and ground mung lentils, these little fritters are crisp and golden on the outside, with a soft, almost creamy interior. They have a naturally earthy, nutty flavor from the lentils, sharpened with green chiles, ginger, and spices.

Moong vadas are best eaten immediately, still hot out of the oil, with a tangy green chutney. The scene reminded me of Diwalis back in Mumbai, when the vadas rarely even made it to the serving platter: Everyone would gather around the kitchen, waiting for the next batch to come out of the kadai, reaching for them before they had a chance to cool. I saw the same thing happening in my kitchen in New York.

In the meantime, my friends Leanne and Christina took charge of the tamarind margaritas, my ode to the soft, sweet-tart tamarind candies I grew up savoring as a kid. The tangy cocktails were a welcome counterpoint to the savory fritters, the perfect way to wake up our taste buds (and made exercising some restraint with those moong vadas before dinner particularly difficult). My brother helped set the table and move furniture around, just as we used to do for our parents back in Mumbai. There was something deeply comforting about watching us fall into these old rhythms.

The table eventually came together with a mix of dishes that felt both familiar and celebratory. There was chana masala from my cookbook, East to East, alongside my dad’s goat kari, slow-cooked with spices until the meat was tender. My mother’s saucy tomato-onion paneer was accompanied by a pile of chapatis that disappeared almost as quickly as they came off the stove. We served everything family-style, laying out the dishes on kansa thalis, traditional Indian plates made from bronze or bell metal, an alloy of copper and tin. They reminded me of the way my grandparents served meals, and I wanted to bring a little of that into our Diwali celebration.

At the center of the spread was a vegetable pulao, fragrant basmati rice cooked with carrots, cabbage, cauliflower, and whole spices. Alongside it, I placed bowls of pickled onions and mango achaar, whose sharp, tangy bite cuts through the richness of the karis. There was also cucumber raita, cool and creamy, offering a welcome respite from the heat of the spices. These accompaniments might seem like small additions, but they are essential to the balance of an Indian meal. Every bite can be a little different, depending on what you bring together on your plate.

For dessert, I made homemade gulab jamun, my brother’s favorite. The soft dumplings are made from milk solids and fried until golden, then soaked in a warm saffron-and-cardamom-scented sugar syrup.

As I sat cuddled among both my families, I realized that while it wasn’t the perfectly orchestrated dinner I’d imagined when I first started planning, it was something better. The family I was born into celebrating Diwali alongside the family I’d chosen and built in New York, all gathered around the same table and enjoying every minute of it. Perhaps keeping the flame alive was never about re-creating the past exactly as it was but about allowing it to illuminate whatever comes next.

#6491. Cranberry Pie

What People Are Saying:“I made 3 desserts this Thanksgiving and this was an absolute hit!! Everyone at the table raved about it including my super picky 7 year old who had herself seconds. Definitely a winner and will be making again.” - PurplePuzzle

Preheat your oven to 350° and grease a 9-inch pie plate with butter.

For the crust, grab a large bowl and mix together the Biscoff crumbs, melted butter, and a pinch of salt. Gently press this mixture into the bottom and up the sides of your greased pie plate.

Bake the crust until it turns golden and feels firm to the touch. Once done, set it aside on a wire rack to cool.

In a small bowl, mix the gelatin with some cold water and let it sit so it can bloom.

Next, for the filling, grab a medium saucepan, toss in the cranberries, brown sugar, orange juice, and zest, and bring it to a simmer over medium heat. Stir occasionally while the cranberries burst and the liquid has thickened slightly, which should take about 7 minutes.

Pour in the coconut milk, ginger, heavy cream, almond extract, and a little salt. Stir everything together and heat until it’s nice and steamy, but not quite simmering. Remove from the heat and stir in the bloomed gelatin until fully dissolved.

Now, blend the cranberry mixture until it’s super smooth—use whatever blender or food processor you have handy. Strain it into a bowl, toss out any solids, and let the mixture cool down to room temperature. Pour the cranberry filling into your crust and refrigerate until set, which should take at least 6 hours.

Serve with homemade whipped cream and enjoy!

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

This pie will keep for up to a week in the fridge and frozen for up to 5 months. Simply thaw it out in the fridge the next day and serve.

#6490. Mexican Seafood and Natural Wines Are in the Spotlight at This New NYC Restaurant

A stacked tuna tostada, puckering shrimp aguachile, and more seafood dishes stun at El Camarón Peludo

Known for their roasted and slow-cooked meats at Taqueria Ramirez, Tania Apolinar and Giovanni Cervantes partnered with chef Carlos Barrera to open a new seafood-focused wine bar this year. Here’s what a full day of prep looks like at El Camarón Peludo in the West Village.

First, fresh shrimp from Sinaloa, Mexico; Ecuador; and more locales are de-shelled and de-veined for three central shrimp dishes. Then, Cervantes starts the fresh salsa for the day, taste testing and comparing each batch to the salsa from last week to make sure the flavor is consistent. A bright red salsa is mixed with mayo to create the sauce on the camarones zarandeados, a shrimp version of a fish dish from the Pacific coast of Mexico that is usually grilled in a flat wire grill basket.

Upstairs, Apolinar prepares the wine bar for opening, laying out chilled seafood on ice in the window and wine bottles that will be placed in chilled buckets for service. She recommends sitting at the long, winding bar to watch the bartenders and chefs work.

Back in the kitchen, Barrera starts breaking down Spanish tuna for a creative tuna tostada layered with spicy mayo, fish eggs, habanero-lime oil, avocado, and crispy leeks. Then it’s taco prep, including the pescadilla (a deep-fried fish taco) and a shrimp taco with queso fresco, refried beans, and slices of roasted poblano peppers. Cervantes and Barrera prep the raw bar area, making salsa verde and salsa negro. The green salsa is made with parsley while the black salsa is layered with habaneros, piquin chile, and squid ink.

Cervantes explains that his original idea to pair the innovative seafood plates with bubbly wine turned into a natural wine bar, with El Camarón Peludo sourcing bottles from all over the world.

Watch the team at the Mexican seafood wine bar prepare tostadas, tacos, and flavor-packed aguachile in the newest episode of Now Open.

NASA's Swift Observatory is about to make a fiery reentry through Earth's atmosphere after a private mission to save it failed. Most of the spacecraft will burn up in orbit.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Editor's note: As of 11:15 a.m. EST on Wednesday (Nov. 4), NASA and the Aerospace Corporation both predict that the Swift observatory could have reentered Earth's atmosphere by now. However, no new details on reentry have been provided. Stay tuned for more updates about where and when the telescope will fall.NASA's decades-old Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is rapidly falling out of orbit and could tumble back to Earth any moment now, the space agency says.

According to NASA's latest estimates, shared Monday (Nov. 2), the roughly 3,200-pound (1,450 kilograms) spacecraft was likely to reenter Earth's atmosphere around 3:30 a.m. EST Wednesday (Nov. 4), with an uncertainty of plus or minus 11 hours — meaning the defunct observatory could have plunged down as early as Tuesday evening, and as late as Wednesday afternoon.

An independent analysis from the private nonprofit Aerospace Corporation, which tracks thousands of objects in orbit, similarly estimates that the telescope should have reentered the atmosphere at 6:56 a.m. EST Wednesday, give or take three hours. Both estimates suggest the Swift spacecraft could have already met its demise as of Wednesday morning, though no official confirmation has been shared.

As with all spacecraft reentries, the risk to humans is minimal. Most of the Swift telescope is expected to burn up in the atmosphere, according to NASA. Any surviving fragments will likely fall somewhere between 20.6 degrees south latitude and 20.6 degrees north latitude — a range that includes parts of Mexico, the Caribbean, Central and South America, the Arabian Peninsula, India, Africa and Oceania, but also a lot of ocean.

NASA predicts that the chances of Swift debris falling over a populated area are approximately 1 in 2,100. For comparison, the odds of a person being struck by lightning in their lifetime are 1 in 15,300, according to the National Weather Service.

NASA will continue to update their predictions as the reentry window draws closer.

Swift has detected thousands of deep-space explosions, including sudden flares from neutron stars (illustrated here).

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is a multiwavelength optical, ultraviolet and X-ray telescope that launched in November 2004 on a mission to study the most powerful explosions in space. Initially designed for a two-year primary mission, the telescope ultimately spent more than 10 times that duration hunting for supernovas, gamma-ray bursts and black-hole-induced eruptions around the universe.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Swift has been rapidly losing altitude for more than a year, after rampant solar activity increased the drag on the aging spacecraft. This past August, a costly mission to boost Swift's orbit with a private spacecraft failed shortly after launch, hammering the final nail in Swift's coffin.

Engineers on the Swift team officially shut down the observatory's science operations on Oct. 20, after the spacecraft fell too low in orbit to continue taking steady observations of the sky.

As Swift goes out with a fiery bang, it leaves behind a trove of scientific data, including contributions to more than 7,000 scientific papers so far, according to NASA. This number will only increase as Swift's final observations are processed.

He holds a bachelor's degree in creative writing from the University of Arizona, with minors in journalism and media arts. His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.

#6488. A Chef’s Guide to Eating and Drinking in Santo Domingo

On a Friday night in July, Nidia Evangelista walked with her arms crossed over the Puente Flotante toward East Santo Domingo. Six lanes of traffic jockeyed inches from her left shoulder, while the black waters of the Río Ozama coursed below. “Oh my God, Oli, what are we doing?” she said. “Nobody does this.” Evangelista is the communications manager for Santo Domingo’s most intriguing restaurant, Casarré. Her boss, Swiss Dominican chef Olivier Bur, was leading Evangelista, photographer Clay Williams, and me beyond the fortified walls of the Zona Colonial, where few travel on foot.

On the other side, we turned a corner and found hundreds gathered around a dance floor in the undercroft of a bigger bridge. Live bachata drowned out the traffic overhead. Bur procured a big bottle of Presidente and plastic cups from a vendor, poured, and raised a “Salud!”

Bur normally walks (or bikes) everywhere. Moving slowly, he’s learned the textures of the city. Still, for the next six days, he took Williams and me to his most beloved restaurants by car. We visited a string of chimi stands where hawkers compete for clientele through the night; a chicharrón spot where couples dance shoeless on the cool tile floor; and a cafeteria where boys shuffle stewed eggplant, beets, and goat to bus drivers en route. Places like these are the “infrastructure for life,” Bur said. “Thirty years ago, there was nothing else.”

Over the last couple of decades, however, another dining scene has sprouted. Dominican chefs have returned from kitchens in Mexico, Japan, or Switzerland to explore the forgotten and sometimes shunned ingredients of their (or their parents’) homes. They served us conch, cassava, breadfruit, and djon-djon mushrooms in sashimis, foams, tostones, and surprising dessert creams. The dishes were fresh and exciting, but local and global traditions have always mingled—as such, the cuisine is not “New Dominican,” it’s simply “Dominican,” fully expressed.

Calle Andrés Julio Aybar 13+1 829 545 7503

The Piantini neighborhood was once verdant and sleepy, according to Bur. Now it’s a bustling business district. Most of the remaining vegetation decorates the façades of restaurants, like Ajualä’s. Brushed palm thatch and a bushy barba de Fidel (Fidel’s beard) tree greet you at the tall aged-steel door.

Venezuelan chef Saverio Stassi is a leader among the culinary new guard. His treatment of local ingredients is virtuosic. He confits guinea hen in cocoa butter and tops breadfruit tostones with local yellowfin and Cambita avocado; and over two days, his team bathes the succulent goat from the northwest—where they famously graze on wild oregano, self-infusing their meat—in Seville orange juice before roasting it in a barbacoa pit.

Calle Max Henríquez Ureña 14+1 809 547 3592

Chef Erik Malmsten has cooked at his parents’ cabaret in Gothenburg, Sweden, at Aquavit in New York, and at Bocuse d’Or competitions around the world. But to take his career to the next level, he returned to his mother’s homeland to open a Nordic-Japanese restaurant.

“You’ll see, it’s really good,” Bur told us. The meal starts with “lobster chicharrón,” with a reduced crustacean bisque, fried into airy orange sheets of bubbly crackling and served with tōgarashi Kewpie. Then, a parade of sashimi, like king fish, served with brown butter soy emulsion, ikura, and lemon zest. It ends with Dominican chocolates, molded, painted, and plated to look like koi fish on a synchronized swim.

If, like me, you come from a pizza region, you might not be inclined to use one of your Santo Domingo meal slots on a pie. But I urge you: Make time for Casa Gazcue. Spanish Dominican chef Francis Pena’s 48-hour-fermented crust comes blistered and sometimes covered in honeyed sesame seeds. Iterations are variously laden with spicy Dominican oxtail, chimi sandwich sauce, pistachio, and jamón ibérico, but you don’t have to choose: For groups, he serves a rosca (a round with an open middle) of six sections arranged like floral pizza petals.

In 1954, the Bonarelli family opened the legendary Italian restaurant Vesuvio. For decades, it was the place—the only place—to go out for a formal sit-down meal around here. Vesuvio closed over 20 years ago, but the founder’s grandson, Giancarlo Bonarelli, now runs Bottega Fratelli in a sleek modern building in Naco (Piantini’s equally upscale neighbor).

You’ll notice a great variety of beet dishes in the Dominican Republic. Farmers harvest them year-round in the cool, pine-forested Costanza Valley. Try them here, roasted and served with blue cheese, chèvre, candied nuts, and honey. Also try a carpaccio of king mackerel, caught off the eastern coast, or any of the risottos, an emblem of the family’s enduring Italian culinary influence.

Hideyoshi Tateyama’s parents opened Samurai in 1990. The restaurant joined Vesuvio, along with one or two others in that era’s small restaurant scene. It still stands out today among the many dozens.

Be sure to order the guatapaná con coco. A tried-and-true combo of shrimp and coconut imbued with native guatapaná leaf, tobiko, sesame seed, and scallion—it’s been on the menu for two decades. Also, don’t miss the chance to sample a sashimi of the meter-long “calamar diamante” from the Samaná region. It’s simply brightened with lemon zest. Meals are capped with a green tea amaro. Once a month, Tateyama personally runs a chef’s-choice omakase service.

On the day we visited Villar Hermanos, lines formed around the block for each of two buffets. Women balanced towers of takeout containers tightly wrapped in plastic. It was the World Cup Final, and people were rushing to get some of the city’s best comfort food to their coffee tables. “This is the place to come for all the Dominican classics,” Bur told us.

We found a large table under the sprawling canopy of a banyan tree and ordered mofongo. It was moist, punctuated with crisp chicharrón crackling. The sancocho, the classic Domincan stew thick with potato and yuca starch, assumed extra body when alternating spoonfuls of broth and rice. While I didn’t have my coveted mangú and tres golpes (salami, queso frito, and eggs), I would trade my house and car to live next door and eat breakfast there every morning under the filtered sun.

Avenida San Vicente de Paúl, Santo Domingo Este 11504+1 809 244 8906

On Avenida San Vicente de Paúl in East Santo Domingo, scooters zip down the busy street all through the night, many popping over a curb into the Plaza Del Chimi. The “plaza” is a stretch of  10 to 15 “chimi” sandwich stalls outfitted with griddles and prep stations heaped with roasted pork shoulders. Dealers quickly slice the meat, lay it on the griddle, flip it onto a squishy pan de agua roll, and top it with cabbage, tomato, and tangy pink sauce before sliding it into your mitts. The stalls are open till 6 a.m. When they run out of beer, a man runs bottles from a cooler at his house and serves them in paper bags.

Avenida Independencia KM 8+1 809 532 2580

Across from a shopping mall on Avenida Indepencia, about a dozen cars cram into five parking spaces for the lunch or late-night staple pica pollo. Behind a crowded serving station, a woman slides eight pounds of chicken into a hotel pan, and the picking begins. Six sets of tongs compete for room, like bird beaks, snapping the chicken into styrofoam containers before barely holding them shut with strained rubber bands. Another eight pounds comes out less than two minutes later.

Pica pollo is one of the lasting influences of Chinese immigrants in Santo Domingo. Usually cooks marinate it in bitter orange, garlic, and oregano before coating it in flour and spice (in this case we detected Chinese five-spice) and deep-frying it to golden brown.

At Parque Mirador Sur, teens and whole families perch along concrete walls and hilltops eating fried yuca and succulent mojo-dipped chicharrón with long toothpicks. It comes from the crowded, steel-barred serving window across the street: Chicharrones Light de la Cayetano.

Among all the chicharrón we ate in the city (there was a lot), theirs stood out. There’s a small covered seating area where you can order beer to share. Bachata plays loud over a hanging speaker. Women take turns kicking off their heels to do the four-step shimmy with their jevos (boyfriends).

The Colmado, Bur says, “is essential to Dominican life. Everything happens there.” For 70 years, Colmado La Venganza has anchored a prominent corner in the Don Bosco neighborhood. It’s hosted thousands of late-night domino games and sports viewing parties. We were there during the World Cup.

At the entrance, a man with a crisp-edged haircut, big sunglasses, and a pressed floral shirt parked his shoe on a milk crate while a boy polished it with a rag. Inside, groups spanning all ages gathered at high-tops and around the bar. Folks shared triple-stacked ham, pickle, and cheese sandwiches, pressed, cubed, and spiked with toothpicks: the “sándwich especial.” Leaving the bar, chef Raniel Cruz (part of our party) texted his mom in Montreal. She responded: “Wait, you’re at Venganza? I used to drink there.”

One couldn’t understand the Dominican Republic’s vast culinary splendor in a lifetime, but if you had just one night to try, you’d want to dine at Casarré. Every Tuesday, the team takes excursions. We accompanied them to meet the countryside cooks, who wrap guáyiga root masa in leaves from the almond trees on Najayo beach and bake it in coal-covered pots. We visited a produce market, where vendors passed fruit samples, like little red “frutas milagrosas” that, when chewed beforehand, make bitter limes taste like sweet limeade.

At night, in a candlelit, contemplative room in the Zona Colonial, Bur and his team showcase their findings in a series of sublime, thoughtful dishes. On our visit, they presented djon-djon mushrooms from the Haitian borderlands in a sweet, guáyiga-thickened foam and in the broth of a citrusy okra and fish soup. Chef Isabella Sánchez explained: “The broth is murky, like the current state of the Río Ozama. It represents the negative aspects of our water—contamination and conflict—and the beautiful: the fish, the beaches, and our grandmother’s tea.”

Smoke from an open Uruguayan-style parrilla floats in the soft light over two stories. Our waiter said, “We want this to feel like a Sunday asado.” Indeed, the smoke, the char, and the Malbec are there. This asado, though, also has Negronis smoked tableside and poured from a glass goose. As we awaited a perfect aged rib eye, we enjoyed paper-thin beef carpaccio with foie, and a paella-esque rice with soft leeks, cilantro, and pork trotters.

Recommendations on where to dine, shop, and stay, wherever you’re headed next.

Oliver Bur, the pioneering chef behind Casarré, offers an inside look at the Dominican capital’s restaurant scene.

On a Friday night in July, Nidia Evangelista walked with her arms crossed over the Puente Flotante toward East Santo Domingo. Six lanes of traffic jockeyed inches from her left shoulder, while the black waters of the Río Ozama coursed below. “Oh my God, Oli, what are we doing?” she said. “Nobody does this.” Evangelista is the communications manager for Santo Domingo’s most intriguing restaurant, Casarré. Her boss, Swiss Dominican chef Olivier Bur, was leading Evangelista, photographer Clay Williams, and me beyond the fortified walls of the Zona Colonial, where few travel on foot.

On the other side, we turned a corner and found hundreds gathered around a dance floor in the undercroft of a bigger bridge. Live bachata drowned out the traffic overhead. Bur procured a big bottle of Presidente and plastic cups from a vendor, poured, and raised a “Salud!”

Bur normally walks (or bikes) everywhere. Moving slowly, he’s learned the textures of the city. Still, for the next six days, he took Williams and me to his most beloved restaurants by car. We visited a string of chimi stands where hawkers compete for clientele through the night; a chicharrón spot where couples dance shoeless on the cool tile floor; and a cafeteria where boys shuffle stewed eggplant, beets, and goat to bus drivers en route. Places like these are the “infrastructure for life,” Bur said. “Thirty years ago, there was nothing else.”

Over the last couple of decades, however, another dining scene has sprouted. Dominican chefs have returned from kitchens in Mexico, Japan, or Switzerland to explore the forgotten and sometimes shunned ingredients of their (or their parents’) homes. They served us conch, cassava, breadfruit, and djon-djon mushrooms in sashimis, foams, tostones, and surprising dessert creams. The dishes were fresh and exciting, but local and global traditions have always mingled—as such, the cuisine is not “New Dominican,” it’s simply “Dominican,” fully expressed.

#6486. The 50 Best Restaurants 2026: The Full List of Winners

Congratulations to Asador Etxebarri in Spain, named the World’s Best Restaurant of 2026

Tonight, the 50 Best Restaurants 2026 were announced at a ceremony in Lima, Peru, with Basque Country restaurant Asador Etxebarri crowned the new top slot on the list. Bangkok tasting counter Gaggan was ranked No. 2, Copenhagen’s immersive, 50-course experience Alchemist was No. 3, Mexico City’s Quintonil No. 4, and Hong Kong’s Wing No. 5, shuffling most of the top rankings from last year. New York City’s Atomix was the only U.S. restaurant to make the 50 Best Restaurants.

Of the specialty awards, Singapore’s Lesley Liu received the Best Sommelier Award (sponsored by Vik), Ghana Food Movement was given the Champions of Change (sponsored by illycaffe), Yiaga in Melbourne was named the One to Watch, Doris Lam received the 50 Best Restaurants Scholarship Award, Jessica Rosval of Al Gatto Verde was named Best Female Chef (sponsored by Lexus), Thailand-based Dej Kewkacha was Best Pastry Chef (sponsored by Sosa), Atomix’s Junghyun Park was given the Estrella Damm Chefs’ Choice Award, and Ferran Adrià was given the SevenRooms Icon Award.

Just as a review, U.K.-based media company William Reed launched the 50 Best Restaurants lists in the early 2000s, publishing the first World’s 50 Best Restaurants list in Restaurant magazine in 2002. The 50 Best gained greater fame in the 2010s, with the top spot going to the likes of Noma (Copenhagen, Norway), El Celler de Can Roca (Girona, Spain), and Osteria Francescana (Modena, Italy). The organization made the wise decision in 2019 to move each year’s winner to a separate “Best of the Best” list — a sort of hall of fame for takers of the top spot — giving new restaurants the opportunity to take the crown. Since then, Geranium in Copenhagen (2022), Disfrutar in Spain (2024), Central (2023), and Maido (2025) in Lima have earned the No. 1 ranking. Noma qualified as a winner again in 2021 because it had “closed and reopened.”

The 50 has also expanded its reach with multiple regional lists, such as the Latin America’s 50 Best, Middle East and North Africa’s 50 Best, Asia’s 50 Best, the 50 Best Bars (which also has its own regional lists), 50 Best Hotels, and even 50 Best Wineries. The entire brand has reached a level of global reputation and fungibility that rivals something like the Michelin Guide ( which has itself ventured into hotels and wineries). But the 50 Best Restaurants is the granddaddy of all listicles, and the one that draws the most attention and criticism regarding its methodology and alleged pay to play. One vocal critic, chef Ana Roš of Hiša Franko in Slovenia, announced earlier this year that she would not attend the ceremony, a move commenters like Top Chef judge Tom Colicchio lauded.

The polling is conducted anonymously among more than 1,100 voters, a mix of industry professionals, food writers, and “well-traveled gourmets,” with at least 25 percent turning over annually. Each voter nominates 10 restaurants in order of preference, up to six in their home region and at least four outside it. The rankings are just a pure tabulation of those votes.

The organization has made efforts to clarify its voting and ranking policies, stating that any restaurant can qualify and that what constitutes “best” depends on each voter. The 50 has also expanded its awards to consider diversity and inclusion, recognizing female chefs (which itself has raised eyebrows), sustainability, sommeliers, pastry chefs, hospitality, and Champions of Change, an award that “celebrates and recognizes unsung heroes” who are “driving positive change in their communities.”

Last week, the “back half” of the list, also known as 51-100, was announced, with the only U.S. restaurant, SingleThread (Healdsburg, California), ranked at No. 93. On the 2025 50 Best Restaurant list, New York’s Atomix was the only U.S. restaurant to make the top 50, ranked at 12. Perhaps in order to remedy the dearth of U.S. and Canadian restaurants on the World’s list, the 50 (the organization previously known as 50 Best), commenced North America’s 50 Best Restaurants in the fall of 2025. Atomix topped that list, followed by Mon Lapin (Montreal), Restaurant Pearl Morissette (Lincoln, Ontario), and other U.S.- and Canada-based restaurants.

A recent rat study hinted that cosmic radiation could pose health risks for future Mars explorers. Live Science asks its readers whether they'd take the journey anyway.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A crewed mission to Mars could be one of humanity's greatest achievements, but getting there may come with serious health risks. Beyond the challenges of surviving in space for months at a time, astronauts would face prolonged exposure to cosmic radiation ‪—‬ high-energy particles in space that can penetrate the human body and potentially damage vital organs.

A new study suggested that cosmic radiation could pose a particular threat to heart health. Researchers found evidence that rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what human astronauts might encounter during a mission to Mars and back developed more scar tissue around the small vessels in their hearts compared with rats that weren't exposed to space radiation.

Although the findings haven't been confirmed in humans yet, they add to the growing concerns about the long-term health effects of sending astronauts on long-duration space missions.

NASA and other space agencies are working on ways to eventually send humans to Mars and beyond. Given these latest findings, would you travel to Mars? Vote in the poll below, and let us know your thoughts in the comments.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry is the Content Manager at Live Science. Formerly, she was the Content Manager at Space.com and before that the Science Communicator at JILA, a physics research institute. Kenna is also a book author, with her upcoming book 'Octopus X' scheduled for release in spring of 2027. Her beats include physics, health, environmental science, technology, AI, animal intelligence, corvids, and cephalopods.

#6484. Interstellar Visitor 3I/ATLAS Shows Water Ice Behaves the Same Across Alien Star Systems

Targets of opportunity sometimes happen in astronomy, and we got a major one when the third interstellar object, 3I/ATLAS, was discovered in July 2025. And it just so happens that in the intervening years between the last known interstellar visitor (2I/Borisov in 2019), we got a major upgrade in our observational capabilities with the launch of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). A new paper from a team of researchers led by Dr. Silvia Protopapa of NASAâs Goddard Space Flight Center and the Southwest Research Institute, and published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, details JWSTâs findings on the water ice content of this most recent visitor from beyond our solar system.

Typically, water ice is pretty easy to spot for astronomers. In infrared, which is JWSTâs specialty, it absorbs light very clearly at 1.5, 2.0, and 3.0 microns in wavelength. Weâve known that for years, and have seen evidence of it in regular comets based strictly on our solar system, such as Hartley 2.

But when JWST looked at 3I/ATLAS, it clearly showed the 3.0 micron absorption line, but the 1.5 and 2.0 ones were surprisingly weak or absent. It also featured a blue near-infrared continuum slope across 1.15â2.50 microns that wasnât typical of the other comets zooming around our solar system. These discrepancies led some observers to question whether 3I/ATLAS actually contained any water ice at all, but the new paper with higher resolution observations quickly put paid to that idea.

Fraser talks about the orbital mechanics of 3I/ATLAS

To prove that it does, indeed, contain water ice, the research team modeled how light scatters through âmixedâ particles that contain both water and dust. This lined up much more closely with the observed spectral lines of 3I/ATLAS, proving that, instead of pure water ice with a clear pattern, the ice is locked up into microscopic grains that blend water and dark rocky minerals, such as pyroxene and carbon.

Light can only travel so far through these aggregates before hitting some dust, causing a shortened optical pathway. That, in turn, mutes the absorption features at the 1.5 and 2.0 micron level, while the longer 3.0 micron wavelength is still able to pass straight through. The tiny grains also scatter shorter wavelengths more effectively, which explains the general blue hue that JWST saw.

In fact, JWST observed this interstellar visitor at three different times during its journey through our solar system, starting when it was about 3.31 astronomical units (AU) out from perihelion all the way through when it was about 5.65 AU past perihelion. And the differences in 3I/ATLASâs spectra were noticeable at each stage. After perihelion, the grains of ice and dust appeared to include a second population of larger, micron-sized, ice-rich aggregates.

Fraser talks about what would happen if we could catch an interstellar object.

Also, after perihelion the researchers noticed a new optical effect known as a Fresnel reflection near 3.1 microns, which indicated that there was also âcrystallineâ water ice in 3I/ATLAS. This differs from the normal, disorganized type of ice normally seen, as its water molecules arrange themselves in neat crystalline lattices rather than in a jumble. According to the paper, these layers were only visible after perihelion either because the Sun itself warmed the surface layers causing them to reconfigure into a crystal, or the solar energy caused the outer dust to blast away, revealing cleaner underlying crystalline structures that were previously hidden.

But perhaps the most interesting part of the paper was the parallels it was able to draw with our own solar system. The infrared patterns of 3I/ATLAS match certain types of Trans-Neptunian Objects (TNOs) in our own solar system. These balls of ice and rock are the planetary leftovers that float out beyond Neptune in the Kuiper belt, and JWST has already spent plenty of time staring at them. Previously, researchers had seen the same 3.0 micron absorption pattern without the 1.5 and 2.0 micron features, but had thought those patterns might be attributable to complex hydrocarbons or organics. Turns out it might just have been dusty ice all along, at least according to the new paper.

Itâs unclear whether there will ever be another opportunity like this in JWSTâs operational lifetime. But thereâs still plenty left to understand about our most recent interstellar visitor. As more and more scientists continue to analyze the data that was collected during 3I/ATLASâs sojourn through our system, thereâs undoubtedly more to be discovered about our latest interstellar visitor, and especially how it can explain more about our own solar system.

SwRI - SwRI-led study uses Webb to compare interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS with icy bodies in our solar system

S. Protopapa - JWST Reveals Refractory-rich Water Ice in Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS: Evidence for a Continuum of Grain Properties across Protoplanetary Disks

UT - 3I/ATLAS Has An Extreme Taste For Heavy Water

UT - 3I/ATLAS Is Very Actively Releasing Water

#6482. All the 2026 National Eater Award Winners, Mapped

The best restaurants, bakeries, chefs, dishes, and bars across the country

The 2026 Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, now in their 17th year, capture the breadth of dining in the U.S., celebrating the best new restaurants across the country. This year’s awards recognize not only restaurants, but also the best in bakeries, pioneering chefs, and standout dishes, as well as the Best New Bars as designated by Eater’s sister publication, Punch. Each winner is a testament to the idea that dining out is still worth the effort and cost it can command — as long as you know where to look.

Eater is partnering with select Eater Award winners to offer special dining perks now through January 31, 2027. To access these exclusive perks, create an Eater account or download and create an account on the Eater app for iOS. (Terms apply)

The best restaurants, bakeries, chefs, dishes, and bars across the country

The 2026 Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, now in their 17th year, capture the breadth of dining in the U.S., celebrating the best new restaurants across the country. This year’s awards recognize not only restaurants, but also the best in bakeries, pioneering chefs, and standout dishes, as well as the Best New Bars as designated by Eater’s sister publication, Punch. Each winner is a testament to the idea that dining out is still worth the effort and cost it can command — as long as you know where to look.

Eater is partnering with select Eater Award winners to offer special dining perks now through January 31, 2027. To access these exclusive perks, create an Eater account or download and create an account on the Eater app for iOS. (Terms apply)

One of Eater’s 2026 Best New Bakeries, the Pastry Project, offers training to people facing barriers to employment in Pioneer Square. Head to the walk-up window for innovative items that rotate weekly — feather-light peanut butter and raspberry jelly cake, elephant ear-esque cardamom croissants, and apple pie cream puffs topped with cider meringue, to name a few. Show up Thursday through Saturday morning, but be prepared for a line. In the summer, the spot doubles as a soft-serve ice cream stand.

Occupying the former SE Division home of a different well-known Northern Thai-influenced restaurant, OK Chicken & Khao Soi was perhaps Portland’s biggest opening of the year. Akkapong “Earl” Ninsom (Yaowarat, Langbaan, and PaaDee, to name a few) and Eric Nelson (Expatriate, Eem, Phuket Cafe) — two of Portland’s most well-respected culinary talents — bring to life Chiang Mai-style dining in a space that feels simultaneously intimate and energetic, in the spirit of a really good dinner party. Named a 2026 Best New Restaurant in the U.S. winner, this spot puts emphasis on its namesake dishes, but don’t ignore the other items on the menu. Slushies and shakes cut the heat of Thai chiles, and richly seasoned and marinated dishes like gai yang chicken legs or sai ouia herbal sausages sing alongside bright basil, crisp cucumbers, and savory side sauces. Reservations are accepted.

Cassis, an Eater 2026 Best New Restaurant, is big in every sense. The nearly 200-seat dining room of the Milwaukee restaurant is an immaculately designed jewel box of gleaming tile, cozy banquettes, and antique mirrors, and even on a Wednesday night, it’s packed and roaring, with a towering, glowing bar at the center of the action. The latest project from Kyle and Meghan Knall, the couple behind nearby acclaimed bistro Birch, channels the conviviality and polish of an old-world French brasserie while remaining distinctly Midwestern in spirit. It’s an all-day restaurant with both heart and panache. — Hilary Pollack

Tucked behind Lonesome Rose, a casual Tex-Mex restaurant in Chicago, a short stairway leads to an unassuming door. There’s no sign, but there is a logo — a snake entwined around a bottle — and the faint sounds of a salsa soundtrack playing Puerto Rican music. This is how you know you’re at Culebra, one of Punch’s 2026 Best New Bars. With cocktails that tap Malta India (a nonalcoholic malt beverage), tamarind, and culantro, this bar is an homage to Puerto Rican flavors and the Latinx influences of the surrounding neighborhood, Logan Square. Owner Diego Garcia-Gonzalez was born and raised there, and worked his way up through Chicago’s bar industry, beginning in 2013 at age 15, then began visiting Puerto Rico in 2024 to do guest bartending shifts. Behind the bar, you’ll spy a menu of $12 daily Daiquiris, made with a different rum blend each day. Take Friday’s offering: It features Uruapan Charanda, Chairman’s 1931 and Cachaça Amburana, brought perfectly into balance for a richly layered drink. — Amy Cavanaugh

Perk: Eater members receive a free order of tostones with the purchase of any two Cocteles Originales through January 31, 2027. (21+ | Terms apply)

Pandemic Instagram sensation-turned-Emily Hotel pop-up Bad Butter, a 2026 Eater Best New Bakery, opened in Bucktown in May. The bakery, founded by Daniel Koester, has attracted substantial (we’re talkin’ 60-plus-minute) lines since its debut — seemingly a feature, not an anomaly of Chicago bakeries lately — so plan to get there early before all the lavish croissants, Danishes, and breads disappear. And they do sell out. Don’t miss the savory monkey bread, which in recent months has appeared variously laced with harissa and salsa macha.

When Creepies opened in mid-2025, the chatter about this Eater 2026 Best New Restaurant centered on its name. Now, those in the know focus on the food that balances French culinary know-how with a Midwestern sensibility to create a restaurant that’s charming in so many ways. Equal parts bistro and chic diner, Creepies is the brainchild of David and Anna Posey — the husband-and-wife chefs behind next-door Elske, stellar in its own right — and chef Tayler Ploshehanski. Start with warm Brie gougères as you linger over the wine list full of intriguing offerings, before moving on to heartier dishes like steamed mussels with fennel, roasted chicken in a liver and wine sauce, and Parisian gnocchi. Save room for one of Anna’s desserts, including a rotating soft-serve sundae.

After three years as Noah Sandoval’s chef de cuisine at two-Michelin-starred Oriole, Larry Feldmeier partnered with the James Beard Award-winner to open All Well in April. Located inside the former La Sardine space, the West Loop restaurant’s menu features a modern American five-course tasting menu ($145) and a la carte bar fare with Japanese and French inflections. Plates like candied beets with sake lees, sea buckthorn, and endive, and sablefish with savoy cabbage, amazake, and genmai, and sweet and briny Hokkaido scallops with celtuce, Virginia ham XO sauce, and coriander, are matched by cocktails like the dirty daiquiri — a martini-adjacent riff featuring white rum, green olive, lime, and Calvados brandy. The puffed grain toast on the tasting menu at All Well is an Eater 2026 Dish of the Year.

This Hingetown newcomer from James Beard-recognized chef Vinnie Cimino, also behind Cleveland critical darling Cordelina, is devoted to ancestral European fare. Rosy’s constantly changing menu is posted on a wooden board above the counter seating. Seasonal vegetables are a major focus, and the majority of the menu is fueled by live-fire cooking. The pickled walleye cheeks, a sometimes special, are an Eater 2026 Dish of the Year; consider starting an order with the restaurant’s bread and spreads variety, and make sure one of their pork sausage dishes is in the mix.

Ahris Kim, one of the forces behind acclaimed NYC restaurants like Atomix and Atoboy, opened her own restaurant in June in Greenwich Village, under parent company Na:Eun Hospitality. Somssi, a 2026 Eater Best New Restaurant, is a neo-bistro with an a la carte menu full of dishes featuring Korean, European, and other Asian touches; see dishes like grilled ox tongue with romesco sauce and the carby Potato Potato Potato.

A new cocktail bar devoted to all things rum opened in Williamsburg in the former Gertie space. Echo Lake, one of Punch’s 2026 Best New Bars, offers $12 daily daiquiris and a lager/rum shot combo cutely called Tiny and a Tot, plus seafood-centric plates like oysters with tepache mignonette and green coconut curry chowder. The new bar comes from beverage power-couple Chloe Frechette (the former executive editor at Eater sibling site Punch) and Paul McGee, who cut his teeth at Chicago’s now-closed tropical bar Lost Lake. The duo is also featuring their own collection of liquid loot within the intimate basement rum bar, Undercurrent.

Perk: Eater members get a free side of soft serve with the purchase of any full-price cocktail through January 31, 2027. (21+ | Terms apply)

With both Afghan and Latin American influences, Diljān, one of Eater’s 2026 Best New Bakeries, gives New Yorkers a bakery with a point of view and innumerable reasons to become a regular. Ali Zaman and Mohamed Ghiasi, owners of Astoria’s Little Flower Cafe, teamed up with Bryan Ford, Honduran American baker and cookbook author, to conceptualize the bakery, now perched on a corner near Atlantic Avenue in Brooklyn Heights. Their combined talent makes for some of the city’s most compelling baked goods. For the Saffron Shah, laminated pastry holds delicate saffron cream in the shape of a crescent, an important Islamic symbol. Halwa tops the sticky bun, while a swirl of samosa pastry wraps halal lamb under a dusting of powdered sugar. Don’t miss the enormous Afghan flatbread crowned by toppings such as halal beef bacon with scallions or sour cherry cream cheese. The team has also branched into pizzas topped with cheese and Afghan cumin, kofta kebabs, or beef pepperoni. Look for specials like the flan with cardamom-poached apricots and conchas stuffed with firni, a rice pudding. — Nadia Chaudhury

Perk: Eater members get a free Afghan chai with the purchase of any pastry through January 31, 2027. Terms apply.

Sunday is a very good night to be at Titusz, a 2026 Eater Best New Restaurant. That’s Schnitzel Sonntag — when the Pittsburgh restaurant, clad in warm wood and gem-toned ceramic tile, offers an irresistible special at an even more irresistible price: a 4-ounce veal cutlet, breaded and fried in lard, for $13. Chef and owner Csilla Thackray honed her craft in some of the city’s top restaurant kitchens. Thackray’s husband, Sean Rosenkrans — another veteran of Pittsburgh’s restaurant and bar scene — has built a stunning list of wines from Central Europe, as well as cocktails fluent in that idiom. Don’t miss the sour cherry soup and the kaspressknödel (cheese dumpling) in charred leek and sauerkraut broth. — Beth Kracklauer

From the team behind Mawn, one of the city’s most beloved and lauded restaurants, comes sibling Sao. Like Mawn, it’s influenced by Southeast Asian flavors, but Sao is more focused on seafood and has a liquor license. That means you can have a well-made martini or glass of wine with your scallops and crab curry from James Beard Award-winning chef Phila Lorn, who is also an Eater 2026 Chef of the Year.

Assuming new ownership of beloved, old restaurants can be a risk, but South Philly local Joey Baldino has the formula down: Keep the trappings, dial in the food. After taking over his family’s private Palizzi Social Club and retaining its members-only allure, Baldino bought Bomb Bomb Bar, which first opened in 1951, and reopened it last year.

In the front room of this Eater 2026 Best New Restaurant, locals analyze Eagles games, and you might hear children playing in the street. In the back dining room, the procession of seafood, priced at $65 per person, feels like a steal in this era of rising prices. The meat for the lobster Française has been removed from its shell, battered and fried, placed on a buttery sauce, and then crowned with its shell once more. The crispy calamari gets enlivened with twangy cherry peppers. But it’s the overall dining experience that’s unbeatable: The restaurant hasn’t reinvented the wheel, but as the Beach Boys play and you sip a pepperoncini martini while watching your server pour hot fudge onto a sundae, you remember (perhaps while still wearing a bib) that complete novelty isn’t always necessary. — Bettina Makalintal

One of Punch’s 2026 Best New Bars, Peach Crease Club’s cocktail menu reads like a list of favorite foods from around the world: Buko Salad from the Philippines, Borscht from Ukraine, Guayaba y Queso from Latin America. But the dishes-turned-drinks are just one half of Peach Crease Club’s identity. The other is music, and the two complement each other like dinner and a show.

Alex Jump, co-owner of the bar (and one of Punch’s Best New Bartenders in 2019), cooked in Denver kitchens like ChoLon before moving behind the stick, and she’s been building culinary-focused cocktails since her Death & Co. Denver days. It’s not a trend she and her husband, co-owner and fellow industry vet Stuart Jensen, are chasing, Jump says; it’s just how they like to drink. Order such cocktails as the Gibson riff the Fattoush and the Guayaba y Queso; the Kik Alicha, named for Ethiopia’s turmeric split pea stew, sits under split-pea foam with a berbere garnish. — Nickolaus Hines

McLain Hedges and Mary Allison Wright of Yacht Club fame run Rougarou, a cozy-cool tribute to Southern cuisine in Five Points, which guarantees that the beverage program is a winner: Cocktails like the Sorghum Daiquiri and the Bananas Foster Julep hit the spot, and the wine selection is small but smart. What’s surprising is the food at this 2026 Best New Restaurant, which is both thoughtful and soulful, prepared by Wright’s brother, exec chef John David Wright. Creative dishes like West Indies crab salad with butter crackers, hot-and-sour catfish, fairytale eggplant with ancho chile peanut butter and ricotta salata, and rice pudding with pumpkin-white chocolate ganache and pecan praline bring something completely new to the Denver table.

Akoya Omakase, a 2026 Best New Restaurant, is the latest project from chef Peter Hoang. The vibe here is relaxed elegance, with affable chefs at the counter showcasing pristine fish in a way that highlights its best qualities, whether pairing golden threadfin bream with umami-laden shiso salt, or smoky juvenile king mackerel with pineapple chutney. Dishes that sound like they might not work on paper sing, like a hirame sashimi accented with kelp salt and both white truffle oil and black truffle pate. Akoya lacks the self-seriousness that some omakases can fall prey to, with chefs explaining dishes in straightforward language, and diners chatting enthusiastically with each other at the counter and even across tables in the small dining room.

D.C. hospitality veterans Jon Sybert and Jill Tyler took a risk when they converted Adams Morgan’s Michelin-starred favorite Tail Up Goat into Rye Bunny, a restaurant that straddles the line between upscale and casual. Rye Bunny, one of Eater’s 2026 Best New Restaurants, encompasses the simple joy of a neighborhood restaurant that’s an equally excellent destination for a weekday date night or a special occasion, and it represents a larger shift in our dining landscape that might save these mid-price-range restaurants as margins get thinner. Be sure to order the Aleppo honey-covered fried chicken, as well as the anchovy and quince jam toasts. — Emily Venezky

Perk: Eater members get a free pour of dessert wine with purchase of dessert; up to two pours per dessert through January 31, 2027. (21+ | Terms apply)

Maru San, a counter spot for Nikkei-style cuisine from decorated Peruvian chef Carlos Delgado, an Eater 2026 Chef of the Year, debuted on Friday, February 20. Delgado, who also runs Shaw’s one-Michelin-starred tasting room Causa and won the 2025 James Beard Award for Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic, adds a sleek, 25-seat counter in Eastern Market for hand rolls and sets, a la carte dishes, and a selection of Japanese beers, sake, and nonalcoholic offerings like a chicha morada and matcha lemonade. During a nightly experience, available for four guests at a time, the Lima-born chef puts a fine dining spin on the fusion food he’s already familiar with. Nikkei cuisine is a specialty at José Andrés’s China Chilcano — the Penn Quarter ceviche spot where Delgado was previously the longtime executive chef.

Bar Roza, one of Punch’s 2026 Best New Bars, can be found down a quiet alleyway that runs through Nashville’s oldest shopping corridor, the Arcade. There, restaurateur Julia Jaksic (who also runs Cafe Roze and Roze Pony) has turned a former storage room into a rose-tinted oasis of pink marble where partner and beverage director Owen Gibler’s cocktails take center stage. Venture into the Polythermal Arcade, a section of the menu where each drink is served two ways, cold and hot. Order the Jet Pilot, a riff on the tiki classic with rums swizzled with grapefruit, lime, and cinnamon over crushed ice, then have it again as the Radio Flyer, topped with steamed almond milk. — Ellen Fort

Perk: Eater members get a free off-menu item or mini croissant with the purchase of any pastry through January 31, 2027. Terms apply.

In an unmarked space in San Francisco’s Nob Hill, chef Patrick Gabon and partner Celine Wuu quietly rewrote the playbook on fine dining with Restaurant Naides, an Eater 2026 Best New Restaurant. Filipino food has not historically held a footing in the Bay Area’s higher-end echelons, but Naides’s dishes make a powerful claim that the cuisine deserves its place there. Be sure to order Gabon’s takes on classic dishes like bagoong, sinigang, and lumpia; the nonalcoholic beverage pairing is also worth exploring. — Dianne de Guzman

San Francisco first came to know chefs Laura and Sayat Ozyilmaz through their pop-up Istanbul Modern, and later through their breakthrough Presidio restaurant Dalida. The duo’s success is grounded in their take on Eastern Mediterranean food, which they made a conscious decision to champion 10 years ago. Fast-forward to 2026, and now Laura Ozyilmaz, an Eater 2026 Chef of the Year, is taking on a personal project of her own, with Sayat by her side, placing foods from Mexico’s Guerrero and Sinaloa center stage at Maria Isabel. It’s a refreshing menu that combines both Mexican and local ingredients through the lens of the Ozyilmazes’ cooking backgrounds. Order such dishes as the ceviche Acapulqueño, duck carnitas enmoladas, and artichoke tetela. — Dianne de Guzman

Perk: Eater members get a free seasonal tepache with the purchase of a tasting menu through January 31, 2027. Terms apply.

Philip Krajeck, the chef behind Rolf and Daughters and Folk, has been building his empire of hip, cozy restaurants since 2012, and his latest is no exception. Junior, tucked into what was once a Dickerson Pike Piggly Wiggly grocery store, is one of Nashville’s hottest new dining rooms. The wine list is a standout, curated by Billy Smith (formerly of award-winning natural wine bar the Four Horsemen, in Brooklyn) and featuring hard-to-find producers and dusty bottles straight from the cellar. Chef Brian Mejia (Rolf and Daughters) is leading the kitchen, showcasing dishes with elegant French techniques and Southern charm, like collard green barbajuan with burnt lemon, blue crab raviolo with herbs and blossoms, and chicory root ice cream with espresso caramel. The cantaloupe verjus terrine on the tasting menu is an Eater 2026 Dish of the Year. Find white tablecloths, red leather banquettes, a shiny, red-lacquered wine station, and an open kitchen with a roaring wood-fired stove here.

Kwame Onwuachi’s arrival in Las Vegas has been a spectacle. Fire dancers, showgirls, a performance from Busta Rhymes, and a poolside drone show helped kick off the highly anticipated opening of Maroon, his Caribbean steakhouse inside Sahara Las Vegas. Maroon is the first West Coast restaurant from the James Beard Foundation Award–winning chef following his acclaimed Tatiana in New York City and Dōgon in Washington, D.C. At Maroon, a 2026 Best New Restaurant, steaks are rum-aged, the fried rice has chunks of oxtail and curry-spiced shrimp, and a jerk pit in the middle of the restaurant turns out jerk chicken, tender lamb chops, and pork tomahawks. Other signatures include wood-fired lobster, crawfish mashed potatoes, and creamed coconut collards.

The only thing about Oklahoma City that feels even vaguely reminiscent of the Caribbean is the sheet-pan-flat horizon. And yet, inside a gaping industrial dining room downtown, there’s Dougla Kitchen, where diners sip fruity rum drinks out of plastic bags, and acclaimed chef Andrew Black digs deep in his past to bring OKC locals a taste of his Indo-Jamaican upbringing. Don’t miss the Island curry crab and callaloo dip, an Eater 2026 Dish of the Year. — Lesley Suter

Los Feliz’s new cocktail bar Vandell, one of Punch’s 2026 Best New Bars, takes over the former Nossa space with a menu of inventive cocktails from industry veterans Shawn Lickliter and Vay Su. Currently, Vandell’s menu features 27 cocktails — 13 original and 14 variations on classics. On the menu, find a handful of takes on a martini, including the Vandell Martini with gin and tarragon vinegar, as well as the Olive Martini with vodka, shio koji, and smoked olive brine. Or, go for one of the market-fresh cocktails named after their main ingredient, like the smoked tomato with mezcal or cucumber with gin.

Karla Subero Pittol’s popular dinner party pop-up Chainsaw, a 2026 Best New Bakery, has found a permanent home in Melrose Hill as a pint-sized Venezuelan cafe slinging arepas, pie, and coffee during the daytime. Grab a chair at the interior counter or among the seating splayed out on the sidewalk, and tuck into cafe quesillo, a Venezuelan flan latte, or a Karlita with grapefruit, honey, and tonic. The menu changes often, but constants include arepas stuffed with carne mechada or black beans and white cheese, as well as the famous passionfruit-lime icebox pie with a bracingly tart filling. But the joy of Chainsaw is trying whatever Subero Pittol’s latest creation is, whether that be a hot dog topped with potato sticks on a potato roll or pescadito frito with a whole fried snapper. A tip: gluten-free icebox pie is available in limited quantities — just ask at the register to see if there’s a lucky slice left. — Rebecca Roland

Henrietta, a charming all-day deli, market, and restaurant, now lives on the edge of Echo Park and Westlake in the same complex as Clark Street Bakery. During the daytime, Henrietta pairs sandwiches like a broccolini panini and turkey porchetta with deli dishes such as lima bean salad made with Rancho Gordo beans. Evening brings a menu of ricotta dumplings, rigatoni topped with short rib, and a half chicken that’s a nod to San Francisco’s Zuni Cafe. Katie Vonderheide, previously of Silverlake Wine, guides the independent producer-focused wine menu, which spans bottles, including an Old World Chianti, French chilled red, and Spanish cava. The restaurant’s enviable roast chicken is an Eater 2026 Dish of the Year.

Perk: Eater members get a free dessert with the purchase of two main dishes through January 31, 2027. Terms apply.

After more than six years of development, Washington D.C. restaurateur Rose Previte’s ambitious Maydan Market, an Eater 2026 Best New Restaurant, debuted in early October in West Adams. The hangar-like building houses an outpost of Previte’s D.C. restaurants Compass Rose (which closed earlier this year) and Michelin-recognized Maydan, alongside stalls from five other Los Angeles-based restaurants like Yhing Yhang, Poncho’s Tlayudas, and Tamales Elena. Maydan Market opens with breakfast in the morning from Compass Rose, while the stalls open for lunch; Maydan, the full-service restaurant, is only open for dinner service.

Perk: Eater members get a free spread for the table with the purchase of any food item through January 31, 2027. Terms apply.

When So. Fox, an Eater 2026 Best New Restaurant, opened in Atlanta’s Virginia-Highland neighborhood in July, chef Myles Moody and sommelier Rachael Pack had an instant hit, bringing new energy to that pocket of the city. The space that formerly housed a burger joint (and before that, an auto repair shop) has been transformed into a bright, perennially packed dining room with grand windows, offering an optimal view of North Highland Avenue. It’s seasonal Southern fare that feels current and relevant, with a refreshingly casual approach. Order the whole roasted chicken; there are only five orders per night. Dishes feature produce from their own Ornewood Park farm, such as the grilled beef with Vidalia onions and braised leeks, and at the end of summer, sugar snap peas with chives and farmer cheese. — Mona Holmes

At Ursa, Tucson-based chef Aaron Lopez, an Eater 2026 Chef of the Year, has created a menu imbued with the techniques and flavors of the Sonoran Desert that spans northern Mexico, Arizona, and southeastern California.

Inside the high-ceilinged, brick-walled downtown space, Ursa serves as a hushed gallery for Lopez and his team’s $150 tasting menu, which merges Indigenous cooking techniques with foraged and locally farmed ingredients. At every turn, with no extraneous adornments, the kitchen lets the produce and meats boast their innate nature. Lopez eschews conventional comfort, reimagining a meal of cactus, corn, sunflower tea, and beans as true luxuries, and the results are evocative and powerful. — Matthew Kang

At Ramen Del Barrio, a 2026 Eater Award winner for Best New Restaurant, chef and owner Chris Krinsky deftly laces together Japanese and Mexican culinary traditions into a fusion izakaya. Here, find dishes like creamy carnitas tonkotsu with two types of pork, confit buche and belly, as well as a chewy tangle of fresh noodles — made in partnership with Austin chef Gary Wu — using flour from a local mill. There is pozole tonkotsu studded with honeycomb tripe and hominy, and mole tsukemen with thick whole wheat noodles and carnitas. The yaki-tacos — hefty yakitori skewers served on top of corn tortillas — feature smoky pulpo or mushrooms accented with pepitas. The new dedicated space features a small television in the dining room that blasts Spanish-dubbed anime. Ramen Del Barrio feels like a loving expression of Krinsky’s culinary fascinations and his commitment to honoring both traditions. — Nadia Chaudhury

Perk: Eater members get a free agua fresca with the purchase of a bowl of ramen through January 31, 2027. Terms apply.

Chef Amir Hajimaleki’s Persian restaurant Roya has been in progress since 2018, and in February it finally opened in its full glory. Located on top of another of Hajimaleki’s restaurants, District Kitchen + Cocktails, the rich blue space sets a sumptuous tone with intricate tilework, art, and unique chandeliers. Drawing from Hajimaleki’s upbringing in Iran, the restaurant serves dishes like mahiche gheymeh (saffron tomato braised lamb shank), wagyu kebabs with fenugreek seasoning and tarragon chimichurri, and a variety of dips, plus a full cocktail menu. Decision-haters can be guided with sofreh, the chef’s tasting menu based in Persian hospitality. Hajimaleki is a 2026 Eater Chef of the Year.

A team with a Michelin-starred pedigree has opened a Cuban omakase in West Palm Beach, and it’s as intriguing as it sounds. Restaurateur Alvaro Perez-Miranda, owner of Michelin-starred Ogawa in Little River, and chefs Osmel González and Camila Salazar, formerly of Michelin-starred Entre Nos, have opened Emelina, named a 2026 Best New Restaurant. The intimate, 16-seat restaurant offers a 10-course tasting menu for $275 that lovingly imagines what Cuban cuisine could be if its native chefs were allowed freedom of creativity and access to the finest ingredients. This imaginative take on Cuban food sources fresh Floridian seafood and produce, utilizing classic omotenashi service for an evening of culinary intention.

For a decade, pint-sized Service Bar has offered creative cocktails and hospitality to fellow bartenders around the world. The bar continues to rank among the top 50 bars in North America for its inventive cocktails and friendly, knowledgeable staff that does Family Meal every Sunday night. Punch selected it as its 2026 Industry Icon, recognizing Service Bar’s decade of creative cocktails and the hospitality that its team has extended to fellow bartenders around the world. The drink menu is arranged by spirits and makes use of seasonal ingredients wherever possible. Fried chicken remains a fan favorite, as do the happy hour deals on Old Fashioneds and classic daiquiris that keep its fan base full of regulars happy. Co-owners Glendon Hartley and Chad Spangler also run Amazonia in Shaw, a pisco-fueled paradise above Michelin-starred Peruvian tasting room Causa.

Perk: Eater members get any two eligible cocktails and three tenders for $25 during happy hour through January 31, 2027. (21+ | Terms apply)
