#6468. Our Sun’s Undiscovered Stellar Nemesis Is Still Out There, Says Physicist

Long period, high inclination comets of the sort that can cause extinction level impacts here on Earth have long been thought to originate from a theoretical Oort Cloud. That is, a roughly spherical cloud of icy cometary objects that number into the trillions at distances that extend up to 1.6 light years away.

More recently, Richard Muller, a well-known professor emeritus of physics at the University of California Berkeley, put forth the idea that long period comets that visit our inner solar system are not just caused by passing stars perturbing the outer edges of the Oort Cloud. But they are also perturbed by a low mass red dwarf star (dubbed Nemesis) that along with our Sun is orbiting around a common center of gravity.

Due to Nemesisâ slightly eccentric oval orbit around the Oort Cloud, it periodically perturbs billions of comets that surround our outer solar system.

Every time Nemesis gets closest to the Oort Cloud is when the comets kick in and this comet shower lasts for maybe a million years, Muller told me via phone. That's when Nemesis is in the densest part of the comet cloud, and that's when the number of deflected Oort Cloud comets into the inner solar system are at a maximum, he says.

Just to be clear, this is not any sort of Planet X. This also doesnât have anything to do with random stellar interlopers that sometimes pass close enough to perturb our Oort Cloud and stir up a plethora of inward bound comets.

In contrast, there is nothing random about Nemesis. This is a phenomenon with a clear periodicity. According to Muller, itâs responsible for 250 million years of clearly defined periodic Earth impacts.

In a 1982 paper in the journal Science, two paleontologists, David Raup and Jack Sepkoski, collected the most extensive record of marine extinctions ever and if you plot those extinctions, you see there's a strong 26-million-year period in the data, says Muller.

The mysterious and hypothetical Oort Cloud is thought to be the home of long-period comets that visit the inner Solar System. Image Credit: ESA. LICENCE: ESA Standard Licence

One of the peaks was at 66 million years ago, the KT boundary extinction which wiped out the dinosaurs.

The challenge was to come up with an explanation, says Muller. I said, "Well, maybe there's a companion star that comes close in to the Oort Cloud every 26 million years, and then triggers a comet hitting Earth," he says.

It's an idea that Muller still very much supports, although he isn't sanguine about being able to directly observe Nemesis.

Despite what others seem to think, there is no clear evidence against this hypothesis, says Muller.

The Oort Cloud, a heretofore unseen, largely spherical cloud of comets and small icy bodies left over from the formation of our solar system some 4.5 billion years ago, very much remains a mystery.

There are three sources for the original material that formed the Oort Cloud, Astrophysicist Sean Raymond, Director of Franceâs Bordeaux Astrophysical Laboratory, told me via email. Planetesimals that originated in our Sun's planet-forming disk; planetesimals that originated around other stars in our Sun's birth cluster, and interstellar objects that were captured during stellar encounters or by scattering by Jupiter, he says.

Why hasnât Nemesis already been directly detected?

Many astronomers assume that if Nemesis is an ordinary red dwarf, somebody would have seen it, and the answer is no, because itâs moving with the Sun around the center of gravity. And as a result, Nemesis doesnât show enough proper motion, or movement across our line of sight, to be detectable.

But it must be big enough to perturb the Oort cloud, which means itâs probably at least five percent the mass of the Sun, says Muller.

The consensus view is the K-T extinction event, which impacted the Yucatan Peninsula some 66 million years ago, was most likely caused by a large asteroid.

Yet the evidence that it's an asteroid rather than a comet is very weak, so people say asteroid because that's what Walter Alvarez, a professor of Earth and Planetary Science also at the University of California, Berkeley, said in his initial K-T Boundary paper, Muller notes. But when I asked Alvarez, I said, "You said asteroid. Could it be a comet?" He said, "Sure, we couldn't tell the difference."

The best near-term chance of characterizing this massive cloud, however, comes from the Rubin Observatory, which is just coming online. Astronomers hope that Rubin will be able to detect more long period Oort Cloud comets.

The next comet shower that could cause serious damage to Earth should not be for another 12 to 15 million years from now, says Muller.

The bad news is that if it's out there, Nemesis almost certainly would lie close to the plane of the ecliptic, which means that from our point of view, it would lie co-planar to most of the bodies of the outer solar system. And as a dim 8th or possibly 9th magnitude star, this would make it even more difficult to spot, certainly impossible to see with the naked eye.

So, Nemesis really is probably lost in a field of view that includes a huge number of other stars, says Muller.

#6467. New Research Identifies the Hidden Rules That Help Brain Cancer Evade Treatment

Glioblastoma is one of the deadliest brain cancers, partly because its cells can change identities to survive treatment. Now, two studies published in Nature reveal that these changes follow predictable patterns, potentially offering new ways to make the tumors less aggressive.

Researchers from EMBL, the German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ), and the Wellcome Sanger Institute discovered that glioblastoma cells transition between distinct states according to specific molecular rules. Some cells resemble neurons, others share features with stem cells, and some adopt aggressive, injury-like states. This flexibility, known as cellular plasticity, helps tumors resist therapy.

To investigate these changes, scientists analyzed DNA, RNA, and epigenetic information from tumors collected from 12 patients, creating one of the most comprehensive molecular atlases of glioblastoma.

“We asked – can we go back to the drawing board?” said Omer Bayraktar of the Wellcome Sanger Institute. “Can we assume that we know nothing about this disease, and reconstruct how a cancer cell behaves in glioblastoma through quantitative approaches?”

“We wanted to figure out whether there is a specific rule-based system that determines how cells transition between these states,” said Oliver Stegle of EMBL Heidelberg and DKFZ. “And we asked not only whether there were rules, but also what would drive such rules.”

The analysis showed that cancer cells follow recurring paths between states rather than switching randomly. Different cell states also occupy specific regions within tumors, a pattern researchers confirmed using laboratory-grown tumor organoids.

“By integrating the single-cell data with spatial transcriptomic data, we found that there is a meticulous and very specific spatial architecture of cancer cell states,” explained Bayraktar. “And this was present in every single glioblastoma tumor in every single patient we studied.”

Researchers then examined gene regulation in more than one million patient-derived glioblastoma cells. Using a deep learning tool called scDORI, they identified molecular regulators that influence how cancer cells change states. Some act as safeguards, keeping cells in relatively stable states and limiting their plasticity.

“A tumor generates an almost endless number of variations on its own regulatory program,” said Stegle. “Instead of seeing this heterogeneity only as an obstacle, we can use AI to learn from it and extract the rules that determine how cells choose their fate.”

The findings suggested that manipulating a small number of regulators might redirect cancer cells toward less aggressive states.

“One of our premises has always been that when we understand these rules, we can not only observe what the cells are doing, but we can also change what they are doing,” said Moritz Mall of DKFZ. “We could perhaps reprogram them, and maybe push them into a state that is less malignant, less dangerous.”

Experiments supported this possibility. Increasing the activity of MYT1L, one of the identified regulators, reduced cellular plasticity and malignant characteristics in patient-derived glioblastoma cells. Mice transplanted with these modified tumor cells survived longer than those receiving control cells.

“The results with MYT1L were interesting, but the findings go much beyond that,” explained Mall. “Our approach predicts the regulators for all of the major tumor cell states, and we tested those predictions experimentally. We were able to steer tumor cells into specific states by manipulating just a handful of regulators.”

Although clinical treatments remain a future possibility, researchers are already applying the approach to other cancers and brain disorders.

“With the help of this atlas and the new AI tool, we identified new regulatory sequences that enable us to potentially drive specific cell states in a tumor-specific setting,” said Mall. “Now that we have this framework, we can apply it to many other questions and cancers.”

#6466. The 2026 Chefs of the Year

Five U.S. chefs making waves in their communities with compelling menus

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Each of the chefs featured in our new national Chef of the Year category made news in a major way. But their most recent projects are just one part of their story.

This year we celebrate five chefs who are making an impact both on the city where they cook and on the larger culinary conversation. — Missy Frederick, editorial director

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

San Francisco diners became acquainted with powerhouse couple Laura and Sayat Ozyilmaz through their championing of Eastern Mediterranean cuisine at Dalida. That restaurant told the story of Sayat’s upbringing and influences in Istanbul, Turkey, opening in 2023 inside a historic building within the lush environs of the Presidio and earning critical acclaim for the duo’s cooking.

In the years since, diners came to know Laura outside of Dalida. She completed an impressive run on Top Chef in 2024, where viewers saw her deftly plant one foot in Mediterranean food and another in Mexican cuisine, showcasing her skill in both fields throughout the season. With the 2026 debut of the Ozyilmazes’ restaurant Maria Isabel, the food feels like an even fuller expression of Laura’s heritage and personal history.

Named after Laura’s sister (Maria) and her mother (Isabel), the restaurant steeps in Mexican matriarchy, highlighting female winemakers, ceramics made by Mexican producers, and indigenous Mexican ingredients. The menu channels Laura’s upbringing in Guerrero and her family’s Sinaloan roots, as recounted through mariscos and maiz, moles and salsa macha. The ceviche Acapulqueño reimagines the Fanta- and ketchup-laden version instead with marigold flowers and preserved Seville oranges dressing tender shrimp and raw scallop; petals — and three fried shrimp heads — adorn the top. Duck enmoladas showcase the power of mole negro against a seasonal mole (sometimes a peach manchamanteles, other times a rhubarb rendition, but always compelling). Chochoyotes, a lesser-seen dish in San Francisco, demonstrates the restaurant’s ability to apply masa in different ways — in this case, dumplings — while harnessing the earthy flavor of huitlacoche. Maria Isabel is both a conduit for diners to connect with complex Mexican flavors and a view into Laura’s vision of the Mexico of her past and future. — Dianne de Guzman, editor, Eater SF

Chef Carlos Delgado’s meteoric rise in D.C. began in 2022 with the opening of tiny tasting room Causa, located in Shaw, where he sends diners on a seafaring voyage along the Peruvian coastline and into the Andes he grew up around, and its accompanying upstairs pisco destination Bar Amazonia. His meticulous sourcing and culinary skills quickly drew critical acclaim.

2026 might be the Lima native’s biggest year yet: His breakout project, Maru San, commanded instant Capitol Hill buzz upon opening in February for its orchestra of Nikkei-style hand rolls, sashimi, and other polished seafood plates he and fellow José Andrés alum Simon Lam pass across a 25-seat black marble counter under a big pink octopus mural, as his favorite tropical house blasts in the background. A rare few get to sample the restaurant’s elaborate tasting menu full of ingredients like high-end uni and dry-aged fish; reservations for the 15-course feast are nearly impossible to get.

The ambitious chef, at 36, isn’t afraid to stretch in many directions. He linked up with the Eaternity Group last year to give the Mediterranean-themed La Vie a needed menu makeover at D.C.’s Wharf development — meanwhile, at least one more Maru San is in the works elsewhere in D.C.

Sounds a lot like his former mentor: Before Causa, Delgado honed his craft under José Andrés as the longtime executive chef at Penn Quarter’s Peruvian mainstay China Chilcano. They still text frequently. — Tierney Plumb, Northeast editor

While Amir Hajimaleki has had American-leaning restaurants in Austin for well over a decade, he hasn’t had the opportunity to fully express himself as an Iranian-born, Texas-raised chef. That is until he opened Roya, his most personal restaurant and a project that has been in the works for more than eight years. Here, he manifests the depth and diversity of Persian cuisine, a bold feat for the middle of Texas. The space, designed with his brother Ali Hajimaleki, feels transportive with intricate tile mosaics, burnished gold and dark blue hues, and delicate chandeliers.

There’s been an electric energy to the Philly restaurant scene in recent years. The city, ever the underdog, has long punched above its weight; now, the rest of the world has come to the same realization. Amid this buzz, two newer restaurants have outrun the shadow cast by the city’s big names: Cambodian noodle house Mawn, which opened in 2023, and Southeast Asian oyster house and raw bar Sao, which opened last September.

At their helm is the slick, stylish Phila Lorn. The restaurants he runs with his wife Rachel feel singular, blending the influences of his Philadelphia upbringing with his Cambodian background in food that feels playfully free and emboldened by a lack of boundaries between cuisines. At Mawn, funnel cake meets coconut macaroons, and vinegar peppers enhance scallops in red curry. At Sao, the crispy rice in the nam khao salad, which features Italian sausage, feels analogous to arancini. Tuna carpaccio is served with crispy shallots and jalapeños, then cured in lime until it picks up the aura of the bowls of beef pho on Washington Avenue.

Hear Lorn talk, with his South Philly-bred bravado (and requisite uses of “jawn”) giving him a commanding presence, and it’s clear that the city’s culinary community is listening, rallying, and getting stoked to eat more of his food. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

Tucson-based chef Aaron Lopez had a vision that started in his small California city of El Centro, an agricultural city near the U.S.-Mexico border. There, he hatched a plan to create a menu imbued with the techniques and flavors of the Sonoran Desert that spans northern Mexico, Arizona, and southeastern California. Trained at top kitchens in Los Angeles and beyond, Lopez researched by going deep into the desert, armed with a camera and his wits. A year later, he and his wife June Chee carried the project to Tucson, a larger venue still deeply embedded in the desert, but with a new audience.

Inside the high-ceilinged, brick-walled downtown space, Ursa serves as a hushed gallery for Lopez and his team’s $150 tasting menu, which merges Indigenous cooking techniques with foraged and locally farmed ingredients. Barrel fruit (a yellow cactus) topped with the tang of pickled chiltepin leaves is the first bite, a luscious treat you may never see on a European plate. Quail breast arrives on a metal skewer dressed in pickled yucca, hovering over a jujube broth like a quiet offering. Goat roasted in agave, pit barbacoa-style, is unveiled tableside and served over softened tepary beans.

At every turn, with no extraneous adornments, the kitchen lets the produce and meats boast their innate nature. Lopez eschews conventional comfort, reimagining a meal of cactus, corn, sunflower tea, and beans as true luxuries, and the results are evocative and powerful. His message — seeing the value and beauty of this landscape, its people, its ingredients, and the way it all comes through the cooking — is the luscious pith of the cactus you find beneath the surface of the American Southwest. — Matthew Kang, correspondent

#6465. Nearby Dwarf Galaxies Show Surprising Lack Of Oxygen, Says Paper

Vital to almost all life as we know it, oxygen has long been valued as a tracer of the chemical evolution of the of the cosmos. As such, it provides a practical means of tracing how the heavy elements of iron, carbon, nickel, magnesium and sulfur --- the real building blocks of habitable planets like our own --- are distributed throughout the galaxy and beyond.

In a paper published in The Astrophysical Journal, researchers using Hubble studied 37 nearby dwarf galaxies â small galaxies containing a few thousand to hundreds of millions of stars â and found that much of the oxygen they expected to see is missing, says NASA.

For the first time, we have measured both how much oxygen produced by stars in low-mass galaxies remains in those galaxies, and how much oxygen has been lost from those galaxies throughout their lifetimes, Grace Telford, the paperâs second author and an assistant professor at the University of Utahâs Dept. of Physics & Astronomy, told me via email.

The findings show that dwarf galaxies can hold onto only a small fraction of the oxygen made by stars, says NASA.

The team used Hubble Space Telescope data; data from NASAâs retired Spitzer Space Telescope as well as the ground based Very Large Array and Australian Telescope Compact Array, NASA notes.

Most of the oxygen does come from core-collapse supernovae, which are the explosive deaths of massive stars, says Telford. Yet a very small fraction is also produced in other types of supernovae caused by the remnants of low-mass stars becoming unstable or merging, she says.

As the cosmosâ third most abundant element, oxygen is relatively easy to detect and measure, and its production is well understood â making it a reliable indicator of how chemical elements are distributed in a galaxy, says NASA.

We found that typically 15 percent of the oxygen produced by stars in these low-mass galaxies is still found inside those galaxies today: mostly in their gas, but small fractions are also in the stars and dust, says Telford. The explanation is that energetic radiation from massive stars and their deaths as supernovae drive oxygen-rich gas out of the galaxies over time, she says.

This means that the missing oxygen is likely in the gaseous halos surrounding the galaxies. That is, the Circumgalactic Medium (CGM). This missing oxygen has also likely traveled even farther into the intergalactic medium.

The Galaxies Losing Oxygen via Winds (GLOW) project, jointly funded by NASA and the National Science Foundation, is a large-scale effort to understand how gas and heavy elements move between low-mass galaxies, their CGM, and the intergalactic medium.

To do this requires combining a large set of new and archival observations of low-mass galaxies from both ground-based and space telescopes, says Telford.

The idea is that most of the oxygen found outside these dwarf galaxies has been driven there by energy from massive stars and supernovae explosions.

Similar measurements of oxygen (and other heavy elements) lost from galaxies have been made for massive galaxies like the Milky Way, says Telford. But low-mass galaxies are expected to lose oxygen more easily due to their smaller gravity and our paper demonstrates that this is indeed the case, she says.

In the Milky Way, there is about one oxygen atom for every 2,000 hydrogen atoms, says Telford. In low-mass galaxies like those in the GLOW project, that value is more like one oxygen atom for every 10,000-20,000 hydrogen atoms, she says.

The GLOW project found that low-mass galaxies lose more oxygen than current galaxy formation simulations predict, implying that we donât yet have a complete understanding of how massive stars interact with their host galaxies, says Telford.

#6464. The Solar System May Have a 6th Dwarf Planet – and It’s Been Hiding in Plain Sight

A newly discovered dwarf planet candidate has a trail stretching back more than a decade in telescope images, giving astronomers a head start in understanding its orbit.

2026 ED138 could become the solar system’s sixth officially recognized dwarf planet. The newly discovered icy body orbits beyond Pluto, and early measurements suggest it is among the largest dwarf planet candidates ever found beyond Neptune.

Astronomers spotted the provisionally named object in data from the Simonyi Survey Telescope at the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. It had likely escaped earlier searches because millions of Milky Way stars crowded the view, making even a world this large difficult to pick out.

Its distance, brightness, and estimated surface reflectivity suggest a diameter of 600 to 1,500 kilometers, or about 370 to 930 miles. Icy bodies that large are expected to have enough gravity to pull themselves into a round shape, one requirement for dwarf planet status. More observations are needed to measure ED138’s exact size and confirm whether it qualifies.

If confirmed, ED138 would join the five dwarf planets recognized by the International Astronomical Union: Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea, and Makemake.

Matthew Holman, a senior astrophysicist at the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, first identified the candidate. He and Mario Jurić, a University of Washington professor of astronomy and leader of Rubin’s solar system team, presented the results at a press conference on October 27, 2026. Jurić contributed additional observations that helped establish the object’s orbit.

“Finding an object this big, roughly 1,000 kilometers across, is something that happens maybe once in a generation,” Jurić said. “It’s the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years, and Rubin turned it up while we were still commissioning the telescope.”

ED138 is currently about 46 astronomical units (au) from the Sun. One au is the average distance between Earth and the Sun, and Pluto’s average distance is about 40 au. ED138 belongs to a population called trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs), which orbit the Sun beyond Neptune.

The sizes, compositions, and orbits of these distant objects offer clues to how the solar system formed. Scientists study them to understand how the giant planets migrated over time and how smaller bodies were scattered as the system evolved.

Finding ED138 required distinguishing its movement from the crowded stellar background near the plane of the Milky Way. Rubin repeatedly monitors the entire southern sky, while powerful algorithms sift through millions to billions of points of light to identify small moving objects. Together, those capabilities allowed the team to pick ED138 out of a field where it had been difficult for other telescopes to detect.

On the evening of October 13, Holman was processing Rubin observations collected earlier in 2026 with search code he had developed with colleague Kevin Napier. The code compares billions of detections of moving objects and determines which detections belong to the same body. When ED138 appeared in the results, its brightness and distance immediately suggested that it was unusually large.

“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” Holman said. “Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong.”

Jurić searched Rubin’s catalogs and images and located 20 more observations stretching back to March 2026. The team also found ED138 in archival images from other surveys dating to 2016. Those records allowed the researchers to trace more than 10 years of its orbit.

“Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth, and precision,” Jurić said. “And the discovery is just the beginning: Once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look. This ability to both discover and ‘precover’ objects is transforming how quickly and accurately we can determine their orbits and understand the distant solar system.”

ED138 adds to a rapidly growing collection of solar system objects discovered by Rubin since it began gathering early data in preparation for the Legacy Survey of Space and Time, or LSST. The survey began in June 2026. In April, before its formal start, Rubin’s solar system team announced observations of more than 11,000 new asteroids, with roughly 380 new TNOs included in the announcement. The team called that submission “the tip of the iceberg” and expressed excitement about the discoveries to come once LSST began.

“If confirmed as a dwarf planet, ED138 would join a very small family of worlds,” Holman said. “Rubin will image the whole southern sky again and again for 10 years, so any others hiding in the places earlier surveys skipped are now within reach.”

Operations of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory are funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Science.

#6463. Can Dubai Become the World's Fittest City?

At 6 a.m. on Sunday, November 22, Dubai's Sheikh Zayed Road will fall silent. For one morning only, the city's six-lane superhighway—usually a blur of Nissan Patrols, taxis, and delivery scooters—will belong to tens of thousands of competitors as Dubai Run takes over the city’s skyline at dawn, following in the footsteps of a record 307,000 participants last year.

Leading the charge is usually Dubai's Crown Prince Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, the driving force behind the Dubai Fitness Challenge (DFC) and one of the city's most ambitious experiments: to turn itself into the fittest city in the world.

"The people of Dubai have created an inspirational fitness movement, sending a powerful message that traveled far beyond our city,” Sheikh Hamdan said during a previous edition of the challenge. “Together, let us transform Dubai into the fittest city in the world.”

An athlete himself, the Crown Prince has long championed cycling, diving, and long-distance running, but the challenge—now in its tenth year—is his most visible legacy. Launched in 2017, it calls on residents and visitors alike to commit to 30 minutes of exercise every day for 30 days each November. Since its inception, more than 16 million people have taken part, transforming what began as a simple invitation to get moving into one of the world’s largest community fitness initiatives.

This year’s landmark edition is running until Sunday, November 29 under the theme What’s Your 30x30?, inviting residents and visitors to find their own way to complete 30 minutes of daily activity. With four flagship events, three free Fitness Villages, and more than 30 Community Fitness Hubs, the program is among the most ambitious yet, transforming everything from beaches and public parks to shopping centers and major roads into places to exercise.

The first Dubai Fitness Challenge took place in 2017

Four major events headline the 2026 calendar: Dubai Ride, which opened the challenge on Sunday, November 1 with thousands of cyclists taking over Sheikh Zayed Road; Dubai Run, the world’s largest free community fun run, on Sunday, November 22; Dubai Stand-Up Paddle, a two-day festival of paddle boarding, kayaking and yoga at Hatta Dam on Saturday, November 7 and Sunday, November 8; and Dubai Yoga, which returns for its second edition on Sunday, November 29, bringing thousands together for a mass sunrise session beneath the DIFC Gate Building.

Three Fitness Villages—at Kite Beach, Zabeel Park and Al Warqa’a—act as free, all-day wellness hubs offering everything from boxing and beach volleyball to spin classes and meditation. More than 30 neighborhood Community Hubs have also been set up across the city, bringing fitness closer to home with pop-up runs, rooftop yoga, skateboarding lessons, padel tournaments, and family-friendly bootcamps.

The calendar aligns with a packed line-up of international sporting events, from the Dubai Premier Padel P1 and T100 Triathlon to the DP World Tour Championship and Emirates Dubai 7s. This year also brings the return of the Dubai Sail Grand Prix, with high-speed catamarans racing off the city’s coastline, while HYROX Dubai will see athletes tackle a grueling combination of running and functional fitness challenges. Elsewhere, the program includes obstacle races, mountain trails in Hatta, and community running events across the city.

It’s all part of what His Excellency Saeed Hareb, Secretary General of the Dubai Sports Council, describes as a lasting change in the city’s relationship with exercise. “It has helped establish a culture of active living, bringing communities together and making sport and physical activity an integral part of life in Dubai,” he said as the challenge marked its tenth anniversary.

Ahmed Al Khaja, CEO of Dubai Festivals and Retail Establishment, says the anniversary is an opportunity to reflect on how far the initiative has come. Speaking at the launch of the 2026 program, he credited the collaboration between government bodies, private businesses, and local communities with making exercise increasingly accessible across Dubai. The aim, he said, is to inspire healthier habits that continue long after the 30-day challenge ends.

The numbers suggest it’s working. Last year’s edition attracted a record three million-plus participants, up from 2.73 million in 2024. More than 307,000 people took part in Dubai Run alone, while Dubai Ride welcomed 40,327 cyclists. Since the challenge launched in 2017, cumulative participation has exceeded 16 million, a remarkable figure for an initiative that began with a simple invitation to exercise for half an hour a day.

The Dubai Ride closes the city's busiest highway for one morning each year

Ethan Matthews, Chief Operating Officer at Reset Fitness and a former professional rugby player and coach in Portugal and Italy, says that Dubai’s greatest fitness asset is its variety. “There are world-class facilities on every block now—not just gyms, but parks, cycling tracks, and sports complexes,” he says. “Try as many things as possible—team sports, group sessions, individual training. It’s about finding what challenges you physically but also what you actually enjoy. That’s how you stay consistent, especially on the tough days.”

For Matthews, the social aspect is just as vital. “The moment you find something you like—padel, CrossFit, running, whatever—you meet people. It opens doors, both personally and professionally. That’s what keeps Dubai’s fitness culture alive.”

Anthony Lee, a personal trainer and owner of Activ8 Lifestyle & Fitness who has spent nearly two decades as part of Dubai’s fitness scene, thinks the timing of the challenge is part of its success. “It’s clever,” he says. “It's just before Christmas, when everyone wants to feel a bit fitter before heading home for the holidays, and when the weather’s perfect for being outdoors.”

He describes the month-long initiative as “a push that gets people back into routine,” and a rare opportunity to sample new workouts without cost or commitment. “You can try boxing on Kite Beach one day, yoga in Zabeel Park the next. It breaks the monotony.” What stands out most, he adds, is accessibility. “You don’t have to be an athlete. It’s about being a better version of yourself—you versus you.”

For visitors, the challenge offers a very different way to experience Dubai as, during November, the city’s hotels, cafes and shopping centers adopt a surprisingly sporty rhythm. At Kite Beach, sunrise yoga sessions fill up fast, while the public running track buzzes with tourists and locals alike, and Zabeel Park hosts evening workouts beneath the skyline. There's no need to sign up—just show up on the day.

Outside of November, the spirit of the challenge remains. Dubai has built more than 557 kilometers of cycle tracks, with a goal of 1,000 kilometers by 2030, and the urban planning department is adding shaded walking routes to make exercise feasible for longer stretches of the year.

Lee, the personal trainer, believes Dubai’s fitness drive has found fertile ground because of the city’s demographic and design. “It’s a young place,” he says. “Most people are working-age expats, and with the beach and pool culture here, people want to look and feel good.”

But vanity isn’t the whole story. “Every new residential tower has a gym and a pool, so exercise is built into daily life,” he says. “When I moved here 18 years ago, you had a handful of hotel gyms and a couple of Fitness First branches. Now every neighborhood has options, from boutique studios to outdoor circuits.” He has also noticed a social shift: “Fitness has become a way to meet people. For newcomers, joining a class or trying padel is how you find your tribe.”

This year’s Dubai Fitness Challenge runs under the theme What’s Your 30x30?

The fitness calendar's cleverest invention, however, might be the Mallathon. With summer temperatures soaring past 45°C, nine of the city’s biggest malls were converted into indoor running routes between June and September, attracting 100,000 participants.

Dr Amir Firouzjaei, a general practitioner and traditional Chinese medicine expert who has lived in Dubai for three years, believes the movement taps into something deeper. “When a city moves, its energy moves,” he says. “It’s not only about training the body but refreshing the mind and spirit.”

He explains that the city’s blend of high-intensity exercise and restorative practices “keeps the balance between energy and recovery,” preventing burnout and encouraging people to “stick with it.”

The trend is filtering into Dubai's hospitality scene, too. New-generation hotels such as SIRO One Za’abeel pitch themselves as “fitness and recovery” spaces, complete with in-room stretching areas, altitude chambers and performance coaches. In Al Quoz, the Matcha Club—a blend of padel courts, co-working space, and cafe—has become the new social hang-out for the health-minded. Even Dubai’s famously indulgent brunches are getting lighter, with restaurants like Eat Well dishing up bowls, turmeric shots, and cold-brew coffee instead of the traditional Champagne towers.

Matthews, who moved to Dubai in 2017—the same year the first Dubai Fitness Challenge launched—says he’s watched the city’s attitudes shift dramatically. “Post-Covid, the appetite for fitness just exploded,” he says. “Gyms, studios and open-air facilities have multiplied, but more importantly, people’s reasons for exercising have changed. They’re doing it to feel good, not just to look good.”

He believes that’s partly because of education and access. “The government has played a big role through campaigns like 30x30, but accessibility is the real game changer. Whether it’s walking paths, beach gyms or purpose-built cycling tracks, there’s always somewhere to move.” For Matthews, that accessibility underpins a healthy, sustainable economy. “When people feel better, they perform better—at work, at home, everywhere. Fitness has become part of Dubai.”

Residents and visitors alike are invited to discover new ways to move, connect and build healthy habits that last beyond the challenge's 30 days

Firouzjaei, the doctor, sees Dubai’s fitness boom as part of a wider cultural shift. “It’s a fast city, and that creates pressure,” he says. “People here work hard and compete hard, so they need ways to recharge and reset.”

He points out that the city’s international mix has made wellness more mainstream. “Residents come from everywhere—Asia, Europe, the Middle East—and many already know yoga, acupuncture, or functional medicine,” he says. “They’re open to new ideas and they understand that health is an investment rather than a luxury.” In his clinic, he’s noticed that even patients who once focused purely on appearance now talk about sleep, stress, and balance.

Behind the lifestyle messaging lies the emirate's urban agenda. Dubai wants to be a ‘20-minute city,’ where every resident can reach work, shops, and recreation within a short cycle or walk. The health argument is compelling. Obesity and diabetes are major public health concerns across the Gulf, and studies show only one in five UAE children meets recommended daily activity levels. City officials believe that building infrastructure—parks, cycle paths, open gyms—is the surest way to shift behavior.

Already, habits are changing. Park footfall has risen 20% year-on-year, while corporate wellness participation has grown by 30%. The once-novel sight of commuters jogging to metro stations has become almost ordinary.

According to experts, Dubai's mix of international residents has made wellness more mainstream

For tourists, taking part couldn’t be easier. The Dubai Fitness Challenge app lists daily events, classes, and pop-ups across the city, most of them free.

Looking back on 18 years in Dubai, Lee says the transformation has been “massive.” When he first arrived, “there were far fewer gyms, and fitness wasn’t part of daily conversation.” Now, he says, it’s as visible as the skyline itself. “Sure, some people join the big events just for the photos—you’ll always have that—but for others it’s the start of something lasting,” he says. “Even if they only do the challenge for a month, it plants a seed. And that’s what counts.”

Matthews agrees, though he cautions against seeing Dubai’s fitness scene as something reserved for the elite. “The biggest misconception is that you have to be in peak shape to take part,” he says. “You don’t. Fitness here is for everyone, from people training for Ironman to those who just want to walk their dogs or join a weekend bootcamp.”

Dubai has always been a city in motion, but now it wants its progress measured not by the height of its towers or the size of its megaprojects, but by footsteps, pedal strokes and heartbeats. It's a city that’s, quite literally, on the move—and inviting the world to keep up.

Dubai’s biggest community running event transforms Sheikh Zayed Road into a traffic-free running track, with participants choosing between a 5km route through Downtown Dubai or a longer 10km course finishing beneath the DIFC Gate Building. More than 307,000 runners took part last year.

Where: Sheikh Zayed Road, starting near the Museum of the FutureWhen: Sunday, November 22, 6.30 a.m.How to take part: Register free at at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

Marking the finale of Dubai Fitness Challenge, thousands of yoga enthusiasts will gather beneath the iconic DIFC Gate Building for a mass sunrise session. The program includes guided breathwork, a sound bath and a 30-minute yoga session, with dedicated areas for families and women.

Where: DIFC Gate BuildingWhen: Sunday, November 29, sunriseHow to take part: Register free at at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

Dubai’s largest beachfront Fitness Village returns with everything from spinning and yoga to padel, beach volleyball, basketball and cricket. There are dedicated activity zones, bookable courts and daily fitness classes, with the Arabian Gulf providing a rather spectacular backdrop.

Where: Kite Beach, JumeirahWhen: Saturday, October 31 to Sunday, November 29; weekdays 3 p.m.–11 p.m., weekends 7 a.m.–11 p.m.How to take part: Register free on-site, with selected activities available to book at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

Zabeel Park’s Fitness Village returns with boxing, spinning, basketball, padel, and daily group workouts, alongside dedicated children’s activities. The village also serves as the official bib collection point for Dubai Run.

Where: Zabeel Park, Gate 2When: Saturday, October 31 to Sunday, November 29; weekdays 4 p.m.–11 p.m., weekends noon–11 p.m.How to take part: Register free on-site, with selected activities available to book at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

Set among palm trees and parkland, this neighborhood-style Fitness Village combines outdoor exercise with family-friendly activities. There’s a 2.8km running and cycling track, bike rentals, daily fitness classes, dedicated ladies-only areas and courts for padel, volleyball, football, and basketball.

Where: Al Warqa’a ParkWhen: Saturday, October 31 to Sunday, November 29; daily 4 p.m.–11 p.m.How to take part: Register free on-site, with selected activities available to book at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

#6462. A Stellar Odd Couple at an Unusual Stage of Evolution

Most of the stars in the Milky Way are what we might call normal stars. They're main sequence stars like our Sun, meaning they're doing what most people probably think stars do: shining as they fuse hydrogen atoms into helium atoms on a vast scale.

But all stars run out of hydrogen fuel eventually, and some stars end up in odd states as they evolve off of the main sequence. White dwarfs represent one of these odd evolutionary statea. Our Sun will become one of these when it runs out of fuel in several billion years. These stars are super-compact and dense; they're about as large as Earth but have about as much mass as the Sun. They shine only with remnant energy.

White dwarfs are strange, but not rare. About 97% of the Milky Way's stars will become white dwarfs eventually, and they're not difficult to detect.

Another strange end-state is the neutron star. They form when massive stars explode as core-collapse supernovae. Since massive stars are rare, so are neutron stars. They're also extremely dense objects, but even more dense than white dwarfs. They can have 2 solar masses and be only 12 km in diameter. It's often said that a teaspoon of neutron star would 'weigh' one billion tonnes.

Not only are neutron stars rare, but they're difficult to detect; they're small, dark, and cold. But some neutron stars do announce their presence as pulsars. Pulsars are rapidly rotating neutron stars that shine beams of light from their poles. If one of those beams is aimed at us, astronomers can see it blinking. They're cosmic lighthouses.

Millisecond pulsars (MSPs) are a specific type of pulsar with rotation periods of 10 milliseconds or less that only form when they have a binary companion. It happens when the companion swells up due to its own evolution. Mass spills over from the companion and spirals onto the millisecond pulsar, giving it angular momentum, or rotational energy that makes it spin rapidly. Finding these binary stars is of great interest to astronomers, and a team of researchers from Italy and Germany have found one with a very young white dwarf partner.

Their research is published in a paper titled "The youngest white dwarf companion to a millisecond pulsar: Insights from NGC 362D." It's published in Astronomy and Astrophysics, and the first author is Greta Ettorre, a PhD student in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the Alma Mater Studiorum University of Bologna, Italy.

Globular clusters are excellent hunting grounds for millisecond pulsars, because the stellar density is so high that neutron stars are more likely to have companions. NGC362D is a millisecond pulsar with a rotation period of only 5.83 milliseconds, meaning it rotates more than 10,000 times per minute. It was first discovered in December, 2022, in the globular cluster NGC 362, about 29,300 light years away.

*Somewhere in this globular cluster (NGC 362), a millisecond pulsar and its binary companion, a white dwarf, are in a rare stage of evolution. The pulsar, which is a dense, rapidly spinning neutron star, has been drawing material away from its less dense white dwarf companion, hastening its evolution into a white dwarf. Image Credit: By ESA/Hubble, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?

"Millisecond pulsars (MSPs) form in binary systems containing a slowly rotating neutron star (NS) that is eventually spun up to millisecond periods by heavy-mass and angular-momentum transfer from an evolving companion," the authors explain. "The recycling scenario for MSP formation predicts that the mass transfer between the non-degenerate companion and the NS typically starts when the donor is either a main sequence or a subgiant or red-giant branch star."

The pulsar's companion, called COM-NGC 362D, is the youngest MSP companion ever found. It's a proto-white dwarf, which indicates that it's only just entering the earliest stages of becoming a white dwarf. "Our analysis robustly shows that this object is a very low-mass (â¼0.18âMâ) He white dwarf (WD) still in the pre-cooling phase," the authors write.

NGC 362D and its companion are important because the astronomers caught them in a rare stage of their relationship. "Interestingly, a detailed comparison with updated binary evolution models indicates that this object completed the mass-transfer phase only recently (â¼0.6 Gyr ago), thus strongly suggesting that COM-NGC 362D is the youngest WD companion to a MSP identified to date," the authors explain. This is especially interesting because as the pulsar draws material from its companion, it drastically shapes the companion's evolution, forcing it to become a white dwarf far sooner than it would on its own. This is called the recycling process.

Astronomers found COM-NGC 362D by cross-referencing radio data from the pulsar itself with ten years of Hubble observations in ultraviolet and near-infrared. By comparing that data with stellar evolution models, they determined its age and other properties. But there was something else: the same models showed less UV radiation than expected for a white dwarf like this. Something was blocking or attenuating some of its UV.

"Remarkably, in this respect, the photometric properties of NGC 362D show, for the first time in this class of objects, significant wavelength-dependent variations that are consistent with the presence of residual circumstellar material," the authors write. This material was likely expelled during the mass-transfer phase, emphasizing how young the white dwarf is.

âWhat makes this system particularly interesting is the possibility of observing it at a very early stage of its evolution,â lead author Ettorre said. âMoreover, the attenuation of the signal that we observed in the ultraviolet could indicate the presence of material still surrounding the white dwarf.â

They acknowledge that it's unclear if the material could've survived for this long, but it's still their preferred explanation.

The purple line in this figure shows the reference model for a young He white dwarf in its cooling phase. The pink points are fitted data from COM-NGC 362D. (The blue points represent data that couldn't be fitted for technical reasons.) "The observed trend, with larger deviations at shorter wavelengths, is consistent with a self-extinction effect likely produced by circumstellar material surrounding the proto-WD companion," the authors write. Image Credit: Ettorre et al. A&A, 713, L14 (2026)

"Our proposed scenario envisages that COM-NGC 362D is an extremely young WD that only recently ended the mass-transfer phase and is surrounded by a residual cloud of material producing self-extinction," the authors write.

This means that they system is a unique opportunity to study the aftermath of the recycling process that generates an MSP. If COM-NGC 362D has only recently had its outer layers stripped away, then the dense core left behind is only in the early stages of transitioning to a white dwarf. So finding this young core could make it easier to identify others.

âNGC 362D currently offers us a unique opportunity to study what happens in the immediate aftermath of the millisecond pulsar recycling process,â said study co-author Emanuele Dalessandro, a researcher at INAF. âIn this context, the possible presence of material around the white dwarf is particularly interesting. In fact, it could produce signatures at radio wavelengths in addition to the optical, similar to those observed in systems with non-degenerate companions, and could therefore help us correctly interpret the properties of other young systems.â

Though their proposed scenario is that COM-NGC 362D is a very young white dwarf at the end of the recycling process, they do acknowledge another possibility. "Alternatively, the material may have been expelled during a previous hydrogen-shell flash," they write.

In any case, pulsars are fascinating objects, and their rapid and regular pulses of electromagnetic energy make them natural clocks. This makes them useful in studying other aspects of the Universe. Understanding how they form will only be helpful.

âMillisecond pulsars rotate with extraordinary regularity and can be used as true natural clocks. Measuring the arrival times of their pulses with extreme precision allows us, among other things, to study gravity under extreme conditions and to carry out increasingly precise tests of general relativity. Understanding their surroundings and reconstructing their evolutionary history is therefore essential to fully exploit what these remarkable cosmic laboratories can tell us.â Ettorre concludes.

#6461. The 2026 Restaurant Dishes of the Year

From an earthy curry crab callaloo dip to a plate of pickled walleye cheeks, these were editors’ most memorable bites

Our editors ate in hundreds of restaurants across the country this year, but certain dishes left a lasting impression, and we’re recognizing them in this new national Eater Award category.

From a textbook execution of the ubiquitous 2026 entree — roast chicken — to an innovative fish preparation offering Midwestern diners a new way to experience a familiar ingredient, these dishes are all worth celebrating. — Missy Frederick, editorial director

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

When experiencing a five-course tasting menu ($145), I wasn’t expecting toast to be a main attraction. But even with competition from luxurious courses featuring everything from a complex Hokkaido scallop to an assertive charred rib-eye with peaches, All Well’s puffed grain toast left a lasting impression.

After three years at two-Michelin-starred Oriole, Larry Feldmeier partnered with Noah Sandoval, fellow Oriole alum and James Beard winner for Best Chef: Great Lakes, to open the ambitious West Loop restaurant All Well, which offers both a la carte bar options and the aforementioned tasting; the toast is only available as part of the latter experience.

The dish arrives to the table amplified with nutty buckwheat butter sweetened with honey, the backdrop for a pasta stuffed with triple-cream Délice de Bourgogne and a cauldron of salty chicken brodo. You’ll dive into the pasta, of course, using the bread to sop up the rich beurre blanc. Like a performer waiting in the wings for their monologue, the puffed grain toast takes center stage. The toast effectively offsets the creaminess and saltiness of the rest of the dish, but can stand on its own even without the accompanying pasta. Its subtle sweetness almost acts as a mid-meal dessert, a distinctive break in a seamless dinner you don’t quite want to end. — Isaiah Reynolds, audience editor

The only thing about Oklahoma City that feels even vaguely reminiscent of the Caribbean is the sheet-pan-flat horizon. And yet inside a gaping industrial dining room downtown, there’s Dougla Kitchen, where diners sip fruity rum drinks out of plastic bags and acclaimed chef Andrew Black digs deep in his past to bring OKC locals a taste of his Indo-Jamaican upbringing. I fully admit this Midwestern-born, California-raised girl doesn’t encounter ruddy callaloo greens as often as she’d like (my hunch is neither do most Oklahomans). No matter. What Black manages to do with this deceiving pile of greenish-brown mush, dank with hand-picked crab and sparkling with curry spices, translates the soul of Caribbean home cooking in a single scoop. I didn’t know it was possible to be overwhelmed by a sense memory from a life that’s not your own, but this heady appetizer does that, served with a side of crisp taro chips and worth lingering over all afternoon with a couple of Red Stripes. — Lesley Suter, brand director

To understand California cuisine in 2026, look no further than Henrietta, a neighborhood bistro that has struck a just-right balance of precision and ingenuity while imbuing a feeling of nostalgia that begs locals and travelers alike to return. The restaurant’s intentions come across most clearly in its roast chicken, served as a just-salty-enough half chicken hunked into handheld pieces with deep, smoky char marks. The prize chicken pile gets tucked onto a plate alongside a scorched lemon half and a heaping, chicory-heavy Caesar panzanella blanketed under a layer of Parmesan that could be a snowcap on a stretch of the San Gabriel Mountains. With the chicken, Henrietta nods to forebears (namely San Francisco’s Zuni), while making the dish its own with a Baja-born Caesar salad that feels distinctly Los Angeles, dotted with torn fistfuls of bread from the neighboring local Clark Street Bakery. Of course, 2026 continues to be the year of the Great Chickening, where roast chicken has become many a restaurant’s calling card — and an easy way into the cultural cache. In Los Angeles alone, Sqirl (with its new dinner menu) and Pasjoli have both put out progressive, near-intoxicating spins on the dish, but Henrietta’s has lodged itself into the collective imagination with its brazen simplicity. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest

The striking cantaloupe and verjus terrine at Nashville’s Junior offers a glimpse into the minds of chef Philip Krajeck and chef de cuisine Brian Mejia, the duo behind the high-technique kitchen. A “terrine” slice arrives with pieces of cantaloupe suspended in a clear gelatin made with verjus, the pressed juice of unripened grapes. One corner is covered in tiny, diced cubes of cantaloupe dressed in citrus-forward turmeric oil; another gets draped in chamomile-steeped cream. The mix of textures and flavors comes together in a dynamic symphony: the bright, acidic cubes of summer-ripened fruit against the calming mellowness of chamomile and gelatin layers that meld cantaloupe juice sweetness with crisp verjus.

The dessert’s structural elegance, which highlights a French variety of melon grown by a local farmer, may not immediately reveal its full complexity: Clear gelatin features a layer of clarified cantaloupe juice with encased melon slices, stacked between two layers of verjus gelatin. The melon gets compressed to intensify its flavors. Somehow, Junior managed to make Jell-O cool again — and dare I say, even sophisticated? — an example of Junior’s steady confidence that makes the restaurant an irresistible experience. — Dianne de Guzman, lead editor, Eater SF

Though people outside the Midwest may not be familiar with freshwater whitefish walleye, there it’s a classic comfort food, a staple of Lenten fish fries, state fair booths, and Lake Erie fishermen’s freezer stashes. At Rosy, chef Vinnie Cimino leans on that familiarity to help convince his customers to experience a beloved ingredient in an entirely new way. Pickled walleye cheeks ($17) have been a recurring staple — if a fleeting one — on Rosy’s Eastern European-leaning menu since the restaurant opened in February 2026. Kate’s Fish in Cleveland’s historic West Side Market provides walleye filets for sister restaurant Cordelia; when breaking down and fileting each fish, the fishmongers save the cheeks until they have a formidable stash. About every three weeks, Rosy can offer pickled walleye cheeks for around four days at a time. It’s a thoughtful move for sustainability, but also for succulence, as fish cheeks are a prized cut for their luscious texture.

Cimino conceived the dish as a nod to Jewish fish-pickling practices (for me, the results also brought to mind a tender ceviche). Seasonal vegetables are pickled with lemon — an earlier version invoked German-style potato salad, spring brought asparagus, and, when I went in June, bell pepper, carrot, and dill were in the mix. They’re then combined with the cheeks, which get a separate hot-pickling treatment involving red wine vinegar, salt, sugar, bay leaf, peppercorns, and coriander. “People really gravitate toward it,” Cimino says. “We’ve built up a great trust with our diners.” While the dish won’t be replacing fried walleye at area fish fries anytime soon, Cimino feels proud that when at Rosy, diners have been more than willing to go along with him for the ride. — MF

#6460. A Monster Solar Storm Turned a Protected Region Around Earth Into a Particle Accelerator

A solar superstorm appears to have turned a normally sheltered region near Earth into a natural particle accelerator, boosting electrons to energies capable of penetrating some satellite shielding.

Protecting spacecraft from radiation means understanding where hazardous particles can appear, especially during severe solar storms. Near Earth, an invisible boundary was thought to keep exceptionally energetic electrons out of a relatively protected region. During and after the geomagnetic superstorm of May 2024, Japan’s Arase space probe, operated by JAXA, detected large numbers of them well inside it. Some had energies exceeding three megaelectronvolts, enough to pass through some satellite shielding.

Researchers led by Nagoya University analyzed Arase’s observations to determine how these electrons appeared in a region that normally excludes them. Their evidence suggests the particles gained energy there, rather than entering it already highly energized. The distinction matters because it means a radiation hazard can develop within the supposedly protected region itself.

Earth’s magnetic field traps charged particles, including protons and electrons, in two doughnut-shaped regions called the Van Allen radiation belts. These particles can damage the hardware and electronics of spacecraft passing through the belts. At the inner edge of the outer belt, roughly three times Earth’s radius from the planet’s center, the most energetic electrons usually seem to encounter an invisible wall. Under typical conditions, the region inside this boundary is devoid of these extremely fast-moving electrons.

Scientists first identified the apparent barrier in 2014, but its origin remains incompletely understood. One possible explanation involves “plasmaspheric hiss,” low-frequency radio waves that sound like static when played through a speaker. These waves occur in Earth’s magnetosphere, the region of space dominated by its magnetic field. Human-made very-low-frequency radio transmissions used to communicate with submarines underwater may also help shape the boundary by scattering radiation-belt electrons into Earth’s atmosphere.

“One of the key questions was how these highly energetic electrons appeared inside the barrier,” said Yoshizumi Miyoshi, a professor at the Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research (ISEE) at Nagoya University and the study’s lead author. “Were they transported inward from the outer radiation belt, or were they accelerated locally within this region?”

The intense solar activity behind the May 2024 superstorm brought northern lights to Hokkaido and as far south as Japan’s Hyogo prefecture. In space, the storm dramatically eroded Earth’s plasmasphere, a region filled with relatively cool charged particles. Its outer boundary retreated unusually close to the planet, leaving the area around the usual electron barrier much less densely populated with plasma. Hotter electrons could then reach farther inward and generate natural, low-frequency electromagnetic waves known as chorus waves.

Arase detected intense chorus waves repeatedly sweeping upward in frequency. “When converted into audio, it sounds like a bird song,” Miyoshi said. These waves ripple through Earth’s magnetic field and can transfer energy to electrons when their oscillations match the electrons’ spiraling motion around magnetic field lines.

“Typically, the plasmasphere recovers on a timescale of about two days,” Miyoshi said. “During the May 2024 superstorm, however, it took approximately 4.3 to 4.7 days for the plasma density to recover to more than half of its pre-storm level in the observed region.”

The resulting low-density conditions persisted for several days, potentially allowing chorus-wave activity and the continued acceleration of electrons inside the previously impenetrable barrier.

To distinguish local acceleration from the inward movement of already energetic electrons, the researchers analyzed electron phase space density, or PSD. This quantity describes how electrons are distributed according to their energies and motion. Using measurements from multiple Arase orbits, the team examined how PSD varied with distance from Earth while accounting for changes in the electrons’ motion.

A distinct local peak developed near the usual barrier boundary and grew stronger over time. That growing peak provided evidence that electrons were gaining energy within the region, rather than simply being transported inward from the outer radiation belt.

Miyoshi said the findings, published in Geophysical Research Letters, show that even parts of near-Earth space considered relatively protected from extremely energetic electrons can experience substantial increases in radiation during severe space weather. The observations also offer insight into how Earth’s magnetosphere responds to extreme solar activity and underscore the value of continuously monitoring the space environment around the planet.

“This discovery highlights the need to understand and predict how energetic electrons behave under extreme space weather conditions,” Miyoshi said. “Such knowledge is important for assessing radiation risks to spacecraft and improving future space weather predictions.”

Reference: “Local Acceleration of Multi-MeV Electrons Inside Earth’s Impenetrable Barrier During the May 2024 Superstorm” by Y. Miyoshi, S. Kurita, A. Shinbori, K. Yamamoto, C.-W. Jun, S. Matsuda, S. Saito, R. Kataoka, D. Wang, I. Shinohara, T. Takashima, T. Mitani, N. Higashio, A. Matsuoka, Y. Kasahara, F. Tsuchiya, A. Kumamoto, T. Hori, N. Kitamura and M. Teramoto, 26 October 2026, Geophysical Research Letters. DOI: 10.1029/2026GL125879

This work was supported by the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science (JSPS) KAKENHI Grants 22K21345, 23K25925, 24K07112, 26K00765, and 26H02088.

The best time to see meteors during the Southern Taurid meteor shower is coming up soon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of autumn's best opportunities to see brilliant "fireballs" arrives overnight Wednesday and Thursday (Nov. 4-5) during the Southern Taurid meteor shower.

Although the Southern Taurids are a minor meteor shower that produces only a handful of "shooting stars" each hour, it occasionally features exceptionally bright meteors called fireballs, which can briefly light up the night sky. According to NASA, fireballs are meteors at least as bright as Venus.

The Southern Taurids are active for several weeks in fall and peak Oct. 14, but the American Meteor Society expects the "fireball swarm component" to peak around Nov. 4-5.

Meteors can streak across any part of the sky, but for this meteor shower, they appear to radiate from the constellation Taurus, which will rise in the eastern sky as night falls and climb higher as the night progresses. That makes the hours around midnight a good time to look for shooting stars. However, unlike major meteor showers such as the Perseids (which peak Aug. 12-13) and the Geminids (which peak Dec. 13-14), the Southern Taurids have a broad peak, so there's no need to be outside at an exact time.

The Southern Taurids are the first of two fireball-rich meteor showers to be visible this month. The Northern Taurids will peak overnight on Nov. 11-12, giving stargazers another chance to spot a fireball. Both meteor showers result from dust and debris left in the inner solar system by Comet 2P/Encke striking Earth's atmosphere.

Discovered in 1786, Encke is a massive comet, measuring 2.98 miles (4.8 kilometers) in diameter, according to NASA ‪—‬ around one-third the size of the object thought to have killed the nonavian dinosaurs. Encke orbits the sun every 3.3 years, one of the shortest known orbital periods of any comet in the solar system. Scientists theorize that Encke is one of many fragments of a giant comet that broke apart 20,000 to 30,000 years ago.

After the Southern and Northern Taurids, the next meteor shower will be the Leonids, which peak Nov. 17-18 and produce around 15 shooting stars per hour, and the Geminids, which peak Dec. 13-14 and can deliver up to 120 shooting stars per hour close to the peak.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

It's best to watch meteor showers with the naked eye, but a good backyard telescope will serve you well in the months to come. As the long nights of winter kick off in the Northern Hemisphere, skywatching opportunities abound — including four consecutive supermoons from Nov. 2026 to Feb. 2027.

His work appears regularly in Space.com, Forbes, New Scientist, BBC Sky at Night, Sky & Telescope, and other major science and astronomy publications. He is also the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com.

#6458. A Common Food Emulsifier Could Solve One of Rocketry’s Oldest Fuel Problems

In propulsion system design, engineers have long faced a trade-off between solid and liquid rocket fuels. Each has advantages and disadvantages, and in an effort to try to min/max the efficacy of different types of fuel, researchers have long placed an emphasis on a hybrid between solids and liquids - in other words theyâve been working with gels. Unfortunately, gels have their own sets of problems to deal with. But a new paper published by Pranay Mudaliar and Jerin John of Concordia in the journal Langmuir uses an uncommon ingredient to elegantly solve some of those problems, but which is typically used in a completely different area of human activity - lecithin.

Solid rocket boosters, like those that powered the Space Shuttle, are very stable, durable, and quick to ignite. However, they are also impossible to turn off - you have to burn through all the propellant at once.

Liquid fuel, on the other hand, is much more flexible, much like automotive fuel. Liquid fueled engines can be throttled up and down, restarted multiple times, and generally are much more controllable than their solid cousins. However, they also float and slosh around in tanks, which is a particular problem in zero-gravity environments, as that sloshing can cause vapor pockets that can break a turbopump if not filtered out beforehand. Liquids also have a tendency to leak or evaporate over long periods, making them less than ideal for multi-year journeys through the solar system.

Fraser talks about some of the difficulties of orbital refueling.

On paper, gels offer a great solution to that. While sitting in a tank, they would act like a dense solid, but can also act like a liquid when forced into a combustion chamber. However, they suffer from their own challenges, such as shelf life and temperature dependent phase changes.

The paper details a new type of fuel that uses an unexpected special ingredient. Lecithin might sound familiar, but not in the context of rocket fuel. Itâs commonly used as an emulsifier in food. Itâs commonly used to keep chocolate smooth, and salad dressing cohesive, and can be found on thousands of supermarket food labels. In the context of rocket fuel, lecithin acts simply as an organic gelling agent.

When combined with a trace amount of calcium chloride salt, lecithin molecules self-organize into microscopic worm-like structures called micelles. Chains of these form an invisible 3D mesh that can trap and hold kerosene molecules, a more traditional type of rocket fuel, in place. Lecithin also has the added advantage of being an organic compound made up of carbon and hydrogen, so it will burn right alongside the kerosene rather than acting as simply dead-weight like may other non-combustible thickening agents previously used to create gel fuels.

Scott Manley talks about the engineering behind solid rocket boosters. Credit - Scott Manley YouTube Channel

But perhaps the most interesting feature of the new fuel is a physical phenomenon known as shear thinning. When the gel is sitting under normal conditions in a tank, it holds it shape firmly like a gelatin, eliminating the sloshing features that cause so many problems in liquid-fuel rockets. However, as soon as thereâs a mechanical pressure or shear force applied - such as when the spacecraft pressurizes the fuel lines - the micellar mesh breaks apart, causing the gel to temporarily quickly collapse into a liquid.

Measurements detailed in the paper show the gelâs viscosity dropping by a factor of more than 100, creating an easily pumpable liquid that can be sprayed through injector nozzles. But when the pressure stops, the material snaps back to its rest state as a gel. There are also two other environmental stimulants that can cause this liquid transformation - if the gel is heated up to between 59 and 68 degrees C, or splashed with a small amount of ethanol. In other words, localized thermal or chemical triggers could easily intentionally force specific amounts of fuel to liquefy without requiring the bulk of the fuel to do so.

Another appealing feature of the gel, from an experimental standpoint anyway, is that itâs clear. Therefore researchers can watch it with optical high-speed cameras and lasers to analyze its structure as well as its spray patterns. And a final appealing feature is its shelf life - the gel stayed stable in a tank for over a year, with no visible signs of a phase separate that plagues many other gelatin-like fuels.

It is still a very long road from the benchtop to the launchpad though. The new fuel hasnât actually been sprayed through the high-pressure injectors that would be used on an actual rocket engine. Nor has it shown that itâs capable of withstanding the vibrations and temperature shocks that come from being launched into space. But as the Concordia researchers continue its development, this new gel is looking promising for potentially powering a future mission.

Concordia University - RESEARCH: New gel fuel could make rocket and satellite propulsion easier to control

P. Mudaliar & J. John - Rheology and Thermal Characterization of Lecithin-Based Kerosene Gels for In-Space Propulsion

UT - A New Non-toxic Propellant is Looking Promising

#6457. Smithsonian Scientists Built a Virtual Universe 1.5 Billion Light-Years Across

Scientists have recreated the universe’s first 2 billion years in a record-breaking simulation that could reveal new secrets about the Big Bang and the birth of galaxies.

Scientists have recreated the universe’s first 2 billion years in extraordinary detail using one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers. The enormous simulation, called “Lumina,” allows researchers to explore how the earliest stars and galaxies formed, how dark matter influenced their development, and how radiation transformed the young cosmos.

Developed by researchers at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, Lumina is among the largest and most sophisticated simulations of the early universe ever produced. It provides a virtual record of cosmic evolution that scientists can compare with observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Nancy Roman Space Telescope.

The research, published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, could help answer fundamental questions about what happened after the Big Bang. By recreating the interactions between ordinary matter, dark matter, and radiation, scientists can test whether their current theories accurately describe the early universe or whether surprising telescope discoveries point to physics that remains unexplained.

Astronomers have spent centuries studying the sky and developing theories to explain the origins of stars, galaxies, and the enormous structures that fill the universe. Modern supercomputers have added a powerful new approach by allowing scientists to simulate how the cosmos should develop if those theories are correct.

These simulations act as virtual laboratories. Researchers can start with conditions in the young universe, apply the known laws of physics, and calculate how matter and energy evolve over billions of years. The results can then be compared with actual telescope observations.

If the simulated universe resembles what astronomers observe, it strengthens confidence in the underlying models. But if important differences emerge, those discrepancies could reveal missing pieces in our understanding of cosmic history.

“With JWST, the early universe has become an exciting new frontier in astrophysics,” said lead author Oliver Zier, an ITC Fellow at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian. “To understand what we are seeing with this telescope, we need to translate our theories into detailed predictions. After several years of work, with plenty of ups and downs, it is incredibly rewarding to see the simulation results and watch our predictions come to life in video.”

Lumina sets a new benchmark for a particular class of cosmological simulations known as radiation hydrodynamics simulations. These models calculate how gas, dark matter, and radiation influence one another as the universe develops, making it possible to investigate the processes responsible for creating the earliest galaxies.

Dark matter is an invisible form of matter whose gravitational influence helps shape galaxies and other cosmic structures. Meanwhile, radiation from stars and other luminous objects affects the surrounding gas, changing its temperature and physical state. Capturing these interactions is essential for understanding how the early universe evolved.

Lumina follows these processes across the first 2 billion years of cosmic history, revealing how young galaxies formed and how their light gradually altered the enormous clouds of gas that filled the space between them.

The simulation’s scale is particularly remarkable. It encompasses a cube of space approximately 1.5 billion light-years along each side, representing more than 100 times the volume covered by previous comparable simulations. That enormous region is similar in scale to the volumes of the universe astronomers can investigate with today’s most advanced telescopes.

One of Lumina’s most important advances involves a process called reionization, which fundamentally changed the gas that filled the early universe.

As the first generations of luminous objects emerged, their radiation stripped electrons from atoms of hydrogen and helium, transforming much of the surrounding gas into an ionized state. This transition helped establish the conditions found throughout the universe today.

Lumina is the first simulation of its kind to model helium reionization as it happened while allowing the resulting changes to immediately affect other processes unfolding within the simulated cosmos.

“We feel incredibly fortunate to be building simulations like Lumina,” said Aaron Smith, an assistant professor of physics at the University of Texas at Dallas and an author on the paper. “For the first time, we can follow along as both hydrogen and helium changed into their modern form across such an enormous volume of the universe, while still resolving the galaxies and other luminous objects driving that transformation.”

By capturing both the large-scale evolution of cosmic gas and the smaller structures responsible for transforming it, Lumina gives scientists an unusually comprehensive view of how the young universe developed.

Building such an enormous and detailed virtual universe required extraordinary computing power.

The team used Frontier, a supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee that ranks among the fastest machines in the world. More than 15,000 graphics processing units worked together to perform the immense number of calculations needed to produce Lumina.

That processing power made it possible to simulate a much larger region of the early universe than previously comparable models while preserving enough detail to investigate individual galaxies, stars, and black holes.

This combination of scale and precision is especially valuable because cosmic evolution involves processes operating across vastly different distances. Changes occurring around individual galaxies can influence the gas between them, while the overall distribution of matter helps determine where galaxies form.

Lumina is designed to do more than recreate the past. It gives astronomers a way to investigate competing explanations for how the universe developed and to make predictions that can be tested against real observations.

Future research will examine how gas travels between galaxies, how radiation left over from the Big Bang influenced cosmic evolution, and how regions of particularly intense star formation emerged and changed over time.

As observations from JWST, Roman, and other telescopes provide increasingly detailed views of the distant universe, Lumina will help researchers interpret what they find.

By comparing the simulated cosmos with the real one, scientists may discover where existing theories succeed, where they fall short, and what new physics might be needed to explain the universe’s earliest chapters.

Reference: “Introducing the lumina project: large-volume radiation-hydrodynamic simulations of the epochs of hydrogen and helium reionization” by Oliver Zier, Aaron Smith, Xuejian Shen, Rongrong Liu, Rahul Kannan, Sonja M Koehler, Volker Springel, Rüdiger Pakmor, Mark Vogelsberger, Teodora-Elena Bulichi and Lars Hernquist, 26 October 2026, Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society. DOI: 10.1093/mnras/stag1469
