There is a constant attempt to use the weak theoretical contention that there is such a thing as dark matter that has no known physical attributes except for its supposed gravitational contributions to try to explain certain galactic and structure formation anomalies. There has been no experimental confirmation of this supposed phenomenon existing except for some manipulated mathematical models to fit the conjecture. Billions of dollars and multiple decades have been invested trying to substantiate this questionable theory and we are no further along. Here’s a shocker, Santa Clause isn’t real either. There are other methods and scientific options, backed by mathematical support to explain the incongruencies of structure formation and gravitational interaction. Dark matter theory will soon reach its unsavory conclusion, at that point real science and physics can continue. Dogma has held back scientific discovery and new scientific discoveries/approaches because of the intransigence of entrenched power brokers who were considered the experts of their time. Let’s move on.

#6456. An Artificial CORTEX to Guide Satellite Rescue Missions

The growing problem of satellites crowding one another is generating concern in the space community, for good reason. Almost 20,000 satellites orbit Earth now, and with more satellite constellations and other satellites being launched every year, Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) is starting to look like it's reaching its limit. Of particular concern are the 3,500+ plus satellites that are basically zombies. They are either completely non-functional or not sending any signals alerting other satellites to their presence.

A collision between two satellites could be catastrophic. Satellite constellations have some built-in redundancy which would help deal with the loss, but there's an additional risk. A collision could also create a debris cloud, multiplying the ongoing risk. The Kessler syndrome describes a cascade of collisions generated from debris created in a single, initial collision, that goes on to create even more collisions. It's like a feedback loop that keeps getting worse.

Somehow, this problem must be dealt with. The existing debris is one thing, but intact zombie satellites are another. These have lost the ability to communicate and warn other satellites of their presence. These can be repaired, and that's the subject of new research in Acta Astronautica. It's titled "CORTEX: An autonomous, end-to-end, convex-based framework for close-range rendezvous trajectory design and guidance with hardware testbed validation," and the lead author is Minduli Wijayatunga, a new aerospace engineering faculty member in The Grainger College of Engineering, at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

This work is all about the growing idea of Rendezvous and Proximity Operations (RPO). Spacecraft docking operations have been custom-designed solutions for individual situations, like docking with the ISS. But with thousands of zombie satellites, custom docking solutions aren't realistic.

"Rendezvous and Proximity Operations (RPO) are shifting from bespoke demonstration missions such as Northrop Grummanâs Mission Extension Vehicles, Chinaâs Tianyuanâ1, and Astroscaleâs ADRAS-J, to routine missions due to the growth of in-orbit assets and the resulting demand for inspection, servicing, assembly, and debris mitigation," the authors write. They point out that while there were only about 13,700 tracked objects in LEO in 2019, there were more than 24,000 in 2025. That's a shocking increase, and there's no signs of it slowing down.

That's forcing scientists to develop autonomous ways to deal with the overpopulation. The growing population of satellites isn't the only thing dictating an autonomous solutions. Autonomous repair is also critical because of the time delay in communications between the ground and LEO, and because satellites are best observed in and maneuvered with in windows when they're illuminated by sunlight.

âThese spacecraft must be able to track the trajectories of uncooperative objects autonomously but also make go/no-go decisions without waiting for the ground to decide,â Wijayatunga said. âSuppose your thruster fails or you encounter high-order orbital perturbations that push you away from your nominal trajectory. In those instances, how do you make those decisions?â she added.

That's what CORTEX is being designed to do.

"This paper presents CORTEX (Convex Optimization for Rendezvous Trajectory EXecution), an autonomous framework for close-range rendezvous trajectory design and guidance under sensing, actuation, and dynamics uncertainties," the authors write.

"Among RPO phases, the close-range rendezvous, where the servicer locates the docking port axes and approaches the client, is particularly safety-critical. It must satisfy strict operational constraints (e.g., keep-out zones, approach corridors, plume/line-of-sight constraints, illumination/eclipses) under limited actuation authority and imperfect relative navigation," the authors write.

Wijayatunga's PhD involved trajectory and guidance using something called convex optimization. Convex optimization is a method that lets a spacecraft approach a target using math and trajectories, not input commands. It basically solves a math problem of trajectories and thruster commands until the lone, best answer is arrived at. The answer should mean a successful docking. The idea is to reach that docking state with minimal fuel use while also following constraints like the targets no-go zones or keep-out zones. Those are places on the target satellite that might house sensitive equipment like sensors or antennae.

This work expanded to include the idea of sunlight windows. Cortex also includes options other than aborting if things went sideways. Instead of calling the docking off, CORTEX can reconsider its options. It even takes into account situations that arise where thrusters can't be fired.

âI wanted to bring that same idea into developing CORTEX and expand it, taking into consideration sunlight windows so we don't have to operate in darkness. That, and the replanning versus abort architecture, are novel in CORTEX,â Wijayatunga said.

âCORTEX has trajectory design and guidance, so if you deviate significantly from your nominal mission trajectory, it replans the trajectory and re-approaches unless you are in severe violation of your keep-out zone, in which case it returns to a passively safe orbit. It's an algorithm to recover from the unexpected. We tried instances where you're supposed to use your thrusters, but you can't for whatever reason. And CORTEX was very robust to that.â

CORTEX is being tested in a particular modelled docking scenario. It's what's called an ISAM, an In-orbit Servicing Sssembly and Manufacturing. It's designed for what will most likely be fairly typical in the future. It involves a Client Spacecraft Object (CSO) in LEO and is designed to test autonomous approach, servicing, and inspection of the CSO by a servicing spacecraft with a Guidance Navigation and Control (GNC) system for proximity operations.

Hold positions are an important part of CORTEX. In the modelled scenario, there are two of them that let the servicing spacecraft pause and re-evaluate in a fixed relative position. One is at the beginning of the fly around, and the other is at the start of the final approach. They are there to let the servicer pause during eclipses, a new idea in CORTEX.

This figure shows some aspects of CORTEX controlling a servicing spacecraft while it approaches and rendezvous with a client satellite. Blue shows the Rendezvous Sphere, orange shows the Approach Sphere, and red is the Keep Out Sphere. The approach axes is identified as CORTEX's successful solution to the docking problem. Image Credit: Wijayatunga et al. 2026. Acta Astronautica.

One way of looking at CORTEX is as a flow chart governed by four things. "The goals of CORTEX are: (i) minimize fuel and time consumption, (ii) ensure that both the fly-around and final approach occur entirely in sunlight, (iii) avoid the KOS during the fly-around phase, and (iv) satisfy the approach corridor constraint and avoid plume impingement during the final approach," the authors write.

This schematic flow-chart shows how CORTEX works. CORTEX has the ability to abort its approach if necessary, and instead of giving up, it can determine how to re-approach its client. Image Credit: Wijayatunga et al. 2026. Acta Astronautica.

In the tests, the servicing spacecraft was forced into an odd, unexpected situation and CORTEX had to deal with it. Its orbit was unexpectedly perturbed, and thruster operation was impaired, not firing when they were supposed to. Other errors were also introduced, corresponding to unexpected factors like solar storms and thrust errors.

CORTEX fared well in the tests and was able to deal with the unexpected situations in the models. "In all cases, the framework either recovered successfully while respecting safety constraints or executed a safe retreat before entering unsafe regions," the authors write.

âIn some of the hardware tests, if the servicer violates the approach corridor, it leaves the keep-out zone and retreats to a safe position and in others, the servicer is able to recover and carry on with its mission,â Wijayatunga said.

Satellite close approach and recovery isn't purely hypothetical. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAX) launched Astroscale's ADRAS-J in 2024. It successfully maneuvered within 50 meters of a typical piece of space debris, a spent rocket stage, considered to be an 'uncooperative target.' It flew around the object, catching multiple images from different angles. It used sensors and autonomous navigation to accomplish this.

Astroscale's ADRAS-J autonomous spacecraft approached a spent rocket booster, a typical piece of space debris, and captured images of it from multiple angles. It's a step toward eventual servicing of zombie satellites. Image Credit: Astroscale/JAXA.

The hallmark of the past few decades is rapidly-advancing technology. Among other things, it's led to a crowded LEO and a growing population of zombie satellites.

Maybe we'll end up using technological tools like CORTEX, enabled by AI and machine learning, to manage the problems technology has helped generate in the first place.

I’ve been skiing my entire life, venturing out for nostalgic winter weekends on the East Coast and fresh powder-chasing adventures out West. Yet somehow, the anticipation of a new ski season never gets old. Like clockwork, every winter brings a new mountain to explore, a favorite run to revisit, and plenty of reasons to start dreaming about the next snowfall. With El Niño in the conversation and ski resorts across the US gearing up for opening day, there’s no better time to get your winter plans in order.

After all, a memorable ski vacation isn’t just about finding the right mountain (though I take my terrain very seriously). It’s also about the cozy ski towns, the lively après-ski scenes, the snow-covered scenery, and of course, the splendid place to retreat to when it’s time for boots to come off. When it comes to the best ski vacation homes, there are some amenities that really do take these trips to the next level: a hot tub to soothe your muscles, an in-unit washer and dryer to freshen up base layers, a nice fireplace or firepit to cozy up around, and a kitchen for easy meals at home—especially ideal after working up a big appetite on the mountain.

Some of the best ski vacation rentals in the US are every bit as enticing as the mountains themselves. Think glass-walled chalets, design-forward A-frames, and tucked-away cabins with easy access to the lifts. From New England favorites to Western powder havens, these 11 standout stays are worth building your next ski or snowboard getaway around.

You might be hard-pressed to leave this homey adobe, but if and when you do decide to venture out, you can enjoy the two hot tubs and pool at the nearby Sundance Tennis and Swim Club.

This corner of the Rockies, roughly 45 miles south of Bozeman, Montana, is a choose-your-own-adventure kind of city. And Big Sky Resort sits at the top of many Montana itineraries for good reason—especially come wintertime. Ski days here mean inviting terrain of wide-open slopes, steep chutes, and picture-perfect runs beneath the hulking silhouette of Lone Peak. Just 10 minutes from the resort itself, this gorgeous mountain home sits on a sprawling 23 acres of land in the Lower Beehive Basin neighborhood—a backcountry ski destination in and of itself.

Inside the home, you’ll find modern cowboy country design and swanky amenities in the places that matter. For one, each of the two bedrooms feature king beds with mattress warmers to keep you cozy during winter nights. Take advantage of the big patio space for stargazing, relaxing in the hot tub, and cooking up some s’mores before heading inside for a movie night. The house can technically host up to eight guests, but it’s more ideal for families or smaller groups. Aside from the two bedrooms, the living room offers one sofa bed and two bunk beds.

When it comes to access to Utah’s renowned slopes and cool ski towns, you can’t get much better than this four-bedroom luxury penthouse. At the base of Park City Mountain, this condo boasts ski-in/ski-out access directly from the mountain's Silver Star lift. Spacious living areas, a chef’s kitchen, a hot tub, and a balcony overlooking the golf course and icy lakes create a refined on-mountain experience. The penthouse’s proximity to both ski runs and downtown makes for a seamless mix—not to mention you’ll be just a 10-minute drive to Deer Valley Resort, accessible from the condo via a free ski shuttle. With bunk beds for families and plenty of lounge areas for après-ski downtime, this Park City gem accommodates groups seeking easy access to slopes in style.

New Mexico ski trips mean a real change of scenery, and this year there’s an extra reason to have this underrated mountain range on your radar. The state is one of the southern mountain regions set to see a spike in snowfall this winter thanks to El Niño. Lucky for those who book this cabin, you’ll be just 23 miles from Taos Ski Valley, and practically at the front door of Angel Fire Resort, a hidden gem famous for wide, smooth, groomed cruiser runs and gentler slopes. (It’s a great one for beginners, featuring the renowned Heading Home 3.2-mile green run that traverses all the way from the summit to the base.)

This home is only around 100 yards away from that exact ski run, with slope access right out the door. Inside, there’s a ton of space to sprawl out and indulge in simple creature comforts: soaking in the hot tub, roasting marshmallows around the firepit on the expansive deck, and playing board games (or one of the vintage arcade games inside the den).

Mammoth is another mountain with an El Niño forecast worth keeping an eye on. Rising to 11,053 feet, the Eastern Sierra resort boasts California’s highest ski-resort summit and 3,500 acres of terrain, with plenty of room for everyone from first-timers finding their ski legs to seasoned riders chasing steeper lines. This unique mountain home near the base of the mountain takes its design cues from Japanese ryokans the host has frequented, with a soaring ceiling, dramatic dome-shaped window framing the surrounding peaks, and a loft-like den. The amenities are equally enticing: a hot tub, sauna, massage chair, optional tatami-and-futon sleeping quarters, yukatas, and an enormous shower room. Locationwise, it’s hard to beat: Canyon Lodge is less than half a mile away and walkable, while the Village and Eagle Lodge are both under a mile from the house. On especially snowy days, you may even be able to ski right down the hill and back home.

There’s something pretty splendid about staying at 8,300 feet, especially when the mountains are quite literally at your doorstep. This standalone cabin in Big Sky’s iconically named Cowboy Heaven neighborhood is a haven for folks who wish to spend their days outside, whether that means skiing straight from the deck in the winter or taking advantage of the area’s wildlife spotting in general.

It’s especially ideal for couples, small families, or friend groups, with one caveat for your crew: The second bedroom has a queen-over-twin bunk, so five adults looking for equal amounts of space may want to book elsewhere. A big plus? Big Sky’s tiny but endearing town center is less than a 10-minute drive away.

Which ski resorts in the US are on the Epic Pass?

The Epic Pass offers skiing and snowboarding at a sprawling collection of USresorts. Major destinations include Vail, Beaver Creek, Breckenridge, Keystone, Crested Butte, Park City, Heavenly, Northstar, Kirkwood, Stevens Pass, and Stowe. There are also regional and partner resorts with more limited access, so check the specific pass tier before booking a trip. Do note that blackout dates and access limits vary by pass, so read the fine print!

Which ski resorts in the US are on the Ikon Pass?

The Ikon Pass has a tempting lineup as well, especially if your winter plans involve chasing snow across the Rockies and Sierras. Its US destinations include Mammoth Mountain, Palisades Tahoe, Steamboat, Winter Park, Aspen Snowmass, Copper Mountain, Big Sky, Jackson Hole, Taos Ski Valley, Deer Valley, Alta, Snowbird, and Sun Valley. Out east, you can head to Killington, Sugarbush, Stratton, Loon Mountain, Sugarloaf, or Sunday River.

Where is El Niño predicted to bring snowfall this season?

For the 2026-27 season, a strong El Niño is shaping the forecast, with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) expecting wetter-than-average conditions across the southern US, from California and the Southwest through the Southeast, as well as along the East Coast. This could mean more opportunities for snowfall in higher-elevation ski destinations, particularly when temperatures cooperate.

However, wetter doesn't automatically mean snowier: NOAA also expects warmer-than-average conditions across much of the West and northern US Seasonal outlooks predict precipitation patterns, not specific snowfall totals, so keep an eye on shorter-range forecasts before planning a powder chase.

#6454. The 2026 Best New Bakeries in America

Precision pastries are sweeping the nation. These bakers are leading the charge.

If there’s one thing we’ve noticed over the past several years, it’s how much bakeries have stepped up their game.

We wanted to recognize these achievements by adding this category to the 2026 Eater Awards, celebrating five examples of excellence in pastry, bread, and sweets across the country. Some embody a personal expression of a baker’s identity, while others push the envelope beyond expected flavor combinations; all excel at a time when “little treat” culture is at its peak. — Missy Frederick, editorial director

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

If one new place in Chicago needs no further hype, it is Bad Butter. You’ll know you’re there when you spot the line cascading out of the whitewashed storefront along West Cortland Street, a queue that doesn’t let up until the pastry case is empty. Formerly a head baker at Soho House Chicago, Dan Koester was stuck at home like the rest of us in 2020, handing off excess home-baked sourdough loaves to friends and family and making some available for free pickup. After he was officially laid off that summer, he launched his own online bakery business, earning a massive following along the way.

One residency at the Emily Hotel later, Koester debuted his Bucktown bakery, demonstrating the full range of his skill. Still warm, charred, and dimpled flats of focaccia showered with scallion furikake rest on its shelves. Impossibly crisp and exquisitely laminated twice-baked almond croissants burst with subtle, aromatic almond paste. A spicy harissa monkey bread with a cloudlike texture is cooled by a pool of creamy labneh drizzled with silky olive oil.

The bakery’s menu has breadth and also manages to arc with the season. Customers snake along the floor waiting their turn to claim a towering cruffin, dusted in fine grains of sugar and piped full of ginger plum jam, or a seasonal tart piled with plump, lacquered blueberries. A pastry box filled with these confections is well worth the wait. — Brenna Houck, dining editorial manager

Born as an underground dinner party operated out of Karla Subero Pittol’s Echo Park garage, Chainsaw finally got its own digs in November 2025 in the form of a lively cafe in Melrose Hill, an unquestionably gentrifying neighborhood that has become home to some of Los Angeles’s best independent restaurants. At the cafe, Subero Pittol channels her Venezuelan heritage through a menu of arepas plump with beans, limey guasacaca, and cheese; a Venezuelan hot dog (“perro caliente”) buoyed by an acidic slaw; and her bracingly tart passionfruit-lime icebox pie, which commands a cult following all its own.

Stepping into Chainsaw feels like you could be in Subero Pittol’s own kitchen as she greets regulars and newcomers as if they are old friends. Customers study a handwritten menu that changes daily — it doesn’t help to come in too attached to any one dish (save the ever-present icebox pie) when you may get tempted by another. The cafe’s impact on Los Angeles feels clear in the near-constant crowds that hover outside, reading their newspapers over an espresso or tucking into the latest of Subero Pittol’s ideas, such as a full English breakfast served for a single day. In a city lacking in untamed Venezuelan cooking, Chainsaw offers a home for Subero Pittol to celebrate the cuisine in a way that feels distinctly Los Angeles. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest

With both Afghan and Latin American influences, Diljān gives New Yorkers a bakery with a point of view and innumerable reasons to become a regular. Ali Zaman and Mohamed Ghiasi, owners of Astoria’s Little Flower Cafe, teamed up with Bryan Ford, Honduran American baker and cookbook author, to conceptualize the bakery, now perched on a corner near Atlantic Avenue in Brooklyn Heights.

Their combined talent makes for some of the city’s most compelling baked goods. For the Saffron Shah, laminated pastry holds delicate saffron cream in the shape of a crescent, an important Islamic symbol. Halwa tops the sticky bun, while a swirl of samosa pastry wraps halal lamb under a dusting of powdered sugar. Don’t miss the enormous Afghan flatbread crowned by toppings such as halal beef bacon with scallions or sour cherry cream cheese. The team has also branched into pizzas topped with cheese and Afghan cumin, kofta kebabs, or beef pepperoni. Look for specials like the flan with cardamom-poached apricots and conchas stuffed with firni, a rice pudding. — Nadia Chaudhury, deputy editor, Eater New York

San Francisco’s pastry game is stronger and more competitive than ever before, and Parachute Bakery steps to the forefront of a crowded field with a mix of patisserie standards and seasonal standouts. At his Ferry Building bakery, pastry chef Nasir Armar marries his fine dining training, honed at Michelin-starred Sorrel and Saison, with flavors that make everyone sit up and take notice (and snap a food photo or two for their socials).

Vegetables and savory complements are given their own footing on the menu. Stalks of grilled asparagus shine in a baton-shaped croissant shell, with fennel jam, sheep’s milk ricotta, and ramp pesto alongside them; one brief, bordering-on-gimmicky croissant got piped with clam chowder, a reference to the soup in a bread bowl famously served on the city’s wharf. Even potato-laden samosas and bright tomato shakshuka get interpreted into pastry form. Parachute succeeds with its experimental vision, a hype well-earned that leaves fans clamoring for what they’ll come up with next. — Dianne de Guzman, editor, Eater SF

#6453. Hidden Brain Signals Could Predict Alzheimer’s Years Before Symptoms Appear

Subtle differences in brain activity may reveal who is most vulnerable to Alzheimer’s disease and who could remain mentally sharp well into old age.

Distinct patterns of brain activity may predict Alzheimer’s disease years before memory problems or hallmark brain changes appear. Stanford Medicine researchers have developed a scoring system that identifies people at greater risk of cognitive decline while also recognizing those whose brains show unusual resilience to aging.

The study, published November 4 in Science Advances, found that these patterns could predict future cognitive decline more effectively than several established risk indicators, including genetics and Alzheimer’s biomarkers.

Researchers analyzed resting-state functional MRI scans from 180 “super agers,” adults aged 75 and older with memory abilities comparable to those of typical 45-year-olds, and 110 similarly aged people diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease.

“Normal, cognitively unimpaired individuals are pretty heterogeneous in terms of their biological abnormalities,” said Yu Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford Medicine. “Simply comparing super agers with such a heterogeneous population makes it challenging to define what is critical in terms of resilient or vulnerable brain patterns.”

The team identified distinct patterns of activity across brain networks and developed the Alzheimer’s resilience-vulnerability connectome (ARC) score. The system distinguished super agers from people with Alzheimer’s with approximately 85% accuracy.

The researchers tested the ARC score in more than 1,300 cognitively healthy adults aged 55 to 70. Although participants initially showed no clear differences in cognitive performance, their brain activity patterns predicted different outcomes over follow-up periods extending as long as 12 years.

People with more Alzheimer’s-like activity experienced faster cognitive decline and were more likely to develop amyloid-beta plaques or receive an Alzheimer’s diagnosis. Those with super-ager-like patterns generally maintained stronger cognitive abilities.

“We used the ARC score to make a prediction of how likely this patient will convert into mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer’s disease,” said Kanhao (Alex) Zhao, PhD, a Stanford postdoctoral scholar and lead author.

“We want to address a major challenge in the Alzheimer’s field nowadays — most studies are looking at well-known Alzheimer’s disease biomarkers, such as amyloid-beta or tau. But those are observable at relatively late stages of the disease,” Zhang said. “What we really care about is defining early markers that can detect earlier signs of cognitive decline and potentially help us deliver timely interventions to people.”

The ARC score performed as well as or better than existing biomarkers at predicting progression toward Alzheimer’s, while offering information at an earlier stage. Combining the score with traditional biomarkers improved predictions further.

“We compared the ARC score with existing biomarkers in predicting people converting to Alzheimer’s disease,” Zhao said. “Our model shows comparable or better prediction ability, and it can do so at an earlier time point. And if we combine our score with the existing biomarkers, the prediction performance improves.”

The researchers also found a relationship between ARC scores and brain age, a broader measure of aging derived from functional MRI data.

“I’m excited we established a signature that can help us better understand the difference between people who can maintain excellent cognitive performance and people who show cognitive decline,” Zhang said.

ARC scores are not diagnostic, and they do not determine a person’s future. Brain activity can change with aging, injuries, and neuropsychiatric conditions. Researchers hope that targeted interventions might eventually shift vulnerable brain patterns toward greater resilience.

Potential approaches include cognitive training and transcranial magnetic stimulation, which uses magnetic pulses to influence brain activity. However, these interventions have not been shown to prevent cognitive decline by changing ARC patterns.

“There are two main components: One is to know which part of the brain to target, the other is how we should change it,” Zhang said. “That’s why identifying the super-ager brain resilience pattern is a critical component — so we know what a good pattern should be.”

Zhang’s team is planning a trial to examine whether cognitive training can alter ARC scores.

“But the critical part is that we have to intervene at an early stage,” Zhang said. “That’s why we focus on the cognitively unimpaired population to identify super-ager-like versus Alzheimer’s-like individuals. If we can precisely identify such as early indicator, I’m optimistic that we can reverse or prevent this process through advanced intervention technologies.”

Reference: “A functional connectome identifies vulnerability to cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s disease progression” by Kanhao Zhao, Hua Xie, Gregory A. Fonzo, Nancy B. Carlisle, Tovia Jacobs, Ricardo S. Osorio, Arpana Church, Feng Vankee Lin, Yu Zhang and Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, 4 November 2026, Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aed9351

The study received funding from the National Institutes of Health (grants R21AG080425, R01MH129694 and R01AG081768), a joint Rosenkranz Foundation-Knight Initiative program, an Alzheimer’s Association grant and a Lehigh University CORE grant.

#6452. A Perseverance Experiment Could Help Astronauts Prepare for Dust Storms on Mars

Martian dust is a major hurdle for human missions to Mars. Like Moon dust, its fine size and electrostatically charged nature allow it to stick to spacesuits, metal, and just about any other surface they come into contact with. Dust storms are also common on Mars, ranging from small whirlwinds that happen daily to global dust storms that occur once every 3 Martian years (~5.5 Earth years) and envelop the entire planet. Due to the low density of Mars' atmosphere, these storms don't generate much physical force.

The danger lies in how the dust plays havoc with instruments, machine parts, and astronaut health and safety. Given how well it adheres to surfaces, Apollo astronauts found that lunar dust accompanied them back into their landing modules, degrading mechanical joints and seals and causing respiratory problems. A recent study led by Washington University in St. Louis (WashU) highlights the need, using data from NASA's Perseverance rover, for sufficient astronaut training to prepare for the Martian environment.

Assistant Professor Scott VanBommel led the research effort along with staff scientist Abigail Knight, both of whom are fellows of the McDonnell Center for the Space Sciences (MCSS). They and their colleagues were joined by an international team of scientists from the U.S., Canada, Australia, and Europe, the MIT Haystack Observatory, Research Institutes of Sweden, the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), the Space Science Institute (SCI), the Astromaterials Research and Exploration Science (ARES) division at the NASA Johnson Space Center, and NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

A very large Martian dust devil. This one reached 20 km high. Image Credit: NASA/JPL/University of Arizona

In addition to its array of sensors, cameras, drilling equipment, and sample cache, Perseverance also carries small swatches of spacesuit material that are constantly exposed to Mars' atmosphere. Using data acquired by the rover's Planetary Instrument for X-ray Lithochemistry (PIXL), the team examined the swatches for signs of wear and tear. They also applied a method developed by VanBommel to estimate the size of each particle in the PIXL data, providing the first direct characterization of fine (â²2.5 Âµm) and ultrafine particles (â²0.1 Âµm).

Their analysis found that the swatches showed little visible wear after 1,645 Martian days (sols) of exposure, largely because the particles observed were much smoother than the jagged grains found on the Moon. In summary, the results showed that Martian dust may be less likely to be abrasive to equipment or harmful to astronaut health than lunar regolith. The PIXL data also allowed the team to analyze the chemical composition of the particles that had caked the swatches.

From this, the team confirmed the presence of perchlorates and other toxins, as well as high levels of sulfur, iron, and silica in the dust grains. In addition, Martian dust can be exceptionally fine, with some ultrafine particles measuring as little as 100 nanometers (nm) in diameter. On Earth, ultrafine particles typically come in the form of smoke and air pollution, which can cause significant health problems because they can sink deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. With Martian dust carrying perchlorates and other toxins, the health risk is magnified.

There's also the way it is electrostatically charged like its lunar counterpart. "The electrostatic properties of Martian dust are likely causing it to preferentially adhere to some surfaces," Knight added, who helped conceptualize and conduct the analysis while a Ph.D. student at the MCSS. So while Martian dust may be less abrasive to surfaces and irritating to the lungs, it poses a hazard because of its toxicity and how easily it can be tracked into habitats where astronauts will not have the protection of a spacesuit.

Mars Perseverance rover - PIXL studies a rock (artist concept). Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

These considerations must be taken into account when mission planners are designing space suits and infrastructure for Mars. As astronauts will be passing in and out of vehicles and habitats regularly, small amounts of dust will likely be introduced that (if left unchecked) will constitute a mounting health hazard. Fortunately, the level of health risk largely depends on dose and duration. With proper mitigation strategies, both can be limited to a point where they do not pose a significant threat.

The particles in the Martian atmosphere have been blowing in the wind for potentially billions of years, so they tend to be well-rounded, like pebbles in a river. We've been operating rovers on the surface of Mars continuously for more than 20 years at this point. We know that dust will be a challenge, but it's something we can prepare for and overcome.

These results highlight the effectiveness of rover missions in advancing human spaceflight and the exploration of extraterrestrial bodies. In addition to providing immense insights into the geological history and conditions on Mars, they've also served as test beds for technologies that will be crucial to human exploration when it begins.

Matt Williams is a space journalist, science communicator, and author with several published titles and studies. Researchers have created a self-charging toothbrush that helps fight the bacteria linked to cavities and gum disease while preventing plaque buildup.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A toothbrush that generates its own electricity with every stroke could offer a new way to fight the microbes behind cavities and gum disease.

Conventional toothbrushes rely on physical scrubbing to remove plaque from teeth and gums. But even after a thorough brush, some bacteria remain and begin rebuilding plaque. To solve that problem, researchers have developed a self-powered toothbrush that converts the friction of brushing into an electrical charge. That electricity is intended to zap the plaque-promoting bacteria and keep them from colonizing teeth.

"It's great to have new approaches that actually enhance the effect of mechanical cleaning," said Nicholas Jakubovics, an oral microbiologist at Newcastle University in the U.K. who was not involved in the study. "The idea that the toothbrush surface itself is actively doing something is really interesting."

The experimental brush has bristles made from polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), a plastic that generates electricity when bent; these types of energy-producing materials are called piezoelectric. As the bristles flex during brushing, they produce an electrical charge that then triggers chemical reactions in saliva and water. These reactions release reactive oxygen species (ROS), which are highly reactive molecules that can damage bacterial cells.

Even when the bristles are not being used to brush, they carry a faint surface charge that helps prevent bacteria from clinging to the brush head when the toothbrush isn't in use, the team reported Wednesday (Nov. 4) in the journal Science Advances.

In laboratory tests where the toothbrush was used on isolated germs, its electrified bristles killed more than half of the Streptococcus mutans bacteria present. These microbes contribute to tooth decay. By comparison, nylon bristles killed just 9% of the bacteria. They also reduced levels of Porphyromonas gingivalis, a bacterium linked to gum disease, by up to 78%, while nylon brushes reduced them by less than 8%.

When the researchers added an antioxidant — a compound that neutralizes ROS — the new toothbrush's antibacterial effect largely disappeared, highlighting that the ROS are likely the key to its effects.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team also found that the activity of certain genes in both S. mutans and P. gingivalis fell after exposure to the electrified bristles. These genes are involved in making ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters — molecular pumps that help shuttle essential nutrients across bacterial cell membranes. The researchers suspect that disrupting this machinery makes it harder for these microbes to survive and cling to teeth.

The new toothbrush still needs to be tested in further safety trials.

But Jakubovics was not convinced by that part of the team's explanation. "ABC transporters transport all sorts of different things," he said, adding that the findings did not clearly show how changes in these genes affected the bacteria.

The researchers also tested the new brush against plaque biofilms — hardy communities of bacteria that stick together and cling to tooth surfaces. For the experiment, they grew human dental plaque on cow tooth enamel and found that the brush removed more than 99% of the biofilm, outperforming a regular nylon brush.

Finally, the team moved to humans, putting the brush to the test in 115 adults with gum inflammation or tooth decay. These study participants were randomly assigned to use either the new toothbrushes or traditional nylon-bristled brushes twice a day for three months. (The study didn't note whether participants noticed a difference in sensation when using the electrified brushes.)

By the end of the trial, the participants who used the electrified bristles had less plaque, less gum inflammation and less bleeding than the participants who used ordinary brushes. Plaque samples also showed that the people who used electrified brushes had lower levels of bacteria associated with oral disease and higher levels of beneficial bacteria, which have previously been reported to suppress harmful oral bacteria and support oral health.

The researchers think that the disease-linked bacteria may have relatively fragile cell membranes, making them more vulnerable to damage from ROS than the beneficial bacteria. That's a theory that requires further study, though, so it's not completely clear how selective the brush is against plaque-causing bacteria.

In a test of the toothbrush's durability, the PVDF bristles retained their structure and electrical properties over three months of simulated use. Lab-grown mouse cells repeatedly exposed to brush material showed no signs of damage, and brushing on cow tooth enamel did not increase surface roughness. However, these tests cannot establish whether repeated use of these brushes is safe for humans.

"We would want to make sure that it is safe on the tissues for long-term use," Jakubovics said. He noted that, in lab tests, bacteria are grown directly on the bristles and exposed to their electricity for hours, "whereas in reality, in the mouth, your bristle is only in contact with the tooth or oral tissue for a very short time."

The trial with humans provides some insight into how the brush works in real life, but it was relatively small. Larger studies will be needed to find out whether the toothbrush offers a meaningful advantage over conventional brushes. For now, Jakubovics sees the recent study as just a proof of concept; more information and more convincing clinical data are still needed, he emphasized.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6450. Mars' Molten Heart is Long Gone, but Some Magma Chambers May Persist

We'll never stop being fascinated by Mars. It's kind of like a failed Earth. It appears as if billions of years ago Mars was warm, wet, and habitable. That ended when its interior cooled and its geodynamo failed.

When its geodynamo failed, its magnetic shield failed. The full force of the Sun bore down on the unfortunate planet, and its warming atmosphere was lost to space.

The loss of atmosphere wasn't the only change. Mars had a powerful volcanic past, and the prominent volcanoes in Tharsis Montes prove that. But the planet is largely believed to have left its volcanic past behind as a consequence of cooling.

But there's growing evidence that the planet isn't totally dormant. Recent evidence from missions like InSight and the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter suggest some ongoing activity. InSight detected more than 1300 Marsquakes, and the Trace Gas Orbiter detected hydrochloric acid.

Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is a highly corrosive acid with multiple natural sources, including atmospheric ones. The ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) collected widespread observations of HCl in Mars' atmosphere at parts-per-billion levels, but initially, it was only detected during perihelion. The HCl detections were attributed to aerosol-atmospheric sources driven by greater warmth from the Sun, a naturally-occurring, seasonal pattern.

But new research in Science Advances shows that not all of the TGO's HCl detections can be traced to perihelion. It's titled "Enigmatic HCl detections as a potential signature of igneous activity on Mars." The lead author is Alexander Trokhimovskiy from the Space Research Institute at the Russian Academy of Sciences.

This Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) image shows Alba Mons near the top, with the three Tharsis Montes volcanoes below it, and the massive Olympus Mons to their northwest. Though not as tall as Olympus Mons, Alba Mons is larger by area. The new HCl detections are curiously close to Alba Mons. Image Credit: NASA/JPL/GSFC

The authors acknowledge that Mars is believed to be volcanically dormant, and that Marsquakes and other evidence of more recent volcanic activity is accumulating. However, there's no clear understanding of Mars' modern activity. For instance, many of the InSight lander's detections were attributed to meteorites.

If we were to witness an actual eruption, and the gases that go with it, a new understanding of Mar's interior would arise. But that hasn't happened, and we have to rely on less obvious evidence for Mars' internal state.

"While sulfur dioxide, so far undetected, could testify to ongoing eruptive activity, evidence of active magma chambers may be better identified by seepage of halogen gases, such as hydrogen chloride (HCl)," the authors write. "Here, we report HCl detections during the cold aphelion season that are isolated in the Alba Mons region." Could these new HCl detections be a window into Mars' interior?

Olympus Mons is known as the largest volcano and the tallest mountain in the Solar System. But Alba Mons is actually the largest volcano by surface area. Like Olympus Mons, it's also in the Tharsis region. (And neither are part of Tharsis Montes, the iconic row of three volcanoes). Alba Mons' volcanic flows reach further than 1300 km from its central summit. One of Alba Mons most significant features is its enormous system of fractures. For multiple reasons, detecting HCl over Alba Mons is intriguing.

"Strongly localized in space and time, aphelion HCl detections, amidst an otherwise absence of HCl at that season on Mars, exhibit marked contrast with prolonged and widespread detections at perihelion," the authors write.

âDetections of HCl at low altitudes, unexplained by observed atmospheric state and models, together with the geological context of the region, hint at an igneous origin of this gas,â Trokhimovskiy et al. write. These most recent HCl directions were in 2025.

This figure show HCl detections by the Trace Gas Orbiter. Blue ones represent perihelion detections, which can be explained by seasonal warming and atmospheric interactions driven by the Sun. Red ones are more enigmatic. They could come from tiny fissures near Alba Mons, almost directly under the detections. Image Credit: Alexander Trokhimovskiy et al. , Enigmatic HCl detections as a potential signature of igneous activity on Mars. Sci. Adv.12, eaeb9422(2026).

The HCl detections alone may not be enough to oveturn the idea that Mars is dormant. As the authors say, they're just a hint. But there's more. "We also identify fresh and narrow (<1 meter) fissures in this area, which we interpret to be potential HCl pathways rooted into magmatic bodies at depth," the researchers explain.

"These structures have not been identified on Mars in earlier works. For instance, systematic geomorphologic mapping of the northern hemisphere did not consider these landforms," the authors explain.

These panels shows some of the important points in the research. (A) shows Alba Mons and the HCl aphelion detections in yellow. (B) is a CASSIS image from the TGO showing a fractured ridge, while (C) and (D) are HiRISE images from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter showing smaller fissures the researchers identify as potential HCl sources. (E) and (F) are geological models that can explain HCl is seeping from these fissures. Image Credit: Alexander Trokhimovskiy et al. , Enigmatic HCl detections as a potential signature of igneous activity on Mars. Sci. Adv.12, eaeb9422(2026).

The researchers calculated the seepage rate necessary to account for the HCl abundance in the aphelion detections. They compared it to the perihelion detections, and included the expected lifetime for HCl to persist in the Martian atmosphere. Their work rules out atmospheric-aerosol interactions as the source for the HCl detected during aphelion. But it also rules out those same interactions for the source of HCl detected during perihelion. That makes sense, since non-seasonal seepage from magma chambers would be happening no matter the season.

"Thus, perihelion HCl is unlikely to be directly volcanic in origin," they write. There could still be a link between igneous HCl and perihelion HCl. "However, a connection between igneous and seasonal HCl may still exist via a mechanism complementary to heterogeneous production," the authors write.

Planets are complicated, as we Earthlings know. Multiple interrelated factors contribute to the whole, and everything changes over time. This work further emphasizes how that's true, even on so-called dormant Mars. "The overall cycle of hydrogen chloride includes irreversible sinks," the authors write, and sinks have to be included in any modelling or understanding of Mars.

"Introducing a volcanic source of HCl, we can propose that a fraction of the perihelion HCl observed in the Martian atmosphere is ultimately of igneous origin," the researchers explain. "Localized igneous sources may therefore act as continuous primary contributors of chlorine, which is subsequently redistributed between atmospheric and surface reservoirs."

But despite the complicated picture of seasonality and surface sinks, their conclusion is clear: "Our results are best explained by ongoing igneous processes in the Martian interior."

#6449. A New Approach Could Eliminate “Zombie” Cancer Cells That Survive Chemotherapy

Some cancer cells survive chemotherapy by blocking their own self-destruct system, but researchers have found a way to switch it back on and kill those cells.

Chemotherapy can leave behind cancer cells that have stopped dividing but remain alive and capable of helping a tumor recover. These survivors can draw support from an unexpected source, the immune system, by activating responses that normally help the body repair damaged tissue.

This “zombie-like state,” called “premature senescence,” involves dramatic changes. Within a few days of exposure to chemotherapy, senescent cells can grow to almost ten times the size of a normal cell and increase the activity of genes associated with wound healing. Their ability to release inflammatory mediators, molecules that attract immune cells, also increases greatly.

The danger lies in the range of jobs the immune system performs. Alongside protecting against infection, it coordinates the repair and replacement of damaged tissue. During wound healing, it stimulates cell division to replace cells lost through injury and triggers the growth of blood vessels that deliver extra oxygen and nutrients. Normally, this complex, carefully coordinated process ensures that new cells appear only where and when they are needed.

Cancers can exploit those repair functions by masquerading as damaged tissue. Instead of destroying malignant cells, the immune system can then help them divide and obtain more oxygen and nutrients. That behavior has led cancers to be described as “wounds that do not heal,” although how they activate the immune system’s wound-healing capabilities remains poorly understood.

Research newly published in Science Advances identifies a mechanism that helps cancer cells survive chemotherapy and enter senescence. Scientists at the Smurfit Institute of Genetics at Trinity College Dublin found that molecules called Inhibitor of Apoptosis Proteins, or IAPs, can protect tumor cells from the killing effects of commonly used chemotherapy drugs. The team was led by Professor Seamus Martin, Smurfit Professor of Medical Genetics, and Dr. Gokhan Gunay, a postdoctoral research fellow.

The researchers found that DNA damage caused by chemotherapy switched on molecules called “Death Receptors,” which can trigger a cell’s self-destruct program. IAPs neutralized their cell-killing effects. That protection allowed surviving tumor cells to enter senescence, where they could coordinate wound-healing responses that benefit the tumor and help it recover after treatment.

But the cells’ continued survival also depended heavily on IAPs, creating a vulnerability. In the study, compounds called IAP antagonists neutralized these proteins and reactivated the Death Receptor self-destruct program, selectively eliminating the senescent cells. The same proteins that helped the cells escape chemotherapy thus remained essential to keeping them alive afterward.

Senescent cells are also relevant beyond cancer treatment. They accumulate in tissues as people age, and that buildup is thought to contribute to age-related inflammation and declining normal function in many tissues.

For cancer treatment, the findings identify both an escape mechanism and a possible way to target the cells that use it. Tumors that evade chemotherapy remain a major challenge for clinicians, and improved treatments could offer patients better survival and quality of life.

Professor Martin said, “Discovering how tumors can evade the cell-killing effects of chemotherapy and enter senescence is an important and challenging problem.

“These new findings suggest ways in which we may be able to lower the defenses of tumors by neutralizing IAPs after the delivery of chemotherapeutic drugs, which should block their entry to senescence and kill more cells of the tumor.”

Reference: “Death receptors regulate entry to therapy-induced senescence and orchestrate addiction to IAPs” by Gokhan Gunay, Seren Hamsici, Vaishnavi Venugopalan, Aoife Costigan, Melanie Fritsch, Aislinn Gallagher Aldave, Anne Huber, Brianna Fernandez, Hande Efe-Cicek, Pavel Davidovich, Pavitha Parathan, Akash Srivaths, Natalie Hudson, Eleanor Noone, Jeffrey O’Callaghan, Lisa A. Mielke, Sarah L. Doyle, Sabrina L. Spencer, Matthew Campbell, Conor J. Kearney, Hamid Kashkar and Seamus J. Martin, 23 October 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aed4541

Work in The Martin laboratory at Trinity is supported by the European Research Council (Project DESTRESS) and Research Ireland.

#6448. Using Vibrations and AI, Future Robotic Missions Could Handle Buried Rocks Autonomously

Knowing a planet's surface and subsurface structure is vital when planning robotic and crewed missions to explore it. Before landers, rovers, or crew modules reach the surface, astronauts and mission controllers need to know what they will be landing on. For rovers with a limited energy budget, it's also crucial that they can determine how far rough, rocky terrain extends beneath the surface. That way, they won't waste time and energy trying to clear obstacles they can't possibly move.

In short, scientists and astronauts need to know what's on a planet's surface (and beneath it) before they attempt to land there and conduct science operations. Thanks to a team from Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University (Virginia Tech), scientists could soon have a new set of tools that will allow robotic missions to make these determinations autonomously. These AI-powered tools measure vibrations in surface terrain to determine what lies beneath and how deep structures extend.

The study was led by Yiyan Ruan, a Ph.D. candidate at Virginia Tech, and Erik Komendera, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering (and Ruan's advisor) who once worked as a researcher at NASA's Langley Research Center. The paper detailing their findings was published in IEEE Sensors Journal. The tools they have developed could have profound applications for both space exploration and life on Earth.

View generated from the digital terrain model and the nadir and color channels of the High Resolution Stereo Camera on ESA's Mars Express. Credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin

As they indicate in their paper, estimating the burial depth of partially embedded rocks is a key capability for energy-limited robotic excavation. When obstacles like rock formations are in the way, mission teams need to know how deep the rock extends so they can decide whether to remove the obstacle or avoid it. Ruan and Komendera's solution leverages AI to interpret vibrational data, allowing robots to make those decisions autonomously. As Komendera said in a Virginia Tech press release:

For as long as humans have built things on Earth, we have had to deal with large and heavy obstacles that cannot simply be ignored or scooped out of the way without careful planning. It's easy enough for us to just look at rocks and make some quick, testable judgments. Is this rock resting or partially buried? Can I move this alone or do I need help and tools? But what if robots need to do this? How can robots make those judgments? Now we have an answer.

To test their approach, their team buried 18 concrete blocks of different shapes and sizes in sand at different depths. They then struck the exposed portions of the blocks with an instrumented hammer and remotely measured the vibrations using a device known as a Laser Doppler Vibrometer (LDV). The results were then input into a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), a type of neural network that learns to identify complex, non-linear patterns from data.

Their MLP mapped 11 measurable features to identify the relationship between impulse excitation, exposed rock geometry, and burial depth. Given the range of factors to consider, the task was rather complex. But by teaching their AI to account for them, Ruan and Komendera created models that could reliably determine the blocks' depth.

When the future rovers set down on Mars, they could determine rock depth and obstacle clearance autonomously. Credit: NASA/JPL

"Estimating how deep a rock is buried using vibrations can be tricky," said Ruan. "The feedback is affected by the rock's geometry and the way the soil holds it. By carefully selecting features from vibration measurements and exposed geometry, we were able to produce reliable data using a compact neural network with just two hidden layers."

These models could help robotic missions excavate subsurface rocks, caches of water ice, and remove obstacles along their travel routes. In the meantime, the team plans to keep building datasets and testing their approach for applications on Earth, such as analyzing construction sites and natural disasters to locate where potentially hazardous materials are buried. They could also be used to study unstable rock formations and underground caverns, assisting with resource and construction planning, and advancing exploration of Earth's subsurface.

Further Reading: Virginia Tech, IEEE Sensors Journal

#6447. Scientists Discover a Hidden Weakness in Prostate Cancer That Could Transform Treatment

A newly identified vulnerability in a cancer-driving protein could pave the way for a different approach to treating prostate cancer.

Researchers at the University of Michigan have identified a potential way to target a protein that helps drive prostate cancer but has long been considered beyond the reach of drugs. Their experimental compound, PBITE-1, interfered with the protein’s cancer-promoting activity in laboratory models, offering a possible starting point for more targeted treatments.

The protein, known as ERG, becomes abnormally active when two genes, TMPRSS2 and ERG, fuse together. This genetic rearrangement occurs in roughly half of prostate cancer cases among patients of European ancestry and promotes tumor cell growth and migration.

For years, ERG has been considered “undruggable” because it appeared to lack the molecular pockets where medications typically attach. In the new study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, researchers discovered an accessible pocket in a region called the PNT domain, which helps regulate ERG’s interactions with other proteins.

After screening more than 1,600 compounds, the team identified a promising molecule and refined it into PBITE-1. In experiments involving prostate cancer cell lines and laboratory models of human and mouse prostate tissue, the compound inhibited ERG activity, triggered cancer cell death, and reduced the ability of cancer cells to invade surrounding tissue.

“Although we were the first to identify the gene fusion as a driver of prostate cancer, it was challenging to find a drug target for ERG,” said Arul Chinnaiyan, M.D., Ph.D., S.P. Hicks Professor of Pathology and member of the Rogel Cancer Center.

Most existing prostate cancer therapies focus on androgen receptors, proteins that respond to hormones such as testosterone. These receptors can activate the TMPRSS2-ERG fusion, helping fuel tumor growth. Drugs that block androgen signaling can slow the disease, but tumors often develop resistance, and treatment can cause side effects that affect quality of life.

Targeting ERG directly could provide an alternative approach for patients whose tumors carry the gene fusion, rather than relying exclusively on treatments that interfere with hormone signaling.

“This work shows that instead of treating all prostate cancer as one disease, we have the potential to personalize therapy for subtypes of prostate cancer.”

PBITE-1 remains an experimental research tool, and its effects have not been established in patients. Further research will be needed to determine whether compounds targeting ERG can be developed into safe and effective medicines.

“Although it is unlikely that PBITE-1 is ready to become a drug any time soon, this study shows that ERG is a druggable target,” Chinnaiyan said.

“It is exciting that we now have a path forward to target ERG in prostate cancer.”

Reference: “A ligandable PNT domain establishes ERG as a directly targetable oncogenic driver in prostate cancer” by Xiaoju Wang, Wenyan Liu, Jiehao Yang, Jean Ching-Yi Tien, Yu Chang, Rahul Mannan, Somnath Mahapatra, Yang Zhou, Lihao Gan, Xuhong Cao, Jiayi Zhou, Yuping Zhang, Sharpkate Shaker, Yichao Huang, Hang Qiao, Rudana Hamadeh, Grafton Ervine, Cynthia Wang, Fengyun Su, Rui Wang, Lanbo Xiao, Raghunath Ranga Sudharshan, Arvind Rao, Zaneta Nikolovska-Coleska, Cole Stephens, Lifeng Pan, James J. Chou, Debashish Sahu, Jeanne Stuckey, Zhen Wang, Ke Ding and Arul M. Chinnaiyan, 7 July 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2537437123
