#6436. Dinosaurs May Have Eaten Far More Fruit Than Scientists Ever Thought

An exceptionally preserved 74-million-year-old forest in New Mexico is revealing unexpected details about ancient plant life.

Dinosaurs may have been eating a much wider variety of fruits than scientists once believed. Fossils from a 74-million-year-old forest in New Mexico show that some flowering plants were already producing surprisingly large fruits millions of years before the asteroid impact that ended the age of non-avian dinosaurs.

The findings, published in the journal Science, challenge the longstanding theory that larger fruits and more complex seed dispersal strategies evolved primarily after the extinction event 66 million years ago. They also suggest that dinosaurs and other prehistoric animals may have helped spread the seeds of flowering plants much earlier than previously thought.

The research centers on an exceptionally preserved fossil forest near Truth or Consequences, New Mexico. James Saulsbury, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Kansas Biodiversity Institute and Natural History Museum, helped collect, classify, and analyze the plant fossils discovered there.

“This paper focuses on a fossil forest in New Mexico and the preserved fruits, seeds and other reproductive structures of the plants that lived there,” Saulsbury said. “These fossils change how we understand the way flowering plants became modern in terms of their reproductive ecology.”

The forest was buried beneath volcanic ash that eventually hardened into rock. The preserved deposit stretches more than a kilometer (about 0.6 miles), capturing plants from approximately the same period and retaining evidence of how they were arranged across the ancient landscape.

“The New Mexico fossil site is exceptional,” Saulsbury said. “My co-authors have referred to it as a ‘botanical Pompeii’ because of its remarkable preservation. The site contains a layer of volcanic ash preserved as rock, known as tuff, that stretches for more than a kilometer. The deposits formed at essentially the same time, preserving many plants where they lived and died. It provides a snapshot of a forest from about 74 million years ago and even preserves aspects of its spatial arrangement.”

Flowering plants first appeared approximately 136 million years ago, but researchers have traditionally believed that their reproductive strategies remained relatively simple throughout much of the Cretaceous Period. Early flowering plants generally produced small seeds and fruits, with wind and other non-animal mechanisms thought to play major roles in seed dispersal.

“For much of their early history, they were relatively small, weedy plants that did not dominate forest canopies,” Saulsbury said. “Although they gradually diversified and occupied more ecological niches, it was thought their seeds and dispersal structures remained small and were primarily dispersed by wind or without fleshy fruit.”

Many early flowering plant seeds were thought to have ranged from dust-sized particles to roughly the size of poppy seeds. By contrast, the New Mexico fossils include fruits approximately as large as modern grapes. Such fruits are much larger than those previously expected from flowering plants of that age.

“The prevailing view has been that this more diverse reproductive ecology emerged only after the end-Cretaceous extinction,” Saulsbury said. “Our study suggests that transition began much earlier. The largest fruits in our fossil flora are about the size of a grape. That may not sound especially large today, but it is remarkably large for flowering plants of that period.”

The team examined hundreds of fossilized seeds, sorting them according to their physical characteristics. Because fossil material often lacks the features necessary to identify an exact species, researchers organized specimens into groups based on their shapes and structures.

“We sorted hundreds of fossil seeds into what we call morphotypes,” Saulsbury said. “These are groupings based on form rather than confirmed species because it is often impossible to determine whether similar-looking fossils represent one species or several.”

The fossil assemblage contains an unusual diversity of fruits, seeds, and reproductive structures. Although the exceptional preservation helped researchers recover this material, Saulsbury believes the forest itself differed from many other known Cretaceous environments.

“However, we don’t believe these findings are simply the result of preservation bias,” he said. “It appears to represent a genuinely unusual forest.”

Fruit size can provide information about the environments in which plants evolved and how their seeds may have spread. Today, many flowering plants produce fleshy fruits that attract animals, which can transport seeds away from the parent plant after eating the fruit.

“Large fruits tend to occur in moist environments with densely packed forests,” Saulsbury said. “Our findings indicate that modern-looking forest structure and reproductive ecology were developing earlier than previously believed. The diversification of flowering plant reproductive strategies did not have to wait until after the end-of-Cretaceous extinction.”

The discovery also complicates an established explanation for the evolution of fruit-bearing plants. Scientists had proposed that large, fleshy fruits became more widespread as mammals diversified following the extinction of non-avian dinosaurs, creating new opportunities for plants to disperse their seeds through animals.

“As mammals expanded into newly available ecological niches, flowering plants were thought to have diversified their seed dispersal strategies in response,” Saulsbury said. “Our findings suggest that story began earlier. If diverse, large fruits already existed in Cretaceous forests, they were likely being dispersed not only by early mammals but also by large dinosaurs and other animals.”

Reference: “Diversification of angiosperm reproductive strategies predated the end-Cretaceous extinction” by Jaemin Lee, Dori L. Contreras, James G. Saulsbury, Garland R. Upchurch and Cindy V. Looy, 25 June 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.adw9457

#6435. A 4,000-Year-Old DNA Mystery Is Rewriting the Origins of the English Language

Ancient DNA is uncovering forgotten migrations that may have shaped the origins of English, German, and Celtic languages, challenging what researchers thought they knew about Europe’s linguistic history.

How can researchers trace a language back thousands of years when no one knows exactly what its earliest speakers sounded like? Although DNA cannot reveal the words ancient people used, it can show where they traveled, offering clues to how the languages we recognize today first spread.

That approach is helping scientists reconsider the origins of English, German, Dutch, and the Scandinavian languages. Spoken by hundreds of millions of people today, these languages share Germanic roots that researchers have long believed reached Northern Europe about 5,000 years ago. New evidence suggests a major part of that history may have unfolded roughly 1,000 years later.

In two studies published in Nature, an international team led by the University of Copenhagen and Leiden University examined DNA from more than 4,500 ancient individuals, including 712 genomes sequenced for the first time. Comparing these genetic records with archaeological and linguistic evidence allowed the researchers to reconstruct population movements that had previously gone unnoticed.

“These studies show what becomes possible when genetics, archaeology, and linguistics are brought together. Questions that have remained unresolved for generations can now be addressed with a level of evidence that was previously impossible,” says Kristian Kristiansen, professor of archaeology at the University of Gothenburg.

One of the clearest discoveries was a previously unknown migration into Scandinavia around 4,000 years ago. The newcomers likely arrived from areas around the Baltic Sea and spread rapidly, leaving a lasting genetic influence on the region. Researchers believe they may have brought an early ancestor of today’s Germanic languages.

“For over a century, scholars have debated when and from where the Germanic languages arrived in Northern Europe. What is exciting is that we can now test some of these ideas directly. We discovered a previously unknown migration that occurred at exactly the time and place where we would expect the earliest form of Germanic to be spreading,” says Hugh McColl, assistant professor at the Globe Institute at the University of Copenhagen and lead author of the study.

The findings also shed light on a separate mystery involving Celtic languages. Although these languages now survive mainly in Ireland, Wales, Scotland, and Brittany, they were spoken across much of Europe around 2,500 years ago. Their origins have been disputed for more than a century, with competing theories pointing to the Atlantic coast or central Europe.

Ancient DNA revealed that people migrated westward from central Europe around 3,000 years ago, reaching France, Britain, Ireland, and the Iberian Peninsula. Researchers consider this the simplest explanation for the spread of Celtic languages, challenging the influential theory that they originated along the Atlantic coast.

“The question of where Celtic languages came from has been debated for more than 100 years. Ancient DNA gives us an entirely new way to evaluate competing theories and brings important new evidence into the discussion,” says Guus Kroonen, associate professor of comparative linguistics at Leiden University and the University of Copenhagen.

The genetic evidence also revealed an unexpected connection between the Vikings and Anglo-Saxons. Around 1,500 years ago, several centuries before the Viking Age, people from what is now northern Germany migrated into Denmark and southern Sweden. In some areas, particularly Zealand, they became a major part of the population.

Their arrival coincided with the emergence of Old Norse, the language later spoken by the Vikings. Many Danish and Swedish Vikings appear to have inherited much of their ancestry from these newcomers, who were closely related to populations that also contributed to the Anglo-Saxons in Britain. That connection may help explain similarities between their languages and artistic traditions.

“This migration came as a real surprise. Archaeologists and linguists had not predicted it, but it helps explain several cultural and linguistic connections between Scandinavia and Britain that have puzzled researchers for a long time,” says McColl.

The researchers caution that migration alone cannot establish which language a population spoke. Their conclusions depend on how the genetic evidence fits with decades of archaeological discoveries and linguistic research.

“DNA sequences do not tell us directly which language people spoke. But by combining ancient DNA with linguistic and archaeological evidence, we can begin to trace how languages spread and changed over thousands of years,” says Eske Willerslev, senior author of the studies and professor at the Globe Institute at the University of Copenhagen.

Reference: “Tracing the spread of Germanic languages using ancient genomics” by Hugh McColl, Guus Kroonen, J. The reentry of NASA's dead Swift space telescope is the end of an era for rapid-response space science.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's the end of an era: NASA's Swift telescope has reached the conclusion of its nearly 22-year mission, burning up in Earth's atmosphere after studying some of the universe's most powerful and mysterious events.

According to NASA, the spacecraft reentered the atmosphere at "7:39 a.m. EST Wednesday over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia, at approximately 3.4 degrees north latitude and 98.6 degrees east longitude." NASA expected most of the telescope's structure to burn up during its passage through Earth's atmosphere, estimating a 1-in-2,100 chance of any surviving debris falling over a populated area. No damage or injuries have been reported.

Weighing approximately 3,200 pounds (1,450 kilograms), the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory was initially designed for a two-year mission, but it far exceeded expectations. Over two decades, Swift became an important tool in the study of gamma-ray bursts, supernovas, black holes and other cosmic phenomena.

Launched in November 2004, Swift was designed to detect gamma-ray bursts, powerful explosions that occur throughout the universe. Its three onboard telescopes let scientists observe cosmic events across different wavelengths, including ultraviolet, optical and X-ray light. The telescope could swivel to focus on different sky targets in a matter of minutes, allowing it to rapidly follow up on sudden events like supernova explosions.

NASA estimates that Swift's scientific observations have contributed to approximately 7,000 research papers, leaving behind an extensive collection that scientists can continue studying for years.

Swift's return was driven by atmospheric drag, which eventually slowed the spacecraft and caused its orbit to decay. Increased solar activity intensified the drag, thus accelerating the space telescope's descent toward Earth.

Earlier this year, NASA explored an ambitious rescue mission to extend Swift's operational life. In August 2026, a privately developed robotic spacecraft built by Katalyst Space Technologies was intended to rendezvous with Swift and boost it into a higher orbit. However, the mission failed after launching, leaving the observatory on its path toward reentry.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

NASA officially ended Swift's scientific operations on Oct. 20 after its declining altitude made observations too difficult. For NASA and the broader astronomy community, Swift's story is a reminder that even missions designed to last just a few years can fundamentally change our understanding of our universe.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry is the Content Manager at Live Science. Formerly, she was the Content Manager at Space.com and before that the Science Communicator at JILA, a physics research institute. Kenna is also a book author, with her upcoming book 'Octopus X' scheduled for release in spring of 2027. Her beats include physics, health, environmental science, technology, AI, animal intelligence, corvids, and cephalopods.

#6433. How Archaeologists Risked Their Lives To Save 30,000 Ancient Treasures From ISIS

Syrian archaeologists rescued roughly 30,000 artifacts from a museum threatened by ISIS, highlighting how protecting human history can depend on trust built before a crisis.

A narrow, highly vulnerable corridor was the Deir ez-Zor Museum’s only connection to the military airport. Access to the Syrian city was severely restricted, and the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS), also known as Daesh, threatened to capture it. Archaeologists trying to move the museum’s collections to safety had to act amid active fighting.

During the summers of 2014 and 2015, Syrian archaeologists risked their lives to rescue approximately 30,000 artifacts. Maamoun Abdulkarim, Professor of Archaeology and History at the University of Sharjah, examines the operation in a study published in Museum Management and Curatorship. He oversaw the rescue as Director-General of Syria’s Directorate-General of Antiquities and Museums (DGAM).

Deir ez-Zor sits on the Euphrates River near Iraq’s border and is the capital of the province of the same name. The region contains some of Syria’s most important oil and gas fields, which made it a fiercely contested battleground during the conflict. As ISIS expanded its control across large parts of Syria and Iraq in 2014, the danger to cultural collections became increasingly clear. Abdulkarim describes the period that followed as “an important example of the sort of looting, destruction, and illicit trafficking of sites and museums that took place in this context.”

“This period formed a critical juncture, as it coincided with the fall of Mosul in Iraq, the looting of its civilizational museum, and the destruction of antiquities from Nineveh and Assyria,” he writes. “These occurrences compelled Syrian antiquities authorities to promptly reevaluate protection policies and expedite emergency measures in cities that were at risk of siege or collapse.”

Before the civil war began in 2011, Syria had 35 archaeological museums. Deir ez-Zor’s was not the largest, but it ranked among the country’s most valuable. Many of its collections came from renowned Mesopotamian civilizations and sites, including Halaf, Dura-Europos, and Mari.

“The 30,000 objects rescued from Deir ez-Zor represent more than just museum pieces; they hold thousands of years of human history and are part of the identity and memory of the communities in the Euphrates region.”

For Abdulkarim, leading the rescue meant making necessary decisions at the right moment, even when none of the choices was easy.

“My foremost priority was the protection of cultural heritage, and I was prepared to bear whatever personal and professional risks and consequences those decisions might entail,” he explains.

“There is rarely a perfect moment to act during an armed conflict; often, delaying a decision in search of greater certainty poses a greater danger than acting under uncertainty.”

The Deir ez-Zor evacuation was part of a much larger effort. During Abdulkarim’s tenure as DGAM’s Director-General from 2012 to 2017, approximately 300,000 museum artifacts were rescued and relocated to secure sites across Syria.

“The artifacts accounted for the overwhelming majority of the country’s museum collections,” he said. “This included approximately 30,000 objects from the Deir ez-Zor Museum.”

Those rescue figures do not provide a complete accounting of the war’s toll. The study gives no precise estimate of how many artifacts were looted during the civil war, which lasted nearly a decade and a half. It also does not specify how many of Syria’s 35 museums escaped destruction or preserved their collections intact.

Even the extent of Syria’s archaeological heritage remains uncertain. Modern-day Syria forms part of the broader Mesopotamian cultural sphere, where some of the world’s earliest and most influential civilizations flourished. There is no official estimate of the country’s total number of archaeologically significant sites. Its antiquities department is said to have records for about 10,000, primarily places that have been excavated or identified through visible remains on the surface. With large areas still archaeologically unsurveyed, the actual number may run into the tens of thousands.

Abdulkarim views responsibility for this heritage as extending beyond the borders of the countries where it is found.

“We did not rescue 30,000 objects simply to save 30,000 museum pieces. We were protecting thousands of years of memory that war threatened to erase,” he said.

His account treats a rescue during active hostilities as more than a logistical operation. “It fundamentally involves decision-making, institutional resilience, trust, and the ability to adapt rapidly to changing circumstances,” he explained.

He identifies competent personnel, effective institutions, meticulous inventories and documentation, and trusted colleagues on the ground as essential to protecting endangered collections. These resources help determine whether an organization can respond when its usual procedures are no longer workable.

“The most valuable resource during a crisis is not always money or technology,” he noted. “Sometimes it is trust, the trust between colleagues who can make the right decision when there is no time left for normal procedures.”

Abdulkarim presents Deir ez-Zor as a case study for heritage professionals confronting war and crisis elsewhere. Museums and archaeological sites in countries including Iraq, Libya, Sudan, and Yemen have also suffered destruction, looting, and illicit trafficking amid war and civil unrest. His analysis emphasizes the timing of decisions alongside the resources available to carry them out.

“In a cultural emergency, waiting for perfect conditions can become more dangerous than acting under uncertainty,” he stressed. “Heritage protection during war is not only about what we save. It is also about when we decide to act, whom we trust, and how quickly we are prepared to adapt.”

The study argues that museum and heritage professionals should make risk management part of their everyday work, rather than introducing it only after an emergency begins.

“The relationships, documentation, professional capacity, and trust required for effective emergency action must be established during periods of stability,” Abdulkarim concluded. “They should not wait until a crisis erupts before taking action. These foundations cannot be built overnight.”

Reference: “The rescue of the Deir ez-Zor museum collections during the Syrian conflict: cultural emergency management, multi-level governance, and lessons for heritage protection” by Maamoun Abdulkarim, 15 August 2026, Museum Management and Curatorship. DOI: 10.1080/09647775.2026.2710063

#6432. High-Tech Drones Reveal Long-Hidden Aboriginal Rock Art Shelters in Australia

Drone-mounted lasers helped locate three unregistered Aboriginal rock art shelters in Australia, offering communities another way to document and protect their cultural heritage for future generations.

In Australia’s Blue Mountains, rugged terrain and dense bushland make searching for Aboriginal cultural sites slow, difficult, and expensive.

More than 200 rock shelters containing cultural and archaeological evidence have been recorded there, but only an estimated 10 percent of the region has been surveyed, according to Dr. Amy Mosig Way, a research archaeologist at the University of Sydney and the Australian Museum.

Researchers from the two institutions, working alongside the Dharug Custodian Aboriginal Corporation, used drone-mounted lasers to help narrow that search. The technology, called LiDAR, short for Light Detection and Ranging, uses laser pulses to create detailed three-dimensional maps of the landscape, helping researchers detect features hidden beneath bushland and tree cover.

After the drone surveys identified potential rock shelters, Way led teams of students and volunteers into the field to verify their locations and assess whether they contained cultural material. The work confirmed the locations of six registered shelters and identified three previously unregistered ones. The newly recorded shelters contain stone artifacts and rock art, including red hand stencils.

“One of the most rewarding aspects of the Gulamada Project has been creating opportunities for students to gain hands-on experience in cultural heritage research in a community-centered project,” Way said.

The research, published in Remote Sensing, also produced much more accurate shelter coordinates than those listed in the official New South Wales sites register, the Aboriginal Heritage Information Management System (AHIMS).

“This work is exciting because it offers an efficient and accurate way to locate sites in rugged environments, which are notoriously arduous, expensive and time-consuming to survey,” said Dr. Jacob Bongers, lead author of the drone research and a digital archaeologist at the University of Sydney. He is also a former AMF/AMRI Visiting Research Fellow at the Australian Museum.

The surveys form part of the Gulamada Project, co-directed by Way and Wayne Brennan, an Indigenous rock art expert at the University of Sydney. Built on the principle of walking side by side, the project brings scientific knowledge and First Nations cultural knowledge together to better understand and care for Country. At the confirmed shelters, Brennan and Erin Wilkins, of the Dharug Custodian Aboriginal Corporation, led the rock art recording.

“From the outset, our vision for the Gulamada Project has been to create a true nexus of science and culture. This work highlights the importance of listening, learning and working together,” Brennan said.

Susan Templeman, the Federal Member for Macquarie, which includes the Blue Mountains, said, “This project demonstrates the power of bringing together First Nations knowledge and new technology to better understand and protect Australia’s rich cultural heritage. I’m proud that the Australian Government’s First Nations Heritage Grants program is supporting important projects like Gulamada here in the Blue Mountains, already renowned for the extraordinary natural and cultural significance within our rugged landscapes.”

The team says the approach allows Aboriginal communities, archaeologists, and heritage managers to search vast areas of challenging terrain much faster than traditional ground surveys. Used alongside existing knowledge and cultural practices, it could help communities locate, document, manage, and protect cultural sites before they are affected by development, erosion, bushfires, or other threats.

“Importantly, our methodology is helping expand the record of Aboriginal cultural sites in the Blue Mountains and has the potential to be applied in other regions,” Bongers said.

The researchers plan to work with Aboriginal communities to test and adapt the approach in different environments, including the tropical savannas of western Arnhem Land and the semi-arid landscapes of western New South Wales.

Reference: “LiDAR-Assisted Survey Locates Unregistered Rock Shelters in the Blue Mountains, Australia” by Jacob L. Bongers, Wayne Brennan, Erin Wilkins, Lauren Roach, Emily Nutman, Joseph W. Lehner and Amy Mosig Way, 11 October 2026, Remote Sensing. DOI: 10.3390/rs18203495

The project “The Gulamada Project: Walking side by side: A Nexus of Science and Culture” was funded under the 2023-24 First Nations Heritage Grants program (Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW) – grant no. FNHI000045 ($248,610), awarded to Amy Mosig Way & Wayne Brennan (the University of Sydney) in collaboration with Erin Wilkins (Dharug Custodians Aboriginal Corporation).

#6431. The 8 Best Air Purifiers for Your Home

Whether you’re dealing with smoke or pet dander, these are the most effective (and affordable) models we stand behind based on testing and research.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Clean indoor air has become more important than ever. While allergens like dust, dander, mold, and bacteria are all teaming up to infiltrate the air you breathe, the widespread wildfire smoke affecting much of the U.S. right now is also proving just how quickly outdoor pollution can make its way inside. According to the EPA, Americans spend about 90 percent of their time indoors, where pollutant concentrations can sometimes be even higher than they are outside. An air purifier protects your airways from airborne irritants while providing clean, fresh air indoors (which is why we think everyone should invest in an air purifier).

We got our hands on air purifiers from brands like Coway, Levoit, and GermGuardian and put them to the test. Filtration was our main concern, so we could determine the air purifiers’ efficiency. Then we moved along to other factors such as noise while running, how well they work in a given room, and convenience features. After our in-home testing, these are the air purifiers that came out on top.

We tried out several air purifiers with a range of filtration systems, noise levels, and features. We tested these models in multiple different apartments, placing them in various rooms of the home to measure their efficiency. We considered the different uses of an air purifier, like if you’re an allergy sufferer or have a home filled with furry friends, and tested special features like light-up displays and automatic shutoff to determine their ease of use and effectiveness. We considered the amount of time it took to set up the different purifiers and install their filter systems.

For units that we haven’t tested, we combed through dozens of potential products and their specifications, reviews, and user complaints to identify what we thought were the best air purifiers. We settled on the following list, which includes options that are budget-friendly, sleekly designed, and high-performing.

The Airmega Mighty2 is the latest version of our previous Best Overall pick, the Coway AP-1512HH. The newest model combines power, quality filters, and robust controls to help you breathe easier.

The Mighty2 uses a three-stage filtration system to capture 99.7 percent of airborne particles, and cleans spaces up to 1,800 square feet in 60 minutes. It has three standard fan speeds, but there’s a turbo mode that will kick on if there’s a big uptick of matter in the air.

The original version just used an indicator light system that let you know basic air quality levels, but this updated model has a built-in air quality index sensor that measures and displays particulate matter counts in real time.

Our tester tried the air purifier in his New York apartment, putting it up against pet odors, litterbox dust, and other household allergens. “Results after about a day were already noticeable. The air in the room seemed clearer and there was less dust on the ground in the area immediately around the litterbox. Not enough that I’m going to have to sweep up any less, mind you, but there was a material difference that I wasn’t getting from using a smaller purifier.”

Full Coway Airmega Mighty2 Air Purifier Review

This air purifier from Clorox uses a three-stage filtration system to trap allergens, pollutants, and VOCs, and it successfully cleared strong scents and odors from the apartment we tested in.

It was quiet enough that you hardly hear it activate, especially if it kicks on automatically while you’re cooking to clear the kitchen of smoke. But on higher settings, you do tend to notice its noise a bit more. The 360-degree, cylindrical shape of the filter offers purification from all directions, and the unit covers 1,000 square feet so you don't have to be as strategic about placement.

We also liked that it has a color-coded indicator light on the front that tells you how hazardous the air is in the room where it's located (though it will add insult to injury when it turns purple while you’re trying your best to sear a steak.)

If you’re a pet owner, specifically with cats, then you know that the litter box smell lingers long after your little fur ball has left the lavatory. The Vital 200S-P from Levoit is a great way to combat the odors that candles and air fresheners just can’t cover up. I set the air purifier up in my living room and noticed a clear improvement in scent after running for the day.

This unit has a traditional air inlet, along with a unique U-shaped inlet that is ideal for trapping pet hair without clogging up the filters. If you pair your air purifier with the app and select Pet Mode, it automatically alternates between fan speeds, too. The pre-filter is easy to remove and wash, so you don't have to purchase replacements as often.

Since we tested the Vital 200S-P in a smaller apartment, it was a bit obtrusive. But the air purifier covers up to 1,875 square feet, so if you live in a townhouse or single-family home, this unit will accommodate.

Full Levoit Vital 200S-P Air Purifier Review

The Airmega 100 is the first cylindrical unit in the Coway line, which is a nice switch-up from the rectangular model that we tested in the past. It tucked nicely into the corner of the living room, and you can change the light between blue, orange, and off, which is ideal if you’re using the purifier in a bedroom.

I tried the fan on various settings, and the lowest mode could barely be heard over the TV playing at an average volume, which aligns with its claimed 20-decibel noise level. You can manually adjust everything on the control panel, or let the purifier do its thing and adapt accordingly as it monitors the air quality of the room.

Setup of the unit was simple; you essentially just need to click the filter into place. This model uses a 3-in-1 filtration system, with a HEPA filter sandwiched between a vacuumable pre-filter and deodorizing filter. The deodorizer layer is especially useful if you have pets, love to cook, or live in an apartment or complex with odors.

Full Coway Airmega 100 Air Purifier Review

For smaller rooms or office spaces, the smart Blueair 511i Max offers much of the same performance and features as larger, more capable models. It only purifies areas of up to 465 square feet, but does so within just 30 minutes on the highest setting. The three-layer filtration system captures up to 99.7 percent of airborne particles, too.

We appreciate that the air quality level is clearly displayed on the front in a five-color scale, and that the display has auto-brightness controls if you're running it overnight while you're sleeping. Advanced features are available through the app, including scheduling and air quality reports.

This unit has a four-stage filtration system, along with Blueair's proprietary HEPASilent filter that uses a combination of electrostatic charge and mechanical filtration to capture 99.97 percent of airborne pollutants and contaminants. This type of filtration technology is less dense than other filter options, so it's designed to run quieter and use less energy.

The value offered by such a small air purifier is unmatched, considering it targets both allergens and odors—all with relatively quiet operation.

If you have a large space or even an entire apartment that needs air purification, the Coway Airmega 400 is the smart model you need. It's designed to cover up to 1,560 square feet in 30 minutes, and has a variety of smart features and sleep settings, all packed into a compact yet capable unit. While this is the most expensive option we recommend, it's relatively affordable considering its capacity, and you shouldn’t have to supplement with an additional air purifier.

It’s surprisingly quiet given its size, reaching only 22 decibels on its lowest setting. We like that it uses multi-stage purification methods, combining a pre-filter, an activated carbon filter, and a True HEPA filter to capture the tiniest of particles. The pre-filter is washable, but the air filter indicator light will let you know when it actually needs to be replaced.

The Airmega 400 has a three-setting smart mode that adapts to its environment, with a fan speed that automatically adjusts based on air quality or lighting conditions. We also appreciate the option to use eco mode, which turns the fan on and off when the room has remained purified for 30 minutes, and there’s also a timer and pollution sensor.

The GermGuardian isn’t a flashy design with robust features, but it aids in keeping the air in my apartment free of pet odors, dust, and smoke.

I have a self-cleaning litter box, which significantly cuts down on smells and dust associated with cat waste, but it doesn’t solve every problem. I let the purifier run during one of the Litter Robot’s cleaning cycles, and thanks to the GermGuardian’s built-in air quality index (AQI) sensor and display screen, I was able to see the particulate matter count in the air reach triple digits in seconds. The automatic fan speed varied as needed, and it wasn’t long before air quality was back to a healthy level.

I put the GermGuardian up against incense smoke, too, and it went to work quickly. The fan had to run at high speed for longer, but by the end, my living room was clear of any lingering haze and odor.

In addition to a HEPA filter and activated carbon, this model also has a UVC light, which is claimed to disinfect bacteria, viruses, and mold. While I did give this feature a try, I didn’t keep it on for long because it’s hard to prove whether these lights are actually useful in an air purifier.

Read Full GermGuardian AC4880B Air Purifier Review

The Sans HEPA 13 air purifier offers quiet operation, whole-home purification, and smart features. This unit runs at only 25 decibels on the lowest fan setting, and I could hardly tell that it was on, even when standing next to the unit.

The air purifier is best used for whole-home use, as it purifies spaces up to 1,854 square feet. The internal sensors monitor and show you the air quality index in real time, and the reading is visible on the touch display. I’m able to view PM2.5, which is particles that are 2.5 microns or smaller, such as dust, smoke, pollen, and pet dander, as well as PM10, which are slightly larger particles up to 10 microns, like coarser dust and mold spores.

This unit pairs a medical-grade HEPA 13 filter with a pre-filter, activated carbon filter, and UV-C light to capture 99.9 percent of particles. This might be overkill for general household use, but I’ve appreciated the multi-stage approach. The only downside I’ve come across is that overall cost will likely be higher, considering the Sans recommends replacing the filter every three months.

There is no shortage of air purifiers on the market, and many of them use a lot of the same tech to achieve better air quality. We’re often testing many different models to find the top recommendations. Ahead are some that haven’t made it to this roundup, but are still worth considering.

Rabbit Air A3 Air Purifier: This air purifier uses a six-stage filtration system to rid your home of smoke, dander, odors, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and germs. The lowest fan setting clocks in around 20 decibels, which is extremely quiet, so you can run this model daily without being disturbed. The build is relatively bulky so it’s not the easiest to tuck into a corner and out of the way, and the $760 price tag is pretty steep.

GermGuardian AirSafe+ XL: This model is shaped like our best portable pick above, and comes with a lot of the same features as the other GermGuardian we recommend, and it has a companion app for tracking air quality metrics. That said, the app doesn’t specify what type or size particulate matter the sensor is measuring, so it’s hard to tell what common allergens are actually floating around your home.

Air purifiers vary in filtration range, so it's important to first consider your room size before buying. To find a model that accommodates your space, the EPA recommends that you first multiply the length and width of the area where you intend to operate the air purifier to calculate the square footage.

Most air purifiers have a maximum coverage area listed, so just compare to your calculations to find an air purifier that is the best fit for your home.

If you have an open floor plan or high ceilings, opt for an air purifier with more coverage. You should also place the air purifier in the room you use most regularly, and make sure it’s in an area where the airflow isn’t obstructed.

The filter system of your air purifier might differ depending on the model and issue you're trying to target such as allergy relief, odor elimination, or germ protection. You’ll often see three-stage filtration (or four-, five-, or six-stage), which includes all three of the filter types detailed below.

Pre-filters are typically the first line of defense in an air purifier and trap larger particles like dust, hair, and fur, which helps extend the lifespan of the main filter and improves the overall efficiency of the unit.

All of our selections on this list involve a multi-step filtration system to target a majority of common pollutants and allergens in your household.

Purvi Parikh, MD, an allergist and immunologist with NYU Langone Health, recommends selecting an air purifier that comes with a HEPA filter. “Make sure it's a HEPA air purifier since these filter down to 0.3 microns and have a robust amount of studies done showing their efficacy.” HEPA filters remove at least 99.97 percent of airborne particles like dust, bacteria, and pollen, and are the gold standard for air purification.

Activated carbon filters are more porous and help get rid of gases and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) that are commonly found in household items like surface cleaners and candles. These filters absorb molecules onto carbon and are best used in environments with strong odors or smoke.

With laundry machines, dishwashers, and fans all emitting their own noise, adding another loud appliance into the mix could be overkill, especially since air purifiers are meant to run the entire day.

Look for models that range from 10 to 30 decibels. A whisper is around 30 decibels, so expect air purifiers in this noise range to be almost virtually silent.

“Air purifiers need to be kept clean, and filters should be changed every six months,” Parikh says. Since air purifier filters are designed to collect and trap different-sized particles, contaminants, and hair, they get gunky pretty easily. This buildup could even reduce the efficiency and the air quality of the purifier if not cleaned often enough. Most air purifiers come with reusable filters, so just rinse them off in between replacements.

App compatibility, savvy control panels, remotes, check filter indicators, and variable settings are beneficial features that make it easier to use your air purifier. If you want to monitor the air quality levels in your home or keep tabs on filter life, look for an air purifier that pairs with an app. If you’re easily overstimulated by loud noises, consider an air purifier that has different modes for adjusting the speed of the internal fan.

Air purifiers use a fan to draw air into the unit, then pass it through a series of filters to remove particles and contaminants. Said filters vary in effectiveness and normally target a specific concern like odors, smoke, and viruses. Once the air has passed through the fan and all of the appropriate filters, it is recirculated back into the room for a cleaner and healthier environment.

“Air purifiers filter out pollutants, improve air quality, remove infectious agents and pollen,” says Parikh. “They limit your level of exposure and reduce lung damage and flare-ups of underlying chronic conditions such as asthma attacks, COPD exacerbations, and heart issues.”

“It can affect everyone’s health by causing inflammation and lung damage over time that may be either reversible or irreversible,” Parikh says. “It is especially dangerous for those with underlying heart disease, lung disease, pregnant women, children, and immunocompromised individuals.”

#6429. Scientists Discover a Strange Form of Iron on the Moon That Shouldn’t Be There

Scientists examining lunar soil collected by China’s Chang’e-6 mission have discovered an unexpected form of iron preserved within microscopic impact glass.

Tiny particles of iron trapped inside lunar glass may preserve evidence of the Moon’s ancient magnetic history. Scientists studying soil returned by China’s Chang’e-6 mission have identified face-centered cubic γ-Fe, an unusual form of metallic iron never before confirmed in natural lunar samples.

The discovery is particularly unexpected because γ-Fe normally exists only at high temperatures and changes into a different crystal structure as it cools. Yet researchers found that this phase of iron had survived inside microscopic glass particles formed during impacts on the lunar surface.

Researchers led by Prof. Haifeng Du of the High Magnetic Field Laboratory at the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science (HFIPS) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) examined impact glass containing numerous nanoscale iron particles. Using focused ion beam preparation, transmission electron microscopy, and chemical analysis, they confirmed that γ-Fe was the dominant iron phase in the two glass samples studied. Their findings were published September 16 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS).

Under normal conditions, γ-Fe transforms into α-Fe as temperatures fall. The team proposed that the extreme conditions created by lunar impacts could prevent this transformation. Rapid cooling of molten material, small amounts of carbon and other elements, and the surrounding glassy matrix may have helped preserve the unusual crystal structure at the lunar surface.

The scientists also investigated whether these particles could retain magnetic information. Using off-axis electron holography, a technique that can map magnetic fields at extremely small scales, they examined the magnetic structure of individual γ-Fe nanoparticles. Relatively large particles displayed a stable single-vortex magnetic state, with their magnetization arranged in a circulating pattern. They also maintained a stable magnetic response when exposed to an external magnetic field.

“This tiny magnetic fossil may help us better understand the Moon’s ancient magnetic history,” said Dr. Long Li of HFIPS, a member of the research team.

Although the Moon no longer possesses a global magnetic field, its rocks and soils contain magnetic minerals that can preserve information about past conditions. The newly identified γ-Fe expands the range of materials scientists can investigate when reconstructing that history.

Because γ-Fe and α-Fe develop under different physical conditions and exhibit distinct magnetic properties, they may retain records from different stages of lunar impact events. Further research will be needed to determine how reliably these minerals preserve ancient magnetic signals and what they can reveal about the evolution of magnetism on the Moon.

Reference: “Magnetic vortex state of natural lunar γ-Fe” by Pengfei Liu, Ziliang Jin, Zheng Gong, Long Li, Kang Wang, Xiandi Zeng, Jing Liu, Dongsheng Song, Haifeng Du, Kelei Zhu, Chuanxin Yan, Jinhua Li, Keke Zhang, Wyn Williams and Ann M. Hirt, 16 September 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2608395123

An analysis of plant fossils preserved in amber from Myanmar revealed that the West Burma Block, a chunk of crust that broke off of Australia, seeded Southeast Asia's lush tropical forests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Southeast Asia's tropical forests owe their rich biodiversity to a tiny fragment of Earth's crust that split from what is now northwestern Australia roughly 150 million years ago, a new study reports.

The fragment transported hundreds of flowering species and a flourishing collection of other ancient plants north across the prehistoric Tethys Ocean, the research reveals. The findings contradict previous theories that the fragment originated closer to what is now Southeast Asia and that Southeast Asia's tropical forests evolved sometime after the extinction of the dinosaurs around 66 million years ago.

At the time the fragment formed, Australia was connected to Antarctica and India within the ancient supercontinent Gondwana, which the Tethys Ocean separated from another ancient supercontinent, called Laurasia.

After drifting northward for 100 million years, the microplate eventually collided with Southeast Asia, seeding tropical forests that evolved into the lush ecosystems found in this part of the world today, the researchers said.

"The rich tropical rainforest flora of [Southeast Asia] is not endemic but owes much of its biota to the great southern land, Gondwana," study co-author Byron Lamont, a distinguished professor emeritus in Curtin University's School of Molecular and Life Sciences in Australia, told Live Science in an email.

But the collision with Southeast Asia was far from smooth, Lamont said. The fragment, which is known as the West Burma Block (WBB) or the Burma terrane due to its location in western Myanmar, wasn't the only piece of crust crossing the Tethys Ocean around 100 million years ago. The Indian subcontinent was also moving north, and it was doing so at a relatively rapid speed of 4 inches (10 centimeters) per year.

Around 80 million years ago, the Indian Plate bumped into the WBB, altering the fragment's orientation. The Indian Plate continued to shove the WBB until they both collided with Asia. The Indian Plate then slid beneath the Eurasian Plate to form the Himalayas, and the WBB ground to a halt to the west of present-day Myanmar, where it created a deep valley between mountain ranges about 35 million years ago, Lamont explained.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both the Indian Plate and the WBB "took some time to stop," he said.

From the time the WBB broke off from Gondwana until its collision with Southeast Asia starting 50 million years ago, the microplate spent tens of millions of years hovering near the equator, where it was humid and hot like it is today. This climate and the fragment's isolation provided a refuge where ancient plant lineages could survive and diversify, Lamont said.

For the study, Lamont and his colleagues examined more than 3,000 plant fossils from Myanmar that were preserved in amber around 100 million years ago. The fossils included flowers, leaves, fruits and seeds. They belonged to at least 392 types of flowering plants and a vast array of conifers, ferns, mosses, cycads and liverworts that reached Southeast Asia by floating on the WBB.

Amber has been mined from the north end of the WBB valley for at least a century, Lamont said. "Its beautiful fossils, preserved in 3D, have long attracted interest for their novelty value alone and there has been much commercial interest in them, especially from Chinese traders," he noted.

Some of the study's co-authors acquired chunks of amber from traders at least a decade ago, and they have been studying these pieces ever since. Advice was often required from experts at other institutions around the world, which is how Lamont got involved in the study, he said.

The findings, published Oct. 27 in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution, reveal the deep evolutionary roots of the tropical forests that grow in Southeast Asia today. The WBB didn't strip Australia of its ancient flora, because the descendants of many plants found in the 100 million-year-old amber still exist in the country's Northeast, which is hot and humid, Lamont said.

It's hard to say what kinds of animals arrived in Southeast Asia via the WBB, because only creatures small enough to be preserved in amber are represented in this fossil assemblage.

"The animals present in the amber are small insects, such as ants and mosquitoes," Lamont said. "Typical Australian vertebrates, such as marsupials, emus and nectar-feeding birds, arrived from South America in Australia over 100 million years later [after the WBB split off], and of course they would not have got caught in the resin even if they had been around."

Wang, S. (2026). A mid-Cretaceous island as a cradle of Southeast Asian plant biodiversity. Nature Ecology & Evolution. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41559-026-03219-7

Sascha is a U.K.-based staff writer at Live Science. She holds a bachelor’s degree in biology from the University of Southampton in England and a master’s degree in science communication from Imperial College London. Her work has appeared in The Guardian and the health website Zoe. Besides writing, she enjoys playing tennis, bread-making and browsing second-hand shops for hidden gems.

#6427. Where to Eat Gluten-Free in Montreal

Recently I’ve noticed more and more food people going to Montreal—and who can blame them? This laid-back bilingual gem on the St. Lawrence River is one of North America’s very best food cities. Personally I’ve loved it since my first visit almost 20 years ago. Montreal’s wonderful food scene draws me back year after year, sometimes multiple times,and by now the six-hour drive from my home in New York City feels like a breeze. It helps to know that my top meals of the year are waiting just across the border.

But for the past two years, following my wife’s celiac diagnosis, I have been navigating the city a little differently. When I was younger, trips to Montreal meant poutine, bagels, smoked-meat sandwiches, and a plethora of other canonical Québécois favorites that happen to be full of gluten. These days we prioritize other local favorites and have developed a dependable roster of businesses we trust—and that don’t feel like a compromise. Luckily there are a ton of them; we’ve been thrilled to discover that Montreal is a paradise for gluten-free eating.

In my opinion the only gluten-free Montreal-style bagels worth sampling are located in Burlington, Vermont. But Montreal is a city that takes its baked goods seriously, and it’s home to a handful of excellent dedicated gluten-free bakeries. You will not miss the bagels. Instead how about a croissant?

Any gluten-free eater knows croissants are one of the hardest pastries to get right without gluten. As a rule my wife and I don’t really bother—unless we’re in Montreal. At Boulangerie Le Marquis, near Jean-Talon Market, and sister business Le Marquis Signature Santé, in Old Montreal, magnificent pains au chocolat and gluten-free croissants—available in plain, almond, and chocolate-almond varieties—arrive hot out of the oven all morning long. Flaky laminated pastry is a near-impossible feat in the gluten-free world, but Le Marquis has perfected it. We favor the pains au chocolat and almond croissants, but it’s tough to go wrong.

Even more unique is the gluten-free manouché at La Bolo à Lolo, a GF market and takeaway in the Plateau. Chef and owner Gordy Moufarrej emigrated from Lebanon to Montreal as a boy and uses his mother’s homemade za’atar in these addictive flatbreads. Made from Moufarrej’s proprietary GF flour blend, they are topped with a paste of olive oil and za’atar, plus cheese if you want (you do). A number of sandwiches made with the same base are available, but we’ve never gotten past the manouché—on our last visit to Montreal, we went three days in a row.

Perhaps unsurprisingly for a French-speaking city, crepes are another great option, and Montreal boasts an amazing spot for 100% buckwheat Breton-style galettes. At Crêperie du Marché, a bustling stall at Jean-Talon Market, cooks turn out a dedicated gluten-free menu of lacy galettes with both savory and sweet fillings. It’s a personal choice, but we like the cheeky selections that mix both: ham, cheese, eggs, potatoes, and a drizzle of maple syrup. Why not?

Nearby is cheery, quirky Cantine Panella, a dedicated gluten-free bakery and café run by the Peruvian chef Alessandra Perona. Her South American sensibility means breads are made with flours like quinoa, cassava, and sweet potato, which gives them a delightful chewiness. We like to stock up on a few of these to bring home, though they sometimes don’t last the drive.

Of all Montreal’s classic foods, rotisserie chicken might be my favorite. At Québécois-style rotisseries it’s slow-roasted on a spit and accompanied by gravy; at Portuguese spots it’s often spatchcocked and grilled over charcoal, then served with piri-piri sauce. In both cases gluten sometimes spoils the fun: Traditional establishments like the legendary Chalet Bar-B-Q and Portuguese eatery Ma Poule Mouillée both use wheat flour in their sauces. No matter—these are far from your only options.

Piri-Piri Chicken at Rôtisserie Coco Rico

At Rôtisserie Coco Rico, a Plateau institution open since 1970, the chicken is spit-roasted and served with GF piri-piri in a mélange of the two dominant local styles. On the side fries from a dedicated GF fryer are among the city’s best (and this is a city with great french fries), but don’t sleep on the roasted potatoes, full of savory chicken flavor.

More refined, and representing the French Canadian tradition, is Little Italy’s Rôtisserie La Lune, from the team behind überpopular restaurant and wine bar Mon Lapin. Gorgeous, plump birds are served with rich gluten-free gravy and excellent fries that come from a blessedly dedicated fryer. The same fryer is also responsible for the unbelievable Croqu’Ailes Farcies XL, which are deboned chicken wings stuffed with more chicken and deep-fried. Every meal here should start with these. But the kitchen has an equally deft hand with seasonal salads and veggie-focused sides—almost always gluten-free and an essential counterweight on the table.

Down the street from La Lune, Mon Lapin is equally adept at catering to gluten-free diners: On two recent visits most of the menu was in play. Dishes change with the seasons, but friendly servers will guide your choices (and help you navigate the impressive wine list). Make sure to save room for the restaurant’s signature buckwheat layer cake, accented with buckwheat honey caramel, fromage blanc, and crisp shards of buckwheat tuile. I’m not sure there’s a better gluten-free dessert on the continent.

Mon Lapin’s co-owners, chefs Jessica Noël and Marc-Olivier Frappier, and wine director Vanya Filipovic, are all alums of the trendsetting Little Burgundy eatery and wine bar Vin Papillon, whose chef and owner happens to be celiac. Best known as half of the duo that opened Montreal icon Joe Beef, Fred Morin now presides over those two restaurants, plus the rotisserie McKiernan and gastropub Liverpool House. His kitchens have airtight allergy protocols and are particularly sensitive to gluten-free diners because of Morin’s own celiac status. And because so many Montreal chefs have passed through Morin’s kitchens, his influence looms large over the city’s fine dining scene—and its spirit of hospitality toward those with allergies and intolerances.

While all of Morin’s restaurants are fantastic, Vin Papillon is the one we come back to every year—its Jambon de la Petite-Bourgogne is one of the world’s great meat-and-cheese plates, featuring house-cured ham, the Quebec sheep-milk cheese le Fleur des Monts, and a sneaky application of brown butter that brings together all the nutty, savory notes. For dessert the restaurant often serves a gluten-free carrot cake ice cream sandwich with caramel sauce in a silver goblet.

Another Joe Beef group alum, Ariel Schor, runs one of our favorite Verdun neighborhood spots with his brother, Pablo. Both natives of Argentina with Jewish roots, the Schors run a restaurant called Beba with a particular affinity for offal (organ meats) and a surprisingly light touch with creative veg dishes that change seasonally. Swiss chard leaves are stuffed with zucchini and chard stems and served with a sweet-and-sour condiment of onions, raisins, and pine nuts. Medjool dates are impishly filled with foie gras and topped with pistachio. Elsewhere on the menu expect things like tongue, rabbit, chorizo, and tripe—dishes that tend to be gluten-free.

When you’re craving Gallic comfort food, Montreal overdelivers. I used to think there were Leméac people and L’Express people, that one couldn’t possibly love Montreal’s two most prominent old-school bistros equally. I was wrong. The late local architect Luc Laporte designed both dining rooms, and they each have the buzzing, joyful energy most restaurants covet.

L’Express is my first love, a Montreal stalwart open since 1980 that I’ve been to more times than I can count. Its main virtues for gluten-free eaters are a dedicated fryer and incredibly good french fries—available as a stand-alone side or, even better, as part of steak frites. There are plenty of other GF mains and entrées, but room must be saved for the enormous île flottante, a classic French meringue-based dessert encased in a hardened caramel dome and surrounded by shards of candied almond. For something on the lighter side, try the unique crème brûlée with wild sweet clover from Quebec, sometimes called boreal vanilla.

Leméac does not have a dedicated fryer, so fries don’t work for celiacs. But I promise you won’t miss them. We favor the textbook duck confit, served with roasted potatoes and a bright green salad. For dessert there’s an unmissable gluten-free chocolate-and-banana moelleux, a decadent cake served with caramel and popcorn ice cream, along with many other classics, including crème caramel.

Montreal is also home to a number of fabulous Middle Eastern and North African restaurants, some of which can cater to gluten-free diners—albeit with asterisks. We love the standout Damas, a Syrian fine-dining spot on a pretty corner in Outremont, though gluten-free choices are limited. Still, it’s worth the trip for the ground lamb and eggplant kebab grilled over open charcoal and accompanied by charred pepper, tomato butter, and gobs of garlic labneh and the dreamy hummus topped with lamb shawarma and pine nuts, which can be served with crudités rather than pita. Both are among the best things I’ve eaten in recent memory.

Le Petit Alep, a neighborhood institution near Jean-Talon, offers more Syrian and Armenian options. The marvelous mezes are largely gluten-free and served—upon request—with crudités; savory, comforting mujaddara is made with lentils and rice, no bulgur, barley, or other glutenous grains. End with the house herbal tea, a beautiful floral mixture of cardamom pods, mint, rosewater, and orange blossom. I’ve tried to make it at home, but I can’t quite replicate it. That’s okay—I’ll be back next year.

#6425. Something Unusual Is Swirling around the Monster Black Hole at the Center of Our Galaxy

Webb’s measurements of metal-rich gas offer clues to the processes that fuel our galaxy’s supermassive black hole, which consumes material more slowly than others.

The gas circling the Milky Way’s central black hole is rich in metals, probably supplied by stars that exploded and released material into its surroundings over time. Researchers at McGill University’s Trottier Space Institute uncovered chemical enrichment around Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), offering clues to the origins of the material available for the black hole to consume.

For astronomers, “metals” means every element heavier than hydrogen and helium. The category includes carbon and oxygen as well as iron and gold.

Sgr A* is closer to Earth than any other supermassive black hole, making it easier to observe. The team studied its surroundings using data from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), launched five years ago. The telescope measures infrared light across a wide range of wavelengths with unprecedented spectral and spatial resolution. Those capabilities allowed the researchers to distinguish the heat signatures of multiple gas clouds orbiting near the black hole and precisely measure each cloud’s metal composition.

The gas also turned out to have a composition similar to that of many stars orbiting Sgr A*. That resemblance suggests the gas and stars may have formed together. The researchers said the findings could help explain how metals are distributed around supermassive black holes in more distant galaxies, as well as the processes that supplied Earth with many of these elements.

Chemical composition also affects what happens to the gas. Metals influence how quickly it cools, which in turn influences how readily the black hole can draw it in.

“We know there’s a black hole at the center of our galaxy pulling material into itself, but we see that it’s eating a lot less material than other supermassive black holes, and more slowly,” said Nicole Ford, the study’s lead author and a PhD student in Professor Daryl Haggard’s research group in McGill’s Department of Physics. “Part of understanding why this is happening means looking at the properties of the materials available for it to consume, including gas, dust and the stars orbiting around it.”

The findings complement a recent study led by Banting Postdoctoral Fellow Mayura Balakrishnan, which examined whether the surrounding gas retained evidence of earlier bursts of energy from the black hole. That study found that local conditions shape the light emitted by the gas, making the black hole’s influence difficult to isolate. The results do not rule out past outbursts. They show that the surrounding gas cannot provide a reliable history of the black hole’s activity.

Ford said understanding how Sgr A* attracts material will require comparing these observations with simulations of how gas evolves over longer timescales.

References: “Ionization Structure and Metal Enrichment of the Galactic Center Minispiral Observed with JWST” by Nicole M. Ford, Mayura Balakrishnan, Sebastiano D. von Fellenberg, Daryl Haggard, Joseph M. Michail, Yuzhu Cui, Joseph L. Hora, Joey Neilsen, Giacomo Principe, Tamojeet Roychowdhury, Nadeen B. Sabha, Howard A. Smith, Zach Sumners and S. P. Willner, 19 October 2026, The Astronomical Journal. DOI: 10.3847/1538-3881/ae994d

“Isolating Sgr A East: The First Uncontaminated X-Ray Maps of a Galactic Center Supernova Remnant” by Mayura Balakrishnan, Adrien Picquenot, Lia Corrales, Q. Daniel Wang, Fabio Acero and Rodolfo Montez, 20 May 2026, The Astrophysical Journal. DOI: 10.3847/1538-4357/ae5dbe

Both studies were funded by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada, the Canadian Space Agency, the Canada Research Chairs program, Fonds de recherche du Québec – Nature et technologies, Centre de recherche en astrophysique du Québec and the Trottier Space Institute of McGill University, and the International Space Science Institute (ISSI).
